The 0.8× activity comparison is relative to bovine α-carbonic anhydrase under the stated assay, and the 61 °C comparison is against the previously reported thermostable γ-CA referenced by the authors. Industrial relevance is a proposed application, not demonstrated process performance.
evidence.ai_role: The generative model learned protein sequence–function patterns, produced candidate enzyme sequences conditioned in a learned latent space, and guided selection for synthesis. The authors measured enzyme function and stability experimentally; AlphaFold was used only for structure predictions of selected designs.

title: TeleProt-guided engineering yields a nuclease variant with improved neutral-pH biofilm degradation
summary: A machine-learning-guided design and high-throughput screening campaign produced a Bacillus licheniformis NucB variant with 19-fold higher measured specific activity than wild type at pH 7. At 1 μM in a laboratory biofilm assay at neutral pH, the selected variant degraded 71% ± 2% of the biofilm versus 13% ± 3% for wild-type NucB.
ai_technology: TeleProt machine-learning-guided protein-library design framework; best-performing ML3 variant selected by model-based optimization with a deep neural network (MBO-DNN)
organization: X, the Moonshot Factory; Google DeepMind; Triplebar; University of Cambridge

evidence.tested: A machine-learning-guided design and high-throughput screening campaign produced a Bacillus licheniformis NucB variant with 19-fold higher measured specific activity than wild type at pH 7.
evidence.unknown: The evidence is from enzyme and in-vitro B. licheniformis biofilm assays; it does not show wound healing, animal efficacy or clinical benefit. At the 1 μM dose, the paper reports the stated biofilm comparison; conditions and estimates are study-specific. This is engineering of a known nuclease, not discovery of a naturally new enzyme or organismal mechanism.
evidence.ai_role: TeleProt combined sequence-evolutionary information with experimental genotype–phenotype data to propose diverse NucB variants for high-throughput microfluidic activity screening. The selected ML-guided variant was then purified and assessed in a lower-throughput nuclease assay and a neutral-pH biofilm degradation assay.

title: FRASE-bot screening identifies a small-molecule ligand that selectively kills CIB1-dependent cancer cells
summary: FRASE-bot used a neural-network nativeness score to triage protein–ligand fragments, then used the retained structural features to seed virtual screening for Calcium and Integrin Binding Protein 1 (CIB1). Of 56 purchased virtual-screen hits, 29 showed dose-dependent CIB1 displacement; compound UNC10245380 (UNC5380) had a TR-FRET displacement IC50 of 8.0 ± 2.5 μM and selectively killed CIB1-depletion-sensitive triple-negative breast cancer cells in the reported assays, with no detected killing in an insensitive line.
ai_technology: FRASE-bot: fragment-in-structural-environment screening with a neural-network nativeness scoring model
organization: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill; University of Missouri

evidence.tested: Of 56 purchased virtual-screen hits, 29 showed dose-dependent CIB1 displacement; compound UNC10245380 (UNC5380) had a TR-FRET displacement IC50 of 8.0 ± 2.5 μM and selectively killed CIB1-depletion-sensitive triple-negative breast cancer cells in the reported assays, with no detected killing in an insensitive line.
evidence.unknown: The authors describe UNC10245380 as a starting chemical probe/lead, not a drug. Binding was inferred from peptide displacement in TR-FRET and a docking pose; the pose is not a solved small-molecule complex. Selective cell killing was in vitro at 30 μM, with no animal or clinical evidence. The earlier Research Square manuscript is the same underlying paper/result and is not counted separately.
evidence.ai_role: The neural network triaged fragments by predicted native-ligand pose likelihood; selected fragments informed pharmacophore construction and virtual screening. The resulting purchased compounds were then tested in TR-FRET binding-displacement and cell-death assays. The model did not perform the wet-lab validation.

title: Chemical language models produce experimentally confirmed dual ligands for three target pairs
summary: A generative chemical language model was fine-tuned on known ligands for paired targets. Prospective synthesis and in-vitro assays found seven of twelve tested designs modulated both intended targets, with confirmed dual activity across FXR/sEH, FXR/THRβ and PPARδ/sEH. Activities varied substantially and were often unbalanced; the strongest reported sEH inhibitor, compound 7, had IC50 17 nM with micromolar PPARδ agonism.
ai_technology: Target-pair-fine-tuned chemical language model (four-layer LSTM recurrent neural network trained on SMILES, pretrained on 365,000 ChEMBL molecules)
organization: Goethe University Frankfurt; Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München; Fraunhofer Institute for Translational Medicine and Pharmacology

evidence.tested: Prospective synthesis and in-vitro assays found seven of twelve tested designs modulated both intended targets, with confirmed dual activity across FXR/sEH, FXR/THRβ and PPARδ/sEH.
evidence.unknown: This is in-vitro activity of a small set of synthesized molecules, not evidence of therapeutic efficacy or synergistic clinical benefit. Potencies were often unbalanced; several selected candidates were active on only one intended target, and the authors caution the success rate may not generalize beyond target pairs with compatible ligand chemistry. Lead optimization remains necessary.
evidence.ai_role: The pooled fine-tuning strategy combined known ligands of each target pair to bias de-novo SMILES generation toward both ligand classes. Researchers used model sampling frequency, similarity and docking to select molecules for synthesis; assays then tested receptor agonism and soluble epoxide hydrolase inhibition. The model proposed chemical candidates, while biological activity was measured experimentally.

title: Iterative machine learning identifies potent inhibitors of alpha-synuclein secondary nucleation
summary: A structure-based iterative-learning workflow combined prior α-synuclein fibril-binding hits, a junction-tree variational autoencoder, a random-forest regressor and Gaussian-process residual model to rank compounds for repeated testing. Prospective iterations produced multiple molecules inhibiting seeded α-synuclein aggregation in vitro; lead I4.05 had a reported kinetic inhibitory constant (KIC50) of 0.52 μM (95% CI 0.45–0.59 μM), compared with extrapolated values of 18.2 μM for its parent and 36.4 μM for Anle-138b in the authors’ assay. Leads also showed activity in lipid-induced and spontaneous aggregation assays.
ai_technology: Iterative structure-based learning workflow using a junction-tree variational autoencoder, random-forest regressor and Gaussian-process residual model
organization: University of Cambridge; US National Institutes of Health, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases; A*STAR; Indiana University School of Medicine

evidence.tested: A structure-based iterative-learning workflow combined prior α-synuclein fibril-binding hits, a junction-tree variational autoencoder, a random-forest regressor and Gaussian-process residual model to rank compounds for repeated testing.
evidence.unknown: Evidence is biochemical/in-vitro inhibition of α-synuclein aggregation, including seeded, lipid-induced and spontaneous assays. The paper does not establish animal efficacy, neuronal protection or clinical benefit. The KIC50 and comparison values are assay-specific; no random-molecule comparator was tested, and model QSAR R² was described as modest. This is related to, but not the same paper/result as, the earlier docking-screen study that supplied starting compounds.
evidence.ai_role: The machine-learning model ranked a ZINC-derived evaluation set for potency using earlier assay measurements, then researchers tested and fed results from successive rounds back into the model. It proposed compounds for experimental testing; aggregation assays measured outcomes. Initial fibril binders came from an earlier docking-and-screening study, so this paper reports iterative optimization rather than an entirely independent start.

title: ClickGen designs PARP1 inhibitors with measured nanomolar activity
summary: ClickGen combines reaction-based molecular generation, reinforcement learning and inpainting to generate synthesizable candidate structures. In a PARP1 case study, researchers selected and synthesized three generated lead molecules; two showed nanomolar PARP1 inhibition in vitro, with reported IC50 values of 19.24 ± 1.63 nM and 69.73 ± 14.57 nM. The two compounds also showed antiproliferative activity in several tested cancer cell lines and lower toxicity in the reported normal-cell assays than the most toxic lead compounds.
ai_technology: ClickGen deep-learning reaction-based molecular generator with reinforcement learning, Monte Carlo tree search and an inpainting generator
organization: Zhejiang University; Chengde Medical University; Hunan University; Macau University of Science and Technology; CarbonSilicon AI Technology Co., Ltd.; Macau Polytechnic University

evidence.tested: In a PARP1 case study, researchers selected and synthesized three generated lead molecules; two showed nanomolar PARP1 inhibition in vitro, with reported IC50 values of 19.24 ± 1.63 nM and 69.73 ± 14.57 nM.
evidence.unknown: Three selected molecules were synthesized and tested in vitro; the article reports two with nanomolar PARP1 inhibition. Cell-line antiproliferative and toxicity assays do not show tumor efficacy or safety in animals or people. The reported IC50 values are from triplicate measurements in the study. This record captures the PARP1 experimental result, not the paper’s model benchmark comparisons.
evidence.ai_role: The system generated candidate molecules by assembling reaction-compatible synthons and using reinforcement learning/inpainting to guide novelty and binding-oriented generation. Researchers computationally filtered and selected compounds, synthesized three leads and tested them; PARP1 inhibition and cell effects were experimentally measured, not generated by the model.

title: Joint molecular modeling identifies seven low-micromolar kinase hits beyond its training chemistry
summary: A joint molecular model combined bioactivity prediction and molecule reconstruction to estimate how unfamiliar a candidate structure was to its training distribution. In a prospective screen of commercial compounds against PIM1 and CDK1, unfamiliarity-informed selection led to seven compounds with low-micromolar potency and limited similarity to training molecules. The authors also evaluated the metric across 33 experimentally labelled bioactivity datasets.
ai_technology: Joint molecular model (JMM): semi-supervised molecular property-prediction and reconstruction model using a SMILES encoder; reconstruction loss defines the unfamiliarity score
organization: Eindhoven University of Technology; Centre for Living Technologies (TU/e, WUR, UU and UMC Utrecht)

evidence.tested: The authors also evaluated the metric across 33 experimentally labelled bioactivity datasets. The reported wet-lab candidate assays directly test the molecular-model predictions within the study.
evidence.unknown: The kinase finding is a prospective in-vitro hit-identification result, not evidence of therapeutic efficacy. Seven low-micromolar hits were reported across PIM1 and CDK1; CDK1 was described as independent of the study’s earlier dataset analysis. The study screened only a small selected set per target after computational ranking. It does not establish the unfamiliarity measure as universally superior or demonstrate animal or clinical benefit.
evidence.ai_role: The model used reconstruction-based unfamiliarity alongside predicted bioactivity and prediction uncertainty to rank molecules for a prospective virtual screen. Researchers tested selected commercial compounds against PIM1 and CDK1; seven compounds showed low-micromolar potency. AI supported prioritization and selection, while wet-lab assays established activity.

title: ESM-guided metagenome mining identifies seven new Cas12a subtypes with distinct activities
summary: AIL-Scan fine-tuned an evolutionary-scale protein language model (ESM) on Cas proteins to search metagenomic sequences and identify previously undocumented Cas12a lineages. The study classified seven previously unreported Cas12a subtypes with distinct CRISPR-locus organization, then biochemically characterized 16 Cas12a proteins from the candidate clades, documenting different DNA-cleavage and PAM-recognition preferences. The authors also demonstrated a specific assay strategy for distinguishing the KRAS G12C variant using a Cas12a variant with broader PAM recognition.
ai_technology: AIL-Scan, using fine-tuned ESM-2 protein language-model embeddings and a machine-learning classifier to identify Cas proteins and predict Cas12a trans-cleavage activity
organization: Zhejiang Lab; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Nanjing Medical University; Tongji University; National University of Singapore; ShanghaiTech University; Zhejiang University; Chinese Academy of Sciences

evidence.tested: The study classified seven previously unreported Cas12a subtypes with distinct CRISPR-locus organization, then biochemically characterized 16 Cas12a proteins from the candidate clades, documenting different DNA-cleavage and PAM-recognition preferences.
evidence.unknown: The paper reports metagenomic classification and biochemical assays, not a clinical genome-editing or diagnostic application. The PAM/SNP detection demonstration is an experimental proof of concept. The trans-cleavage prediction model was trained on a small labeled set (69 proteins), with two unreported candidates used as an explicit prediction check; CRISPR loci and small-gene annotation in metagenomes remain incomplete. Distinct from other Cas-protein discovery papers by target family, candidate set and measured result.
evidence.ai_role: The fine-tuned ESM model screened metagenomic proteins for Cas identity and generated embeddings; supervised models on small experimental labels predicted trans-cleavage activity to help select uncharacterized candidates. Researchers then manually inspected candidate loci and experimentally measured binding, cleavage and PAM preferences. AI supported sequence-family identification and candidate prioritization; laboratory assays established the reported biochemical properties.

title: Evo genomic language model designs functional toxin-antitoxin and anti-CRISPR systems
summary: Evo used genomic context to generate functional bacterial defence-system components. The paper reports an AI-generated toxin and low-sequence-similarity antitoxins that neutralized it in growth assays, including antitoxins that also acted against multiple natural toxins; it also reports five generated anti-CRISPR proteins that protected bacteria against Cas9 activity in cell and phage assays. Two generated anti-CRISPR proteins lacked significant sequence similarity to known proteins. These experiments demonstrate function-guided genomic design beyond simple copying of natural sequences.
ai_technology: Evo 1.5, a long-context generative genomic language model trained on prokaryotic DNA sequences
organization: Arc Institute; Stanford University

evidence.tested: The paper reports an AI-generated toxin and low-sequence-similarity antitoxins that neutralized it in growth assays, including antitoxins that also acted against multiple natural toxins; it also reports five generated anti-CRISPR proteins that protected bacteria against Cas9 activity in cell and phage assays.
evidence.unknown: This is a set of functional in-vitro bacterial assays, not evidence of therapeutic use, broad host range or ecological performance. One generated toxin had 71% sequence identity to a known RelE toxin; novelty is especially supported by low-similarity antitoxins and anti-CRISPRs, two of which lacked significant sequence identity to known proteins. Earlier Evo phage-genome design and Evo 2 regulatory-sequence work are different papers and different functional results; this row is limited to the toxin-antitoxin/anti-CRISPR findings in the cited Nature article.
evidence.ai_role: Researchers prompted Evo 1.5 with genomic contexts that associate functionally related bacterial genes and used it to generate candidate toxin-antitoxin and anti-CRISPR sequences. Candidates were filtered computationally, synthesized/expressed and tested in bacterial growth, Cas9-protection and phage assays. AI generated candidates; the biological activity was established experimentally.

title: AI-generated virtual spatial proteomics reveals lung-cancer tumor–immune niches associated with immunotherapy response
summary: HEX, a pathology-image AI model, predicts spatial expression of 40 protein biomarkers from routine H&E slides. In retrospective NSCLC cohorts, combining HEX-derived virtual spatial proteomics with histology improved prognosis prediction and, in a separate 148-patient immune-checkpoint-inhibitor cohort, improved response prediction over H&E-only and virtual-proteomics-only models. The authors interpreted virtual maps as showing co-localized T-helper and cytotoxic T-cell niches among responders and immunosuppressive macrophage/neutrophil aggregates among non-responders.
ai_technology: HEX (H&E to protein expression), using a pathology foundation-model backbone; MICA (multimodal integration via co-attention)
organization: Stanford University; and collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: In retrospective NSCLC cohorts, combining HEX-derived virtual spatial proteomics with histology improved prognosis prediction and, in a separate 148-patient immune-checkpoint-inhibitor cohort, improved response prediction over H&E-only and virtual-proteomics-only models.
evidence.unknown: Retrospective observational cohorts; predictive associations do not establish causal mechanisms or improved patient outcomes from model-guided treatment. The 148-patient immunotherapy cohort is separate from the prognosis cohorts. The paper itself says extensive clinical validation remains necessary; do not describe the finding as a clinically validated diagnostic or prospective treatment-selection tool.
evidence.ai_role: HEX predicts expression of 40 proteins and produces spatially resolved virtual proteomics from H&E images; MICA fuses the original image with AI-derived maps for outcome prediction. Researchers used predicted marker distributions to interpret therapy-associated tumor–immune spatial patterns. These are retrospective model analyses with cohort-based clinical associations, not prospective treatment evidence.

title: Contrastive-learning biomarker discovered from phase 2 data retrospectively generalizes to phase 3 immunotherapy outcomes
summary: The Predictive Biomarker Modeling Framework (PBMF), an ensemble neural network trained with a treatment-versus-control contrastive objective, identified a composite clinicogenomic biomarker using phase 2 POPLAR data for atezolizumab versus docetaxel. When applied retrospectively to the phase 3 OAK trial, its biomarker-positive group had a treatment-versus-control overall-survival hazard ratio of 0.59 (95% CI 0.47–0.74); an interpretable distilled decision tree produced HR 0.55 (95% CI 0.43–0.70). The tree used baseline ctDNA maximum allele frequency, lesion diameter, and mutation status in KMT2D, TSC1, ATM, PDGFRA and LRP1B.
ai_technology: Predictive Biomarker Modeling Framework (PBMF), an ensemble of neural networks using a contrastive treatment/control objective; knowledge-distilled decision tree
organization: AstraZeneca; Tempus AI

evidence.tested: The Predictive Biomarker Modeling Framework (PBMF), an ensemble neural network trained with a treatment-versus-control contrastive objective, identified a composite clinicogenomic biomarker using phase 2 POPLAR data for atezolizumab versus docetaxel.
evidence.unknown: Retrospective reanalysis; the biomarker has not prospectively guided patient selection or treatment. The outcome comparisons do not establish benefit from applying PBMF clinically. The authors call for prospective validation and note potential cohort comparability limitations. The identified feature set includes previously studied biomarkers; the paper’s novel result is the composite PBMF-derived predictive subgroup and retrospective generalization, not discovery of each individual feature.
evidence.ai_role: PBMF searched clinicogenomic features for a treatment-specific predictive subgroup, using phase 2 POPLAR training data and contrasting atezolizumab against docetaxel outcomes. Researchers transferred the derived model/biomarker to phase 3 OAK data and distilled it into an interpretable tree. This was a retrospective analysis of trial data, not prospective trial stratification.

title: Deep-learning splice prediction links a PARP2 variant to altered protein isoforms and influenza susceptibility
summary: By combining single-cell splicing-QTL analysis during influenza A infection with SpliceAI/Pangolin annotation and statistical fine-mapping, researchers prioritized causal splice variants. They experimentally characterized rs2297616 in PARP2: its A allele creates an alternative 5′ splice donor, adding 39 nucleotides and producing a protein isoform 13 amino acids longer. CRISPR-edited A549 cells showed the predicted splice and protein changes; the A-allele edited cells also had higher influenza A infection than G-allele cells. The variant was associated with higher viral burden in a panel of 96 lymphoblastoid cell lines.
ai_technology: SpliceAI and Pangolin deep-learning splice-effect predictors, integrated with single-cell scHi-HOST sQTL mapping and SuSiE statistical fine-mapping
organization: Duke University

evidence.tested: They experimentally characterized rs2297616 in PARP2: its A allele creates an alternative 5′ splice donor, adding 39 nucleotides and producing a protein isoform 13 amino acids longer.
evidence.unknown: The 96-donor LCL association is observational and modest (the paper reports p=0.029 for the genotype association). Infection experiments used edited A549 lung epithelial cells, not patients or an in-vivo infection model. The same locus had been linked to alternative splicing previously, but the paper provides new evidence connecting genotype to PARP2 protein isoform expression and to influenza susceptibility. Broader viral-susceptibility implications remain unproven.
evidence.ai_role: Deep-learning splice models prioritized variants predicted to alter donor/acceptor sites; statistical fine-mapping and sQTL association narrowed causal candidates. The AI-supported analysis nominated rs2297616; the authors then tested its splice and protein-isoform effects using reporter assays, CRISPR-edited A549 cells, sequencing and western blotting, and assessed influenza infection in edited cells.

title: AlphaFold2-guided mining identifies context-independent cytidine deaminases for efficient base editing
summary: Researchers used AlphaFold2 to predict structures for 1,483 cytidine deaminases, clustered the predictions and experimentally characterized representatives. The screen identified previously uncharacterized enzymes with high editing efficiency, and CD0208^P52A showed little sequence-context preference across AC/GC/TC/CC motifs, a narrow editing window and relatively low off-target activity. In mammalian cells, its base editor introduced stop codons in single- and multicopy genes without DNA double-strand breaks.
ai_technology: AlphaFold2 protein-structure prediction, followed by structural clustering of candidate cytidine deaminases
organization: Agricultural Genomics Institute at Shenzhen, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences

evidence.tested: Researchers used AlphaFold2 to predict structures for 1,483 cytidine deaminases, clustered the predictions and experimentally characterized representatives.
evidence.unknown: The base-editing experiments were preclinical cell experiments, not animal or clinical efficacy tests. AlphaFold2 supplied predicted rather than experimentally solved structures. The paper reports multiple promising deaminases; CD0208^P52A is the specific context-independent editor highlighted here. No therapeutic safety or in-vivo delivery claim is implied.
evidence.ai_role: AlphaFold2-predicted structures at scale were used to mine and cluster 1,483 putative deaminases; representatives were then selected for experimental characterization in cytosine base editors. The model enabled structure-guided candidate selection; editing outcomes were measured experimentally in mammalian cells.

title: GPT-3.5 reasoning helps connect MRE11 to social-context sleep regulation in Drosophila
summary: A study combined GPT-3.5-generated gene-function context with a genome-wide Drosophila RNAi behavioral screen. It identified MRE11 knockdown as reducing sleep in group-housed flies, a result the authors report as previously unrecognized in this social context. GPT-3.5 reasoning proposed a link from MRE11 to Dop1R1/dopaminergic signaling; treatment with a Dop1R1 antagonist partially rescued sleep, locomotor and social-activity phenotypes in MRE11-RNAi flies.
ai_technology: GPT-3.5, prompted for genome-wide Drosophila gene-function interpretation and chain-of-thought relationship hypotheses
organization: Huazhong University of Science and Technology; and collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: It identified MRE11 knockdown as reducing sleep in group-housed flies, a result the authors report as previously unrecognized in this social context.
evidence.unknown: The experiments are in Drosophila and concern sleep in the presence of conspecifics. Dop1R1 antagonist treatment only partially rescued phenotypes; this does not establish direct MRE11 regulation of the receptor or dopamine pathway. GPT-3.5 had high false-negative rates in the authors’ known-gene evaluation and contributed knowledge summarization/hypothesis generation, while the broad RNAi screen itself was experimental. No mammalian or human result is implied.
evidence.ai_role: GPT-3.5 was queried about fly gene functions and used to construct hypothesized relationships among behavioral-screen candidates; it proposed a MRE11–Dop1R1 link that researchers tested pharmacologically. The RNAi screen and behavioral measurements were experimental, while direct molecular regulation was not demonstrated.

title: GET and interaction assays link a leukemia-risk PAX5 variant to stronger NR2C2 binding
summary: The General Expression Transformer (GET) model inferred cell-type-specific transcription-factor motif interactions from regulatory data and nominated a lymphocyte-specific interaction between PAX5 and nuclear-receptor-family factors. AlphaFold multimer modeling and PAX5 proximity-labeling in a B-ALL cell line supported interaction with NR2C2; the leukemia-associated PAX5 G183S variant showed increased PAX5–NR2C2 proximity signal. The variant-specific expression profile was enriched for predicted NR/3 and shared PAX5/NR/3 target genes, suggesting a possible regulatory mechanism for the germline risk variant.
ai_technology: GET (General Expression Transformer) foundation model for cell-type-specific regulatory grammar; AlphaFold2/AlphaFold Multimer for structural hypothesis assessment
organization: Columbia University; Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence; collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: The General Expression Transformer (GET) model inferred cell-type-specific transcription-factor motif interactions from regulatory data and nominated a lymphocyte-specific interaction between PAX5 and nuclear-receptor-family factors.
evidence.unknown: This is a cell-line interaction and expression analysis, not proof that the variant causes leukemia or directly alters disease risk through NR2C2. PAX5–NR2C2 interaction itself was consistent with prior evidence for the paralogue PAX2 and mouse pre-B cells; the specific reported distinction is increased interaction signal with PAX5 G183S and associated transcriptional enrichment. The authors call the disease-driving mechanism possible and identify limitations in cell-state and variant resolution.
evidence.ai_role: GET learned regulatory syntax across 213 cell types and used motif co-regulation to predict TF–TF interactions, which nominated PAX5/nuclear receptor family interactions in B cells. Structural modeling prioritized candidate binding interfaces. Researchers then used proximity labeling and mass spectrometry in a B-ALL cell line to compare wild-type PAX5 with the G183S leukemia-risk variant.

title: Paper2Agent integrates perturbation datasets to prioritize GPR137 at a psoriasis risk locus
summary: Paper2Agent-generated agents used AlphaGenome to prioritize GPR137 as the top predicted gene affected by psoriasis-associated variant rs887314 in CD4+ T cells, then integrated that prediction with existing MPRA-coupled scCRISPRi and CD4+ T-cell Perturb-seq data. A cross-screen correlation of gene-expression signatures supported GPR137 as the probable causal gene under stimulated conditions (Spearman rho 0.613 at 8 h and 0.630 at 48 h; FDR < 0.05), but not at rest. The paper presents this as activation-dependent computational evidence.
ai_technology: Paper2Agent-generated AlphaGenome, MPRA-coupled scCRISPRi and CD4+ T-cell Perturb-seq agents, coordinated through an AI co-scientist
organization: Stanford University; collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: Paper2Agent-generated agents used AlphaGenome to prioritize GPR137 as the top predicted gene affected by psoriasis-associated variant rs887314 in CD4+ T cells, then integrated that prediction with existing MPRA-coupled scCRISPRi and CD4+ T-cell Perturb-seq data.
evidence.unknown: The analysis reuses existing published datasets and does not report new wet-lab experiments for this psoriasis case. AlphaGenome supplied a model prediction; cross-dataset signature correlation supports, but does not establish, causal biology. The GPR137 concordance was significant only after stimulation, and the authors describe it as probable/activation-dependent. A human researcher selected which AI-proposed strategy to run. Primary paper source checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: The AlphaGenome paper agent scored and ranked candidate genes at rs887314. Under human-in-the-loop supervision, the AI co-scientist inspected two other paper agents' datasets, proposed ten validation strategies, and the researcher selected signature-correlation analysis. The resulting cross-screen, cross-modality analysis found significant concordance for GPR137 only under stimulated conditions.

title: Machine learning links mycobacterial protein disorder to targeted degradation potential
summary: Researchers combined a genetic chemical-proximity platform and experimental screening of 72 Mycobacterium smegmatis protein candidates with machine learning. A Lasso model trained on measured degradation data identified N-terminal disorder propensity as associated with degradation potential and predicted candidate targets among 348 essential proteins conserved between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis. Experimentally induced degradation of selected essential M. smegmatis proteins inhibited bacterial growth and, for some targets, potentiated antimicrobial compounds.
ai_technology: Lasso regression model trained on sequence and structural protein descriptors, including AlphaFold2 confidence and predicted disorder propensity
organization: Harvard Medical School; Massachusetts Institute of Technology; collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: Researchers combined a genetic chemical-proximity platform and experimental screening of 72 Mycobacterium smegmatis protein candidates with machine learning.
evidence.unknown: Most mechanistic and growth evidence was generated in M. smegmatis, a non-pathogenic model, not in clinical treatment or an animal efficacy study. The machine-learning target predictions for the larger set of 348 essential proteins require orthogonal experimental validation. The study reports that targeted degradation of some proteins inhibits growth and potentiates antimicrobials; this does not establish a deployable drug or clinical benefit. Primary paper source checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: Machine learning connected measured degradation constants from experimentally screened protein substrates to protein sequence/structure features, identifying N-terminal disorder propensity as a predictor of degradation potential; the trained model then ranked candidate targets among essential proteins conserved between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis. Experiments—not the model alone—showed degradation and antibacterial phenotypes for selected targets.

title: Machine-learning-guided closed-loop synthesis experimentally realizes unreported dye molecules
summary: A closed-loop molecular discovery platform combined machine-learning property prediction, automated synthesis and characterization, and iterative model updates to explore dye-like molecules. In the published Science abstract, the team reports experimentally realizing 294 previously unreported molecules across three design–make–test–analyze cycles on four rarely reported scaffolds, while also identifying six top-performing molecules in a second case study using pre-existing chemical-space examples.
ai_technology: Autonomous molecular-discovery platform integrating generative and property-prediction machine-learning models, Bayesian optimization, and synthesis-planning software with automated chemical synthesis and characterization
organization: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: In the published Science abstract, the team reports experimentally realizing 294 previously unreported molecules across three design–make–test–analyze cycles on four rarely reported scaffolds, while also identifying six top-performing molecules in a second case study using pre-existing chemical-space examples.
evidence.unknown: This is molecular discovery in dye-like chemical systems, not a validated drug or biological effect. The 294 number is from the published Science abstract; an earlier ChemRxiv preprint describes 312 unreported molecules, so version-specific counts differ and the published figure is used here. The measurements addressed absorption wavelength, lipophilicity and photo-oxidative stability; no environmental, toxicological or commercial benefit is claimed. Primary-source abstract and author-lab description checked; independent replication not assessed.
evidence.ai_role: Generative ML proposed candidate dye-like structures; property-prediction models ranked molecules against absorption, lipophilicity, and photo-oxidative-stability targets; automated multi-step synthesis and measurements generated training data for model retraining and the next cycles. The closed-loop process converted model-guided suggestions into synthesized and characterized compounds.

title: Sequential model-based optimization discovers two previously unreported chemical reactions
summary: A programmable robotic synthesis platform used inline HPLC, Raman or NMR feedback and closed-loop optimization to explore selected reaction spaces. In a tosMIC campaign, sequential model-based optimization with a Gaussian-process surrogate identified a reaction between toluenesulphonylmethyl isocyanide and benzylidenemalononitrile; subsequent optimization increased yield from the 27% initial condition to 49% (22 percentage points) over 50 reactions. The article also reports a second previously unreported reaction and an exploratory trifluoromethylation campaign that discovered new molecules.
ai_technology: ChemputationOptimizer, a sensor-integrated reaction engine with sequential model-based optimization (Gaussian-process surrogate); the platform also exposes random search, design-of-experiments, Bayesian-optimization and genetic-algorithm routines
organization: University of Glasgow

evidence.tested: The article also reports a second previously unreported reaction and an exploratory trifluoromethylation campaign that discovered new molecules.
evidence.unknown: The platform's reported yield gains are specific to these selected reaction spaces and objectives, not general chemistry performance. The tosMIC and phloroglucinol campaigns are reported as previously unreported reactions; product characterization and complete procedure details are in the article/supplement. The system includes several optimization algorithms and the authors note random search can be a strong baseline; the reported tosMIC optimization used SMBO with a Gaussian-process surrogate. No claim is made that the reactions are industrially useful or broadly generalizable. Primary source checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: For the tosMIC and phloroglucinol explorations, machine-guided combinatorial search proposed reaction parameters and inline spectroscopic feedback supplied product-yield measurements; a Gaussian-process sequential-model-based optimizer guided the reaction-space exploration and follow-up optimization. Human chemists defined reaction space and experimental constraints, and performed/characterized the experiments.

title: CHAI image-only histology biomarker stratifies metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer outcomes in independent trial data
summary: A computational histology AI platform built a prognostic signature from diagnostic whole-slide images in 507 CHAARTED participants and evaluated the locked signature in 684 ENZAMET participants. In the independent ENZAMET cohort, the unfavorable-risk group had worse overall survival (HR 2.6, 95% CI 2.0–3.4) and progression-free survival (HR 2.2, 95% CI 1.7–2.7); associations remained after adjustment for clinical variables. The article also reports treatment-interaction analyses, but this retrospective secondary analysis does not establish prospective treatment-selection benefit.
ai_technology: Computational Histology Artificial Intelligence (CHAI) platform
organization: Valar Labs; and the CHAARTED/ENZAMET trial collaborators

evidence.tested: In the independent ENZAMET cohort, the unfavorable-risk group had worse overall survival (HR 2.6, 95% CI 2.0–3.4) and progression-free survival (HR 2.2, 95% CI 1.7–2.7); associations remained after adjustment for clinical variables.
evidence.unknown: The locked image-only biomarker was independently evaluated across two prospective randomized-trial datasets, but this article is a post hoc secondary analysis, not a prospective biomarker-directed treatment trial. The treatment-interaction result is suggestive and does not prove that choosing triplet therapy by this score improves outcomes. No clinical deployment or benefit claim is made. Primary journal abstract checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: CHAI extracted quantitative histomorphologic features from H&E diagnostic whole-slide images and learned an image-only risk signature on CHAARTED data; the locked signature was tested in ENZAMET. Humans specified cohorts/endpoints and analyzed the trial outcomes.

title: Prospective multicentre study combines EV protein biomarkers and machine learning for preclinical oesophageal cancer detection
summary: The BarFlare assay and an interpretable multi-criteria decision-making classification-fusion machine-learning framework combined extracellular-vesicle SCC and MMP13 biomarkers with clinical factors. The model was evaluated in prospective multicentre diagnostic cohorts and two population cohorts; the longitudinal cohort contained baseline samples from 30 people who later developed oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, with a reported median lead time of 34.9 months and AUC 0.864. The paper also reports external diagnostic validation in two cohorts.
ai_technology: Multi-criteria decision-making Classification Fusion (MCF) machine-learning framework; 289 candidate feature-selector/classifier pairs were compared and three base models fused
organization: Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center; and collaborating hospitals/cohorts

evidence.tested: The BarFlare assay and an interpretable multi-criteria decision-making classification-fusion machine-learning framework combined extracellular-vesicle SCC and MMP13 biomarkers with clinical factors.
evidence.unknown: This is a prospective observational diagnostic study, not an intervention trial or proof that screening improves outcomes. The longitudinal preclinical cohort had 30 incident cases and matched controls; performance estimates require external replication in larger populations. The source reports an association and lead time, not guaranteed individual prediction. Primary publisher full text and abstract checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: The MCF framework integrated newly identified EV biomarkers with clinical variables, selected and fused machine-learning classifiers, and produced the risk score evaluated in diagnostic and prospective population cohorts. BarFlare is the high-sensitivity EV assay platform, not the AI model.

title: Machine-learning selection of a six-protein panel for atherosclerosis severity and patient stratification
summary: Five machine-learning classifiers integrated clinical and serum-proteomic data from carotid atherosclerotic stenosis (60 participants), dyslipidemia (55) and healthy controls (66). A consensus approach identified a six-protein panel (B2M, GPV, MMP9, PLF4, TSP1 and fibrinogen/FB isoforms) that distinguished the atherosclerosis group from the comparison groups, with reported ROC-AUC above 0.9 across the tested classifiers. Protein levels were evaluated by flow cytometry and ELISA in an independent external cohort that included patients with acute atherothrombotic stroke.
ai_technology: Five machine-learning classifiers: Naive Bayes, linear SVM, random forest, Extra Trees and AdaBoost
organization: Biomedical Research and Innovation Institute of Cadiz, University of Cadiz and collaborating clinical institutions

evidence.tested: A consensus approach identified a six-protein panel (B2M, GPV, MMP9, PLF4, TSP1 and fibrinogen/FB isoforms) that distinguished the atherosclerosis group from the comparison groups, with reported ROC-AUC above 0.9 across the tested classifiers.
evidence.unknown: The discovery cohorts were small (60 atherosclerosis, 55 dyslipidemia and 66 healthy controls); external validation supports the measured panel but does not establish population-wide performance, prospective clinical utility, or improved patient outcomes. The proteins have prior biological associations, so the finding is the specific integrated panel and cohort discrimination rather than discovery of six new proteins or a new mechanism.
evidence.ai_role: Five classifiers integrated clinical and serum-proteomic features and selected a consensus six-protein panel for patient-group discrimination. The authors then evaluated the selected proteins in an independent clinical cohort using flow cytometry and ELISA.

title: ESM-FEP combines protein-language-model fitness screening and free-energy calculations to engineer herbicide-detoxifying maize dioxygenase
summary: ESM-FEP was applied to Zea mays dioxygenase ZmHSL1B and nominated a quadruple mutant (Q140H/Y205F/L332R/K336F) with approximately sevenfold higher catalytic efficiency for mesotrione detoxification than wild type, measured by in-vitro assays and kinetic analysis. Arabidopsis thaliana expressing the engineered variant showed enhanced herbicide tolerance in the reported transgenic tests.
ai_technology: ESM-FEP (fine-tuned ESM-2 protein language model plus alchemical free-energy perturbation)
organization: Central China Normal University, State Key Laboratory of Green Pesticide

evidence.tested: ESM-FEP was applied to Zea mays dioxygenase ZmHSL1B and nominated a quadruple mutant (Q140H/Y205F/L332R/K336F) with approximately sevenfold higher catalytic efficiency for mesotrione detoxification than wild type, measured by in-vitro assays and kinetic analysis.
evidence.unknown: Reported results concern one maize dioxygenase and mesotrione in specified in-vitro and Arabidopsis tests. They do not establish crop-field performance, commercial efficacy, or generality across herbicides/enzymes. Primary PubMed abstract and publisher citation metadata checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: Fine-tuned ESM-2 screened saturation-mutagenesis variants for retained global protein fitness; free-energy perturbation then estimated substrate-binding effects and prioritized mutants. The selected M5 mutant was assayed in vitro and in transgenic Arabidopsis by the researchers.

title: ESM-Ezy mining identifies multicopper oxidases and asparaginases with experimentally improved catalytic properties
summary: The ESM-1b semantic-embedding mining strategy nominated low-sequence-similarity enzyme candidates. In the reported experimental assessment, 44% of tested multicopper oxidases outperformed their query enzymes in at least one measured property (including catalytic efficiency, heat/solvent tolerance or pH stability); 51% were reported to excel in environmental-remediation applications. Among mined L-asparaginases, 40% had higher specific activity and catalytic efficiency than query enzymes.
ai_technology: ESM-Ezy, using ESM-1b protein-language-model embeddings and semantic-space similarity
organization: Westlake University; and collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: In the reported experimental assessment, 44% of tested multicopper oxidases outperformed their query enzymes in at least one measured property (including catalytic efficiency, heat/solvent tolerance or pH stability); 51% were reported to excel in environmental-remediation applications.
evidence.unknown: Percentages describe the selected candidates and tested property comparisons in this study, not the fraction of all database enzymes that will be superior. The reported remediation suitability is assay-specific; environmental or industrial deployment is not established. Primary abstract/full-text search result checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: ESM-1b sequence embeddings and semantic-space similarity ranked low-similarity candidate enzymes from sequence databases for experimental follow-up; assays assessed catalytic properties of selected multicopper oxidases and L-asparaginases.

title: PepMLM designs experimentally binding target-conditioned peptide ligands, including peptides used for targeted protein degradation
summary: PepMLM fine-tunes ESM-2 using masked-language modeling conditioned on a target protein sequence to generate de novo linear peptide binders without structural input. In the reported experiments, selected peptides showed sequence-specific binding to targets including NCAM1 and AMHR2; incorporation into ubiquitin-based antibody constructs enabled targeted degradation of disease-relevant proteins, including Huntington’s disease drivers and viral phosphoproteins.
ai_technology: PepMLM, ESM-2 fine-tuned with target-sequence-conditioned masked language modeling
organization: Cornell University; and collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: In the reported experiments, selected peptides showed sequence-specific binding to targets including NCAM1 and AMHR2; incorporation into ubiquitin-based antibody constructs enabled targeted degradation of disease-relevant proteins, including Huntington’s disease drivers and viral phosphoproteins.
evidence.unknown: The reported evidence is preclinical binding/degradation assays, not therapeutic efficacy, pharmacokinetics or safety. The article notes that experimental optimization/stabilization of its selected peptides was not performed and further validation is needed for viral-target applications. Primary publisher full text/abstract checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: Given a target protein sequence, PepMLM generates candidate linear binder peptide sequences by reconstructing masked peptide regions. The authors tested selected designs in binding and degradation assays and reported target-specific activity in the stated systems.

title: Machine-learning analysis of plasma metabolomic fingerprints yields a 21-metabolite gastric-cancer panel validated across multicentre cohorts
summary: In a multicentre study, machine-learning analysis of plasma metabolic fingerprints from 1,944 retrospective participants selected a 21-metabolite panel that differentiated gastric-cancer from non-cancer cohorts; five model types achieved AUCs of 0.921–0.971 in discovery and 0.907–0.940 in external verification. Prospective testing in 264 participants using both NPELDI-MS and UPLC-MS reported diagnostic AUCs of 0.855–0.918 and 0.856–0.916, respectively. The paper also reports a four-metabolite prognostic score based on retrospective survival data.
ai_technology: Neural network, lasso regression, ridge regression, support-vector machine and random-forest models applied to plasma metabolic fingerprints
organization: Zhejiang Cancer Hospital; Shanghai Jiao Tong University and six collaborating clinical centers

evidence.tested: In a multicentre study, machine-learning analysis of plasma metabolic fingerprints from 1,944 retrospective participants selected a 21-metabolite panel that differentiated gastric-cancer from non-cancer cohorts; five model types achieved AUCs of 0.921–0.971 in discovery and 0.907–0.940 in external verification.
evidence.unknown: The panel was evaluated in selected clinical cohorts and is not established for routine screening or clinical use. Prospective validation was at one lead center, and only six panel metabolites were robustly detected by confirmatory UPLC-MS under the reported testing. Model performance does not show that the panel is causal or improves outcomes. Primary full text/abstract checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: The study used machine-learning feature selection/modeling (including logistic-regression coefficient filtering) to identify and evaluate a 21-metabolite diagnostic panel from high-throughput mass-spectrometry fingerprints; classifiers were then validated on independent retrospective and prospective cohorts.

title: Machine-learning-guided CsrA homolog screens reveal divergent bacterial regulatory activities
summary: A Swarm-seq assay tested more than 500 bacterial CsrA homologs for regulation of Bacillus subtilis swarming and found two functional classes: several homologs strongly inhibited swarming while others failed despite conserved sequence and canonical GGA motifs in the hag transcript. A random-forest model trained on these assays predicted homolog activity across thousands of sequences; experimental testing supported predicted Class I regulatory activity for Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus CsrA and Pseudomonas putida RsmA. The findings indicate sequence conservation and the canonical RNA motif do not alone determine these tested regulatory effects.
ai_technology: Random-forest machine-learning classifier trained on Swarm-seq functional assay data
organization: University of Chicago

evidence.tested: A Swarm-seq assay tested more than 500 bacterial CsrA homologs for regulation of Bacillus subtilis swarming and found two functional classes: several homologs strongly inhibited swarming while others failed despite conserved sequence and canonical GGA motifs in the hag transcript.
evidence.unknown: Activity classifications are based on the reported B. subtilis swarming assay and tested proteins; they do not establish all native targets or regulatory functions in each source organism. The predicted function landscape across thousands of homologs is not experimentally validated wholesale. Primary publisher abstract checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: High-throughput swarming assays generated a functional dataset; machine learning was then trained to classify homolog functional activity across the bacterial domain and nominate homologs for validation. Selected CsrABb and RsmAPp predictions were experimentally validated.

title: GRACE designs two carbonic-anhydrase-like enzymes with measured catalytic activity
summary: The GRACE workflow combined RFdiffusion structure generation, ProteinMPNN sequence design, CLEAN enzyme classification and solubility/structure filtering to select two carbonic-anhydrase-like sequences from 10,000 candidates. The authors report experimental expression and carbonic anhydrase activity: dCA12_2 at 400 WAU/mL and dCA23_1 at 260 WAU/mL in the reported assay.
ai_technology: GRACE (RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN and CLEAN, with computational solubility/structural filters)
organization: National Cheng Kung University; and collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: The authors report experimental expression and carbonic anhydrase activity: dCA12_2 at 400 WAU/mL and dCA23_1 at 260 WAU/mL in the reported assay.
evidence.unknown: The reported activity values are from the study's carbonic-anhydrase assay and do not establish purified-enzyme kinetics, physiological CO2-fixation performance, or industrial utility. The designs and validation are a two-protein proof of concept; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: The generative-design workflow produced structures/sequences and machine-learning function classification prioritized two candidates from a 10,000-sequence pool; researchers expressed both and measured carbonic-anhydrase activity.

title: Self-iterative learning finds RNA-targeting prokaryotic Argonautes and an RNA-modification-sensing activity
summary: The self-iterative hierarchical ensemble model (SIM) nominated six high-confidence prokaryotic Argonaute candidates; five were experimentally validated as RNA-targeting proteins. The study identified three uncharacterized Agos with a novel N-terminal domain, defining a previously unrecognized subclass. Biochemical and in-vivo experiments on Haloferax profundi Ago (HpAgo) established RNA cleavage and a distinctive RNA-modification-sensing capability, which the authors used to build a method for quantifying modified RNA.
ai_technology: Self-Iterative hierarchical ensemble Model (SIM), an ensemble-learning and self-training pipeline
organization: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; ShanghaiTech University and collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: The self-iterative hierarchical ensemble model (SIM) nominated six high-confidence prokaryotic Argonaute candidates; five were experimentally validated as RNA-targeting proteins.
evidence.unknown: Five of six selected candidates were validated; the broader predicted sequence space was not experimentally tested. The specific RNA modification-sensing mechanism and assay performance are supported for HpAgo and tested conditions, not all Argonautes. No therapeutic or universal detection claim is made. Primary abstract/citation record checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: SIM iteratively expanded its training labels to rank prokaryotic Argonautes for RNA targeting from sparse initial data; it prioritized candidates and identified a previously unrecognized domain-containing subclass. The researchers validated RNA cleavage and RNA-modification sensing biochemically and in vivo.

title: Machine-learning models identify carbon-source-dependent metabolic reactions that control Escherichia coli growth
summary: Elastic-net and multilayer-perceptron models integrated genome-wide gene-deletion data and simulated fluxes to predict beneficial and detrimental reactions for E. coli growth on 30 carbon sources. Beyond training-set examples, the authors experimentally validated model predictions about the glyoxylate shunt, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and redundant purine-biosynthesis reactions. The findings showed that effects of energy-generating pathways depend on carbon source, while biosynthetic pathways were more generally growth-promoting across the tested conditions.
ai_technology: Elastic-net regression and multilayer-perceptron models
organization: Konkuk University

evidence.tested: Beyond training-set examples, the authors experimentally validated model predictions about the glyoxylate shunt, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and redundant purine-biosynthesis reactions.
evidence.unknown: Reported reaction effects are for E. coli under the tested carbon-source and genetic-perturbation conditions; they do not establish universal metabolic-control rules. The results should not be interpreted as direct clinical or industrial outcomes. Primary PubMed abstract and PMC article record checked; no independent replication assessed.
evidence.ai_role: The models combined gene-deletion phenotypes with simulated metabolic fluxes to prioritize reactions whose perturbation would benefit or harm growth across carbon conditions; selected out-of-training-set predictions were experimentally tested.

title: Deep-learning-guided mining of NRPS scaffolds yields active naturally inspired antimicrobial peptides
summary: The team mined 216,408 bacterial genomes, identifying 335,024 NRPS clusters and 328 dereplicated peptide scaffolds. Deep-learning scoring selected five synthesized peptides; P2 showed MIC50 values of 1–2 μM against Vibrio parahaemolyticus and V. alginolyticus. Deep-learning-guided sequence optimization produced P2.2, which showed increased antibacterial activity, membrane effects and reduced hemolysis in assays.
ai_technology: Deep-learning peptide activity scoring and sequence-optimization algorithms
organization: Zhejiang University of Technology; and collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: Deep-learning-guided sequence optimization produced P2.2, which showed increased antibacterial activity, membrane effects and reduced hemolysis in assays.
evidence.unknown: The study calls the peptides naturally inspired; it did not establish that the synthesized sequences are the native products of the mined clusters. P2's MIC50 of 1–2 μM did not mean 80% inhibition: its MIC80 exceeded 128 μM under the reported 24-hour conditions. P2.2's measured MIC80 values were 32 μM for V. parahaemolyticus and 64 μM for V. alginolyticus. These are in-vitro findings, not clinical efficacy.
evidence.ai_role: AI-ranked peptide candidates inspired by nonribosomal peptide synthetase cluster scaffolds from bacterial genomes and guided amino-acid optimization of P2 into P2.2; the selected sequences were synthesized and tested in vitro.

title: KPPepGen generates experimentally active pathogen-specific antimicrobial peptides
summary: KPPepGen combines Gene Ontology and pathogen-knowledge-graph prompts with a diffusion model to generate pathogen-conditioned peptide sequences. The paper reports valid peptide generation for 56 pathogens and wet-lab evaluation of nine novel peptides for Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, reporting antimicrobial activity and low cytotoxicity. Its Magainin 2 optimization result is a separate model-comparison metric, not a clinical outcome.
ai_technology: KPPepGen knowledge-aware prompt diffusion model
organization: Huazhong Agricultural University

evidence.tested: The paper reports valid peptide generation for 56 pathogens and wet-lab evaluation of nine novel peptides for Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, reporting antimicrobial activity and low cytotoxicity.
evidence.unknown: The source reports nine experimentally evaluated peptides for E. coli and S. aureus, not experimental validation for all 56 pathogens. Antimicrobial activity and cytotoxicity are in-vitro outcomes; therapeutic efficacy, safety in animals or people, and resistance outcomes are not established by this report.
evidence.ai_role: The model used pathogen-specific knowledge prompts to generate and optimize antimicrobial peptide sequences; researchers synthesized candidates and evaluated the nine reported novel peptides in wet-lab antimicrobial and cytotoxicity assays.

title: Latent diffusion designs antimicrobial peptides active against fungi and drug-resistant bacteria
summary: A latent-diffusion and molecular-dynamics pipeline generated and filtered peptide sequences; 40 synthesized candidates were tested, and 25 met the study's MIC threshold for antibacterial or antifungal activity. AMP-29 showed activity against Candida glabrata and efficacy in a murine skin-infection model, while AMP-24 showed in-vitro Gram-negative activity and efficacy in murine Acinetobacter baumannii skin and lung infection models.
ai_technology: Latent diffusion model coupled to molecular dynamics and peptide filtering/ranking
organization: Shandong University; and collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: A latent-diffusion and molecular-dynamics pipeline generated and filtered peptide sequences; 40 synthesized candidates were tested, and 25 met the study's MIC threshold for antibacterial or antifungal activity.
evidence.unknown: Twenty-five of 40 tested peptides met the authors' stated MIC ≤200 μM activity threshold, which includes a broad range of potency. The murine efficacy reports concern selected peptides and infection models, not human treatment. Some fungal peptides showed hemolysis; favorable safety cannot be generalized to the whole set.
evidence.ai_role: The diffusion model generated a diverse peptide sequence set, and computational filtering selected 40 candidates for chemical synthesis and experimental antimicrobial testing; the selected peptides included leads taken into mouse infection models.

title: CAIMAN validates AI prescreening of typical and atypical large-bowel biopsies across UK and Portuguese cohorts
summary: CAIMAN is a weakly supervised deep-learning model trained on pathologist-labeled whole-slide images to classify typical, atypical non-neoplastic and atypical neoplastic bowel biopsies. In three external cohorts comprising 1,536 slides from the UK and Portugal, it detected atypical biopsies with AUROC values of 0.9431, 0.9576 and 0.9636. At 99% sensitivity, it outperformed the prior IDaRS pipeline on two external cohorts, but not the third.
ai_technology: CAIMAN (Colorectal AI Model for Abnormality Detection), a weakly supervised deep-learning whole-slide image classifier
organization: University of Warwick; University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Foundation Trust, collaborating UK hospitals and IMP Diagnostics (Portugal)

evidence.tested: In three external cohorts comprising 1,536 slides from the UK and Portugal, it detected atypical biopsies with AUROC values of 0.9431, 0.9576 and 0.9636.
evidence.unknown: Retrospective validation on archived biopsies does not establish clinical deployment or improved patient outcomes. CAIMAN did not outperform IDaRS at 99% sensitivity in one of the three external validation cohorts; the authors call for larger multicentre validation and a clinical trial. The reported 99% sensitivity is paired with cohort-specific specificity, not a universal performance guarantee.
evidence.ai_role: AI learned biopsy-level histological patterns from slide-level diagnostic labels, then classified whole-slide images into typical, atypical non-neoplastic or atypical neoplastic classes. The trained frozen model was evaluated on three external cohorts; the reported finding is a specific retrospective clinical diagnostic-validation result.

title: Multi-centre validation tests AI-empowered OncoSeek across 15,122 participants and four assay platforms
summary: A 2025 study added four cohorts to evaluate the seven-protein-marker OncoSeek test, which combines blood protein tumor markers and clinical variables with AI. Across seven cohorts from seven centres in China, Brazil and the United States, totaling 15,122 participants, the reported overall sensitivity was 58.4% at 92.0% specificity; the symptomatic cohort had 73.1% sensitivity at 90.6% specificity. The study also tested performance across four platforms and two sample types.
ai_technology: OncoSeek AI-empowered blood test combining seven protein tumor markers with individual clinical data
organization: SeekIn; Henan Cancer Hospital, Peking University Shenzhen Hospital, First Saúde, Yonsei University and collaborating clinical centres

evidence.tested: A 2025 study added four cohorts to evaluate the seven-protein-marker OncoSeek test, which combines blood protein tumor markers and clinical variables with AI.
evidence.unknown: This is a retrospective/observational cohort validation of a blood test, not evidence that screening improves outcomes or reduces mortality. Aggregate sensitivity was 58.4% and performance varied by cancer type; several cancer-specific groups were small. The article adds validation to a previously published OncoSeek test, so this record is limited to the new expanded-cohort/platform result, not a claim of first test discovery.
evidence.ai_role: The AI-assisted test integrated measured protein-marker values and clinical variables for multicancer classification. This paper evaluated its performance in four additional validation cohorts, including a prospective blinded study and symptomatic case-control cohort, and aggregated results across seven cohorts.

title: HiDDEN finds malignant-like cell signals in early multiple-myeloma precursor samples
summary: HiDDEN refines sample-level case labels at single-cell resolution. In human bone-marrow single-cell RNA-seq data, its labels tracked manual neoplastic-cell annotations in mixed precursor samples and inferred malignant-like cells in three low-purity MGUS samples that the original manual analysis had labeled as containing only healthy cells. The inferred cells were enriched for previously described malignancy-associated gene signatures. In a separate mouse demyelination dataset, HiDDEN identified an early endothelial subpopulation with expression changes associated with angiogenesis, blood–brain-barrier breakdown and extracellular-matrix responses.
ai_technology: HiDDEN, a machine-learning framework for refining disease/condition labels at single-cell resolution
organization: Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: HiDDEN refines sample-level case labels at single-cell resolution.
evidence.unknown: The MGUS finding is a transcriptomic inference in previously collected samples, computationally supported by known gene signatures and sample-purity estimates; the paper does not report independent pathology confirmation, clinical follow-up, or validation as a diagnostic test. The endothelial subpopulation was found in a mouse lesion model; its association with blood–brain-barrier dysfunction does not establish causality.
evidence.ai_role: The model inferred which individual cells in case samples were affected rather than assigning the sample-level case label to all cells. This enabled the paper’s reanalysis of human myeloma precursor single-cell data and mouse demyelination single-nucleus data, yielding the specified malignancy and endothelial-population findings.

title: MILTON-augmented disease cohorts surface putative new gene–disease associations in UK Biobank data
summary: MILTON uses machine learning on routine clinical biomarkers, quantitative traits and plasma proteomics to predict disease phenotypes and augment case labels in UK Biobank. In a phenome-wide analysis of 484,230 genome-sequenced participants, the authors report 182 putative novel gene–disease associations that were not genome-wide significant in baseline cohorts or explained by biomarker associations; 38.9% of the 167 mappable signals were nominally supported with the same direction in FinnGen.
ai_technology: MILTON (Machine Learning with Phenotype Associations), an ensemble machine-learning framework for disease prediction from clinical and molecular biomarkers
organization: AstraZeneca Centre for Genomics Research; and collaborating UK Biobank/FinnGen research institutions

evidence.tested: In a phenome-wide analysis of 484,230 genome-sequenced participants, the authors report 182 putative novel gene–disease associations that were not genome-wide significant in baseline cohorts or explained by biomarker associations; 38.9% of the 167 mappable signals were nominally supported with the same direction in FinnGen.
evidence.unknown: The authors classify the 182 associations as putative novel; they are computational associations, not experimentally established causal genes. FinnGen nominal same-direction support applied to 38.92% (65/167) of the mappable putative novel PheWAS associations, while the paper also reports other aggregate exome-wide results. A separate example, APOB–thyrotoxicosis, showed FinnGen support. These signals require further biological validation.
evidence.ai_role: MILTON predicted cases from clinical biomarkers and other quantitative traits, augmenting phenotype labels for genetic association analyses. The AI-enabled cohort enrichment yielded putative novel gene–disease signals; the study compared them with baseline analyses, orthogonal prioritization tools and FinnGen.

title: SCimilarity links fibrosis-associated macrophage states across diseases and validates a matching in-vitro cell state
summary: SCimilarity searched a 23.4-million-cell reference atlas spanning 412 single-cell RNA-sequencing studies using query profiles from interstitial-lung-disease macrophages and fibroblasts. It identified fibrosis-associated macrophage-like states in other fibrotic diseases, COVID-19 and selected tumour datasets, and a 3D hydrogel culture as a high-ranking in-vitro match; the authors report experimentally demonstrating that this system reproduces the queried macrophage state.
ai_technology: SCimilarity, a deep metric-learning model for querying cell-state similarity across single-cell atlases
organization: Genentech; and collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: It identified fibrosis-associated macrophage-like states in other fibrotic diseases, COVID-19 and selected tumour datasets, and a 3D hydrogel culture as a high-ranking in-vitro match; the authors report experimentally demonstrating that this system reproduces the queried macrophage state.
evidence.unknown: Most cross-disease and tumour-context links are computational similarity observations in previously published single-cell datasets; they do not establish causal roles in those diseases. Some rare tissue/cancer matches are from individual datasets or samples. The in-vitro 3D hydrogel assay is the experimentally tested part; broad disease associations need further biological validation.
evidence.ai_role: The model ranked cell profiles in a 23.4-million-cell atlas by similarity to ILD-derived macrophage/fibroblast query profiles, linking these states to disease/tissue contexts and nominating the 3D hydrogel culture for experimental follow-up.

title: Machine-learning analysis identifies a plasma protein signature associated with ALS years before symptoms
summary: In a plasma-proteomics study, machine learning selected a 17-protein panel from 33 proteins that differed between 183 people with ALS and 309 controls. The panel distinguished ALS from healthy participants and other neurological diseases in a held-out test set (AUC 96.2%, balanced accuracy 89.3%) and was assessed in independent cohorts, including UK Biobank samples. Applying the model to presymptomatic samples from people who later developed ALS showed risk-score shifts up to about 10 years before symptom onset.
ai_technology: Machine-learning classification model trained on Olink plasma proteomic features
organization: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke; and collaborating ALS registry and research institutions

evidence.tested: The panel distinguished ALS from healthy participants and other neurological diseases in a held-out test set (AUC 96.2%, balanced accuracy 89.3%) and was assessed in independent cohorts, including UK Biobank samples.
evidence.unknown: This is a candidate biomarker result, not a clinically available diagnostic or screening test. The discovery and neurological-disease test cohorts are modest; the presymptomatic analysis is retrospective, and broader ancestry representation and prospective longitudinal validation remain needed. The paper reports multiple cohort-specific metrics; the summary uses the detailed held-out test-set AUC and balanced accuracy rather than the abstract’s 98.3% model figure.
evidence.ai_role: The model selected a multiplex protein signature and classified ALS versus healthy and neurological-disease controls; the researchers then applied its risk score to presymptomatic samples to estimate disease-associated changes before onset.

title: A seven-gene machine-learning score shows an Alzheimer-associated signal in an independent plasma cohort
summary: A machine-learning pipeline selected a seven-gene lactylation-related transcriptomic score (LDS) from nine Alzheimer disease cohorts. The study evaluated the signature in seven independent brain transcriptomic datasets and a single-center clinical plasma cohort of 540 participants (180 controls, 90 with amnestic mild cognitive impairment and 270 with Alzheimer disease). Plasma LDS had AUC 0.772 for Alzheimer disease; combining LDS with p-tau181 and p-tau217 had AUC 0.859. LDS scores increased across control, aMCI and Alzheimer groups and correlated with MMSE and Braak stage.
ai_technology: Lactylation-Derived Score (LDS), a random-forest feature-screening and partial least-squares logistic-regression model
organization: Southeast University Zhongda Hospital; and collaborating clinical and research institutions

evidence.tested: A machine-learning pipeline selected a seven-gene lactylation-related transcriptomic score (LDS) from nine Alzheimer disease cohorts.
evidence.unknown: The plasma validation cohort was recruited at one center and the analyses are retrospective and observational. The score does not establish lactylation as a causal mechanism, clinical benefit, or readiness for routine diagnosis; broader and prospective validation is needed. This is a transcriptomic signature and a different result from previously reported Alzheimer spectral-protein/chemical biomarker studies.
evidence.ai_role: Machine learning selected a seven-gene expression signature from lactylation-related genes across multi-cohort brain transcriptomic data; the resulting score was measured by RT-qPCR in a separate clinical plasma cohort and evaluated alone and with plasma p-tau markers.

title: A machine-learning plasma panel classifies some REM sleep behavior disorder participants years before motor Parkinson diagnosis
summary: Researchers developed a targeted multiplex mass-spectrometry assay for eight plasma proteins and applied machine learning to distinguish Parkinson disease from healthy controls and classify people with isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD). In the reported longitudinal iRBD cohorts, the model classified 79% of participants up to seven years before motor Parkinson disease or dementia with Lewy bodies onset. The work connects a targeted protein panel to a pre-motor disease signal in measured blood samples.
ai_technology: Machine-learning classifier using recursive feature elimination on targeted plasma proteomic measurements
organization: University of Oxford; University Medical Center Göttingen and collaborating European research institutions

evidence.tested: Researchers developed a targeted multiplex mass-spectrometry assay for eight plasma proteins and applied machine learning to distinguish Parkinson disease from healthy controls and classify people with isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD).
evidence.unknown: The discovery phase used only 10 Parkinson cases and 10 controls. Although the study includes larger targeted-assay cohorts, the longitudinal iRBD groups were small (18 and 54 participants), and the finding is not a validated screening test or proof that intervention changes outcomes. The model’s apparent early classification needs larger prospective cohorts.
evidence.ai_role: The classifier selected an eight-protein panel from targeted mass-spectrometry measurements, then classified motor Parkinson cases and iRBD participants; the longitudinal analysis linked panel scores with later clinical conversion.

title: Machine learning selects CSF and serum protein panels associated with early Alzheimer disease
summary: In a proteomic study, researchers measured paired CSF and serum samples in a discovery cohort and used random-forest machine learning to select a 19-protein CSF panel and an eight-protein serum panel to distinguish mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer disease from cognitively normal participants. Targeted proteomics verified candidate proteins in an independent multicenter cohort. In small held-out test groups, the CSF panel reached AUC 0.984 and the serum panel AUC 0.881; the CSF panel also distinguished Alzheimer-related MCI from frontotemporal dementia, ALS and Huntington disease in the reported analyses.
ai_technology: Random-forest machine-learning classifiers on CSF and serum proteomic profiles
organization: Capital Medical University; Westlake University, Zhejiang University and collaborating Chinese clinical institutions

evidence.tested: In a proteomic study, researchers measured paired CSF and serum samples in a discovery cohort and used random-forest machine learning to select a 19-protein CSF panel and an eight-protein serum panel to distinguish mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer disease from cognitively normal participants.
evidence.unknown: The AUC test sets were small (CSF: 9 Alzheimer-related MCI and 21 controls; serum: 8 and 21). The study used separate independent multicenter targeted-proteomics validation for candidate proteins; that does not make the small classifier test cohorts large or establish clinical utility. The serum panel was less effective at distinguishing Alzheimer-related MCI from other neurodegenerative diseases than the CSF panel. These are research panels, not routine tests.
evidence.ai_role: Random forests prioritized 19 CSF proteins and eight serum proteins to form disease-specific MCI classifiers after proteomic discovery and targeted validation; the selected panels were evaluated in held-out samples and against other neurodegenerative diseases.

title: LightGBM links a three-protein blood panel to biopsy-staged MASLD fibrosis
summary: A translational study combined a disease-related mouse gene-expression signature, human liver-biopsy transcriptomes and serum protein measurements to select IGFBP7, SSc5D and Sema4D as a three-protein panel for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). A LightGBM model classified biopsy-staged fibrosis, with AUCs 0.82 for F0/F1, 0.89 for F2 and 0.87 for F3/F4 in the development/testing data. In an independent Danish cohort of 156 patients, AUC was 0.84 for F0/F1 and F3/F4; performance for F2 was lower (AUC 0.62).
ai_technology: LightGBM classifier (TLM3) using the three serum proteins IGFBP7, SSc5D and Sema4D
organization: TNO; Amsterdam UMC, Leiden University Medical Center and collaborating Dutch and Danish clinical institutions

evidence.tested: A translational study combined a disease-related mouse gene-expression signature, human liver-biopsy transcriptomes and serum protein measurements to select IGFBP7, SSc5D and Sema4D as a three-protein panel for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).
evidence.unknown: The model is an early translational biomarker result. Its independent cohort replicated better classification at F0/F1 and F3/F4 (AUC 0.84) but was modest for F2 (AUC 0.62).
