The authors say mechanistic claims could not be tested in the single-biopsy cohorts and call for prospective and intervention studies before clinical utility is established. TNO disclosed a patent application related to the biomarkers.
evidence.ai_role: The LightGBM model combined the three protein measurements selected from a translational mouse/human fibrosis signature to classify liver-biopsy fibrosis stages. The authors compared the model with Fib-4, APRI and FibroScan in held-out and independent cohorts.

title: A machine-learning-selected P4 serum panel detects hepatocellular carcinoma and signals cirrhosis-to-cancer progression
summary: A staged serum-proteomics study across 1,002 individuals used random-forest machine learning to select a four-marker panel, P4 (HABP2, CD163, AFP and PIVKA-II). In an independent validation set, the panel distinguished hepatocellular carcinoma from cirrhosis (AUC 0.979; sensitivity 0.925; specificity 0.915) and from healthy controls (AUC 0.992). In a prospective external cohort of cirrhosis patients followed for HCC, it predicted conversion with AUC 0.890 and median lead time of 11.4 months before imaging diagnosis.
ai_technology: Random-forest machine-learning model for serum-protein panel selection and HCC classification
organization: Mengchao Hepatobiliary Hospital of Fujian Medical University; Fujian Cancer Hospital, Zhejiang University and collaborating Chinese clinical institutions

evidence.tested: In an independent validation set, the panel distinguished hepatocellular carcinoma from cirrhosis (AUC 0.979; sensitivity 0.925; specificity 0.915) and from healthy controls (AUC 0.992). The prospectively collected cirrhosis cohort was split into 177 training and 76 validation participants for predictive-model construction; collection timing alone does not establish a prospective locked-model evaluation.
evidence.unknown: The prospective cohort included 253 cirrhosis patients, with 36 developing HCC; 8 of 65 participants were false positives for conversion by the reported endpoint. This is source-reported research performance, not proof of improved survival or a clinically implemented screening test. The lead time is measured relative to imaging diagnosis in the study cohorts.
evidence.ai_role: The random-forest model evaluated serum protein panels and selected the four-marker P4 panel; researchers then tested classification in an independent validation set and assessed prediction of cirrhosis-to-HCC conversion in prospective follow-up data.

title: Mal-ID maps disease-associated immune-receptor patterns across infections and autoimmune conditions
summary: Mal-ID analyzed B-cell and T-cell receptor repertoires from 593 people, including patients with COVID-19, HIV, systemic lupus erythematosus and type-1 diabetes, influenza-vaccination recipients and healthy controls. Its combined models classified held-out immune states and highlighted disease-associated receptor patterns; interpretation identified distinct autoreactivity features in lupus and type-1 diabetes and antigen-associated receptor sequences in COVID-19. The authors also evaluated classification on independent COVID-19 cohorts.
ai_technology: Mal-ID (MAchine Learning for Immunological Diagnosis), an ensemble using repertoire feature models and ESM-2 protein-language-model embeddings
organization: Stanford University; Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation, Duke University, University of Pennsylvania and collaborating institutions

evidence.tested: The authors also evaluated classification on independent COVID-19 cohorts.
evidence.unknown: This is a patient-sample diagnostic-validation and immune-biology study, not evidence of clinical deployment or benefit. Validation cohorts and disease-specific sample sizes are limited; external COVID-19 classification involved small cohorts and thresholds were tuned in some analyses. Additional disease-specific validation, threshold calibration, sequencing-depth assessment and interpretation alongside standard clinical assessment remain necessary. Its 2024 bioRxiv preprint is the same work, not a separate finding.
evidence.ai_role: Three machine-learning representations of B-cell and T-cell receptor data were combined to classify immune states and prioritize disease-associated receptor sequences, gene segments and isotypes for biological interpretation.

title: Active learning identifies a higher-activity streptavidin variant for gold-catalyzed hydroamination
summary: An iterative active-learning campaign engineered a streptavidin artificial metalloenzyme for the known-to-the-authors gold-catalyzed hydroamination of 2-ethynylaniline to indole. Gaussian-process models guided screening across five residues in a 3.2-million-variant sequence space. The final-round library contained 38% variants more active than the prior reference, compared with 3% in the initial library. The leading variant, Sav CTNLV, showed 18-fold higher cell-specific activity than wild-type Sav and threefold higher activity than the previous reference variant in replicate testing.
ai_technology: Active-learning Gaussian-process regression model with optimized sequence descriptors and experimental-noise estimates
organization: ETH Zurich; University of Basel and University of Regensburg

evidence.tested: The leading variant, Sav CTNLV, showed 18-fold higher cell-specific activity than wild-type Sav and threefold higher activity than the previous reference variant in replicate testing.
evidence.unknown: The hydroamination reaction and streptavidin–gold artificial metalloenzyme were established in earlier work by the same group; this record is specifically the later AI-guided identification of a higher-activity five-residue variant, not discovery of a new reaction. Activity was measured in an E. coli periplasmic whole-cell assay; purified variants did not retain the same rank order in vitro. Industrial utility or catalytic scale-up was not demonstrated.
evidence.ai_role: The model used measured sequence-activity data from thousands of variants to select exploratory and exploitation libraries across five residues, then prioritized variants for experimental testing. It enabled identification of a high-activity sequence in a large combinatorial space; the paper reports considering experimental uncertainty in its rankings.

title: MODIFY-guided library screening identifies a cytochrome c variant active in both carbon–boron and carbon–silicon bond formation
summary: Researchers applied MODIFY, an ensemble model combining protein language models and sequence-density models, to design a diverse high-fitness library for Rhodothermus marinus cytochrome c. Experimental screening identified variant MLYPPT, which catalyzed both non-natural borylation and silylation: reported total turnover numbers were 2,880 and 2,740, with enantiomeric ratios of 94:6 and 97:3, respectively. The same library yielded distinct high-performing variants for each reaction.
ai_technology: MODIFY (ML-optimized library design with improved fitness and diversity)
organization: Georgia Institute of Technology; University of Pittsburgh; University of California, Santa Barbara

evidence.tested: Experimental screening identified variant MLYPPT, which catalyzed both non-natural borylation and silylation: reported total turnover numbers were 2,880 and 2,740, with enantiomeric ratios of 94:6 and 97:3, respectively.
evidence.unknown: The C–B and C–Si reactions had previously been demonstrated with separately evolved cytochrome c variants; this finding is the discovery of additional, structurally distinct variants and a generalist MLYPPT catalyst. The reported yields and enantiomeric ratios are from the study's assays; industrial scale-up was not shown.
evidence.ai_role: MODIFY used evolutionary sequence models and protein language models for zero-shot fitness estimates, then co-optimized predicted fitness and residue-level diversity to propose a 1,000-variant library. Researchers synthesized and assayed sampled library members; the model-guided library contained experimentally measured new cytochrome c variants, including MLYPPT with activity in both reactions.

title: Active learning identifies a protoglobin variant with 99% yield and cis-selective cyclopropanation
summary: An iterative machine-learning campaign engineered the protoglobin from Pyrobaculum arsenaticum (ParPgb) for non-native cyclopropanation of 4-vinylanisole. After two model-guided rounds following an initial library screen, variant MPFDY gave 99% total cyclopropane yield and a 14:1 cis:trans ratio in the reported assay, compared with a parent variant that produced about 40% yield and favored trans product. The result demonstrates a specific sequence combination with improved yield and stereoselectivity in this enzyme scaffold.
ai_technology: ALDE (Active Learning-assisted Directed Evolution), using a bootstrapped deep-neural-network ensemble and Thompson sampling
organization: California Institute of Technology; University of California, Berkeley; Elegen Corp

evidence.tested: After two model-guided rounds following an initial library screen, variant MPFDY gave 99% total cyclopropane yield and a 14:1 cis:trans ratio in the reported assay, compared with a parent variant that produced about 40% yield and favored trans product.
evidence.unknown: Cyclopropanation is an established non-native enzyme reaction class; the study's distinct result is the ALDE-guided ParPgb sequence and its measured product yield/selectivity. The 99% yield and 14:1 ratio are study assay results, not evidence of industrial process readiness. The study is a single enzyme-engineering campaign.
evidence.ai_role: ALDE trained on measured sequence–yield data, quantified model uncertainty, and selected variants across two iterative rounds in a five-residue, 3.2-million-sequence design space. Experimental screening measured product yield and stereoselectivity; the model-guided variants included MPFDY, whose combined mutations improved the targeted cis-product objective where tested single mutations and their naive recombinations did not.

title: An ML-generated MinE homolog restores bacterial cell division patterning in vivo
summary: A machine-learning-generated MinE homolog, synMinEv25, restored Min oscillations and wild-type-like cell growth and morphology when substituted for the native minE gene in an E. coli strain lacking minDE. Researchers generated variants with a multiple-sequence-alignment variational autoencoder, used AlphaFold2-based structural scoring to select candidates, and screened them in synthetic-cell mimics before in-vivo testing. The validated variant is a distant homolog with less than 50% sequence identity to E. coli MinE.
ai_technology: Multiple-sequence-alignment variational autoencoder (MSA-VAE), AlphaFold2 Multimer, and a structure-based divide-and-conquer scoring pipeline
organization: Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry

evidence.tested: Researchers generated variants with a multiple-sequence-alignment variational autoencoder, used AlphaFold2-based structural scoring to select candidates, and screened them in synthetic-cell mimics before in-vivo testing.
evidence.unknown: This is a proof-of-principle result in one engineered E. coli MinDE system, not a general demonstration that generated proteins can replace natural genes. The paper notes weak correlation between several in-silico scores and individual measured protein properties; it reports one best-performing variant and does not establish applications outside this assay.
evidence.ai_role: The MSA-VAE generated MinE homolog sequences; structure-based scoring estimated membrane binding, MinD complex formation and dimerization to prioritize 48 candidates from 4,000 generated sequences. Cell-free synthetic-cell assays identified 14 variants with Min oscillations, and researchers tested these in E. coli; synMinEv25 restored oscillations, growth and morphology. AI generated and prioritized candidates, while wet-lab experiments established function.

title: Closed-loop learning links donor–acceptor molecules’ photostability to higher triplet states
summary: A closed-loop synthesis and learning campaign found that solution photostability across a donor–bridge–acceptor molecular series correlated with the high-energy portion of the triplet excited-state manifold, beyond the commonly considered lowest triplet state. Researchers tested the model-derived hypothesis on an experimental set and changed solvent triplet energy to test the proposed Dexter triplet-energy-transfer degradation pathway. The study used Bayesian optimization and interpretable supervised learning to extract the chemical hypothesis from measured photostability data.
ai_technology: Closed-loop transfer (CLT), combining Gryffin Bayesian optimization with physics-feature supervised learning
organization: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; University of Toronto; Vector Institute; University of Chicago; University of California, Berkeley

evidence.tested: Researchers tested the model-derived hypothesis on an experimental set and changed solvent triplet energy to test the proposed Dexter triplet-energy-transfer degradation pathway.
evidence.unknown: The finding concerns solution photostability in the studied donor–bridge–acceptor chemical space; it does not by itself establish a universal law for all organic molecules or performance in processed films/devices. The work used human expertise in the loop and experimentally tested the model-generated hypothesis. Device deployment was not demonstrated.
evidence.ai_role: Bayesian optimization recommended molecules for automated modular synthesis and photostability assays; an interpretable supervised model using physics-based features identified a triplet-state hypothesis, which researchers tested with experimental test sets and solvent-energy perturbation. AI guided experimental selection and surfaced a specific chemical relationship; the follow-up measurements tested it.

title: Machine-learning search of archived spectra reveals vinyl–NHC coupling products in palladium catalysis
summary: MEDUSA Search mined archived high-resolution mass spectra and uncovered previously unreported vinyl–N-heterocyclic-carbene (NHC) coupling products in Pd/NHC-catalyzed Mizoroki–Heck reactions. Researchers retrieved the corresponding reaction records and independently tested the proposed transformation with multiple palladium–NHC complexes; ultrahigh-resolution mass spectrometry and MS/MS supported the product formulas and structures. The work also found an ethyl–NHC product across tested reaction mixtures, suggesting additional catalyst-transformation pathways.
ai_technology: MEDUSA Search, an isotope-distribution-driven HRMS search engine with machine-learning ion-threshold regression and false-positive classification
organization: Zelinsky Institute of Organic Chemistry, Russian Academy of Sciences; Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology

evidence.tested: MEDUSA Search mined archived high-resolution mass spectra and uncovered previously unreported vinyl–N-heterocyclic-carbene (NHC) coupling products in Pd/NHC-catalyzed Mizoroki–Heck reactions.
evidence.unknown: The claimed novelty is specific to vinyl–NHC coupling products in the studied Pd/NHC catalytic context. HRMS formulas alone cannot distinguish structural isomers, so the paper's MS/MS, ultrahigh-resolution measurements, reaction notebooks and independent experiments are essential evidence. The authors state that most other detected ions could not be associated confidently with reaction conditions because of incomplete metadata; those are not counted here.
evidence.ai_role: Researchers generated candidate product-ion formulas from reaction fragments and catalysts; MEDUSA Search screened archived spectra using isotope-pattern matching, with two ML models estimating ion-presence thresholds and filtering likely false positives. It surfaced previously overlooked ions in old spectra; follow-up experiments with different NHC ligands and MS/MS tests checked the proposed vinyl–NHC products.

title: Deep learning on routine pathology slides prescreens FGFR-altered bladder cancers in a global study
summary: A deep-learning device analyzed routine H&E whole-slide images to estimate whether advanced urothelial tumors carried selected FGFR2/FGFR3 alterations used for erdafitinib eligibility. In a separate 350-slide retrospective validation set, the device achieved 88.7% sensitivity and 31.8% specificity; it was also prospectively integrated into a non-interventional study spanning 89 sites in nine countries. The paper projected a 28.7% reduction in molecular tests assuming 15% biomarker prevalence; that estimate was simulated, not a measured population-level reduction.
ai_technology: FGFR Device, a multi-instance-learning attention model with a convolutional neural-network backbone
organization: Janssen Research & Development, LLC (Johnson & Johnson)

evidence.tested: In a separate 350-slide retrospective validation set, the device achieved 88.7% sensitivity and 31.8% specificity; it was also prospectively integrated into a non-interventional study spanning 89 sites in nine countries.
evidence.unknown: The 350-slide retrospective validation set was deliberately enriched (150 FGFR-positive and 200 negative; 43% prevalence), and the device fell slightly short of the prespecified 90% sensitivity target. Prospective real-time workflow validation covered only 17 samples in one month (15 predictions; two quality-control failures); production deployment reported 24 samples, with only 20 receiving molecular testing. The 28.7% test reduction is a simulation assuming 15% prevalence, not an observed clinical outcome. This is prescreening support, not a stand-alone diagnosis or evidence of patient benefit.
evidence.ai_role: Trained on more than 3,000 urothelial-cancer slides with molecular test labels, the deep-learning model inferred selected FGFR alteration status from H&E images and returned a likelihood for prescreening before confirmatory molecular testing. The device was prospectively integrated into a non-interventional study workflow; molecular tests remained the reference standard.

title: Machine-guided synthetic regulatory DNA drives cell-type-specific expression across cell lines and vertebrates
summary: The CODA platform used the Malinois deep-learning model and sequence-search algorithms to design synthetic cis-regulatory elements (CREs). In massively parallel reporter assays, 94.1% of the synthetic sequences met the authors’ cell-type-specificity criterion, versus 73.6% of model-selected natural sequences and 40.6% of chromatin-mark-selected natural sequences; synthetic sequences also had higher measured target/off-target separation across K562, HepG2 and SK-N-SH cells. In transgenic zebrafish, two of three liver-directed and two of three neuron-directed CREs showed the intended activity. One neuron-directed sequence, synN1, retained cortical and neuronal expression in mice, including postnatal neocortical layer 6 and subplate neurons.
ai_technology: CODA (Computational Optimization of DNA Activity) with Malinois deep neural network and AdaLead, simulated annealing, and Fast SeqProp sequence search/design algorithms
organization: Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; The Jackson Laboratory; Yale University

evidence.tested: In massively parallel reporter assays, 94.1% of the synthetic sequences met the authors’ cell-type-specificity criterion, versus 73.6% of model-selected natural sequences and 40.6% of chromatin-mark-selected natural sequences; synthetic sequences also had higher measured target/off-target separation across K562, HepG2 and SK-N-SH cells.
evidence.unknown: The in-vitro work used three transformed human cell lines and reporter assays. In-vivo testing covered a small selected set: two of three liver-directed and two of three neuron-directed elements were active in zebrafish; mouse validation focused on neuronal synN1, with n=3 synN1 mice for postnatal cell-type analysis and n=6 for the 5-week cortical reporter assay. These are transgenic reporter results, not therapeutic delivery or evidence of clinical utility. Earlier synthetic enhancer studies existed; this paper’s counted result is its CODA/Malinois comparison against natural sequences plus selected vertebrate validation, not the general idea of AI-designed enhancers.
evidence.ai_role: Malinois predicted MPRA activity of candidate DNA sequences in K562, HepG2 and SK-N-SH cells; CODA iteratively optimized sequences for specified cell-type specificity. Researchers synthesized and experimentally measured the designs by MPRA, then tested selected CREs with reporter constructs in zebrafish and mice. The paper attributes the novel sequences and their measured expression specificity to this model-guided design loop.

title: AI-derived histology biomarker stratifies first-line chemotherapy outcomes in advanced pancreatic cancer
summary: The CHAI computational-histology platform generated a locked H&E-based biomarker intended to distinguish advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma patients with differential outcomes on fluoropyrimidine-based versus gemcitabine-based chemotherapy. In an independent validation cohort of 299 patients from the prospectively collected COMPASS and Know Your Tumor cohorts, the 173 patients classified F-pref had longer time to next treatment or death (8.6 vs 7.5 months, P=.035) and overall survival (14.4 vs 11.7 months, P=.003) on F- versus G-based therapy. Among 126 G-pref patients, G-based therapy was associated with longer time to next treatment or death (9.6 vs 7.2 months, P=.038), but not significantly different overall survival.
ai_technology: Computational Histology Artificial Intelligence (CHAI) platform
organization: Cedars-Sinai Medical Center; Valar Labs; Johns Hopkins University; University of Pittsburgh Medical Center; Pancreatic Cancer Action Network; University Health Network / Princess Margaret Cancer Centre

evidence.tested: In an independent validation cohort of 299 patients from the prospectively collected COMPASS and Know Your Tumor cohorts, the 173 patients classified F-pref had longer time to next treatment or death (8.6 vs 7.5 months, P=.035) and overall survival (14.4 vs 11.7 months, P=.003) on F- versus G-based therapy. The locked biomarker was applied to assembled data from prospectively collected cohorts; prospective validation of treatment selection is still needed.
evidence.unknown: Validation used 299 patients in two prospectively collected but nonrandomized cohorts; treatment assignment was not randomized, and the authors also used propensity weighting and target-trial emulation. The primary endpoint was time to next treatment or death, not progression-free survival. In the biomarker’s G-pref subgroup, the OS comparison was not significant. The authors call for further prospective validation before clinical adoption. An earlier CHAI study concerned adjuvant gemcitabine outcomes in resected disease; this entry is limited to the distinct locked first-line fluoropyrimidine-versus-gemcitabine biomarker and external-cohort results in advanced disease.
evidence.ai_role: Deep-learning models segmented H&E biopsy slides and quantified more than 30,000 histomorphologic features. Using the development cohort, the investigators statistically selected and weighted features into a treatment-preference biomarker and locked its threshold before applying it to an independent validation cohort. The platform supplied the image-derived feature measurements used in the biomarker; this is a biomarker-development and validation result, not autonomous treatment assignment.

title: PlantRNA-FM identifies translation-associated RNA motifs and structure motifs in plants
summary: The PlantRNA-FM model, pretrained on sequence and predicted RNA structure from 1,124 plant transcriptomes, identified 5′-UTR motifs associated with translation efficiency across plant transcriptomes. Reporter assays in plants tested selected predictions: mutating a high-translation-associated RNA secondary-structure motif reduced measured translation efficiency by up to 5.3-fold, while disrupting a model-prioritized low-translation-associated RNA G-quadruplex motif increased it by up to 5.8-fold. The paper reports the rG4 motifs as translation-repressive, consistent with prior evidence on individual rG4s; the transcriptome-wide model prioritization and tested instances are the scoped findings here.
ai_technology: PlantRNA-FM, an interpretable RNA foundation model integrating RNA sequence and predicted structure
organization: Northeast Normal University; Chinese Academy of Sciences; University of Exeter; John Innes Centre; Alan Turing Institute

evidence.tested: Reporter assays in plants tested selected predictions: mutating a high-translation-associated RNA secondary-structure motif reduced measured translation efficiency by up to 5.3-fold, while disrupting a model-prioritized low-translation-associated RNA G-quadruplex motif increased it by up to 5.8-fold.
evidence.unknown: Experimental reporter validation was limited to selected motifs and had n=3, as reported in the figure caption. The model’s transcriptome-wide associations are not individually causal validations. The repressive role of rG4 motifs was previously known for individual cases; the paper’s contribution includes model-prioritized plant 5′-UTR motifs and experimental effects for selected constructs, not first discovery of rG4 biology. Reporter assays do not establish whole-plant phenotype or crop benefit.
evidence.ai_role: PlantRNA-FM was pretrained with plant RNA sequence and structure data, then fine-tuned on translation-efficiency data. An attention-contrast interpretation framework prioritized 5′-UTR sequence/structure motifs associated with translation; researchers tested selected motif predictions by mutating reporter constructs and measuring translation efficiency in plants.

title: Deep learning mines venom proteomes for antimicrobial peptides active in vitro and in a mouse infection model
summary: The APEX deep-learning model screened 16,123 venom proteins by generating and scoring 40,626,260 venom-encrypted peptides. After activity prediction and filtering for low similarity to known antimicrobial peptides, the authors selected 58 for experiments; 53 showed antimicrobial activity against at least one tested pathogen. Three selected peptides reduced bacterial counts after topical treatment in a mouse Acinetobacter baumannii skin-abscess model; the wolf-spider-derived Arachnoserver-5 peptide produced a reported three-log reduction versus untreated controls through day four, without significant body-weight change under the study conditions.
ai_technology: APEX deep-learning model for bacterial strain-specific minimum inhibitory concentration prediction
organization: University of Pennsylvania

evidence.tested: After activity prediction and filtering for low similarity to known antimicrobial peptides, the authors selected 58 for experiments; 53 showed antimicrobial activity against at least one tested pathogen.
evidence.unknown: Only 58 of the 386 low-similarity candidates were experimentally tested, and activity was measured against a defined panel of 11 strains; some tested peptides were cytotoxic. The mouse study was a topical single-dose skin-abscess model with six animals per group, not systemic treatment or human efficacy. The paper notes possible ion-channel activity for many candidates and calls for follow-up safety testing. A related APEX study mined archaeal proteomes (10.1038/s41564-025-02061-0); this entry is limited to the separate venom-protein source library and its distinct peptide set and experiments.
evidence.ai_role: APEX scored 40.6 million candidate peptide fragments generated from venom proteins for predicted antimicrobial activity. The authors filtered predicted hits for sequence dissimilarity to known antimicrobial peptides, synthesized a selected subset, and experimentally tested antimicrobial activity, cytotoxicity and selected animal-model efficacy. The AI model narrowed an otherwise very large peptide search space; assays established which selected candidates were active.

title: CHANCE uses tumor genomes to prioritize non-cancer drugs with activity in patient-derived cancer cells
summary: CHANCE, a supervised machine-learning model integrating patient-specific coding and non-coding mutations with drug and protein-interaction information, screened 5,197 TCGA/ICGC tumors against 923 FDA-approved non-oncology drugs. For ex-vivo validation, the investigators sequenced tumor cells from seven patients with pancreatic or esophageal cancer and tested CHANCE-prioritized drugs; at least one predicted non-oncology drug showed anticancer activity in tumor cells from five of the seven patients. This is patient-specific cell-assay validation, not a treatment-response study in patients.
ai_technology: CHANCE, a supervised gradient-boosted-tree model integrating coding/non-coding variants, protein–protein interaction networks, drug targets and drug-response data
organization: Tianjin Medical University; collaborating Chinese cancer research and clinical institutions

evidence.tested: For ex-vivo validation, the investigators sequenced tumor cells from seven patients with pancreatic or esophageal cancer and tested CHANCE-prioritized drugs; at least one predicted non-oncology drug showed anticancer activity in tumor cells from five of the seven patients.
evidence.unknown: Only seven patient-derived samples were tested, from pancreatic or esophageal cancers; at least one prioritized non-oncology drug showed activity in five. This was an ex-vivo drug-sensitivity assay, not clinical treatment, and the study does not establish efficacy, safety, dosing or patient benefit. The 5,197-tumor/923-drug screen is computational prediction; only the small patient-derived subset had experimental validation. Drug-response predictions may include drugs represented in training, as the article notes 149 of 923 screened drugs were in the training data.
evidence.ai_role: Trained on drug-sensitivity measurements from 318 cancer cell lines across 647 drugs, CHANCE maps each patient tumor’s whole-genome mutations to drug-target/pathway features and ranks non-oncology drugs by predicted patient-specific anticancer activity. Investigators used these predictions to select drugs for ex-vivo testing in tumor cells from seven patients; the reported five-patient activity result tests the model’s personalized prioritization.

title: AlphaCD maps experimentally measured catalytic properties across cytidine deaminases and supports a high-fidelity editor
summary: The researchers measured catalytic efficiency, editing windows, motif preferences and off-target activity for 1,100 APOBEC-like cytidine deaminases fused to nCas9 in HEK293T cells, then trained AlphaCD to predict these properties. They applied it to 21,335 UniProt deaminases and experimentally checked a 28-protein subsample. As an application, the team used AlphaCD to identify a high-efficiency deaminase and alanine scanning to produce the E100A variant, which retained editing activity while reducing off-target activity; cell experiments tested editing at endogenous loci and a PCSK9 splice site.
ai_technology: AlphaCD, a machine-learning model trained on sequence, predicted structure and related protein features
organization: Agricultural Genomics Institute at Shenzhen, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences

evidence.tested: The researchers measured catalytic efficiency, editing windows, motif preferences and off-target activity for 1,100 APOBEC-like cytidine deaminases fused to nCas9 in HEK293T cells, then trained AlphaCD to predict these properties.
evidence.unknown: The large functional dataset was measured in HEK293T reporter assays. The 21,335-protein landscape is model-predicted, with a 28-protein validation subsample. The engineered E100A editor was tested in cells; these experiments do not establish therapeutic safety, in-vivo efficacy or clinical benefit. This is distinct from the earlier AlphaFold2 structural-clustering papers: the named discovery and assay here concern the 1,100-enzyme dataset, AlphaCD predictions and A0A2R2Z4E4 E100A variant, not CD0208^P52A or the 2023 DddA-like clade findings.
evidence.ai_role: AlphaCD learned experimentally measured activity, editing-window, motif and off-target properties across 1,100 deaminases, predicted properties for 21,335 database sequences, and was applied to select a high-efficiency candidate for subsequent alanine-scanning engineering. The authors report the model's predictions validated on 28 sampled deaminases; the E100A mutation itself was experimentally produced by alanine scanning, not generated by the model.

title: Deep-learning design produced soluble analogues of membrane-protein folds with preserved binding functions
summary: A deep-learning pipeline based on inversion of AlphaFold2 and ProteinMPNN designed soluble proteins with claudin, rhomboid-protease and GPCR-like folds. Experiments reported stable, folded soluble designs and structural agreement with target folds. The researchers grafted functional motifs, including a ghrelin-receptor epitope that bound its antibody and active/inactive A2A-receptor-like designs that differed in mini-Gs binding; a binding-site knockout served as a control.
ai_technology: AF2seq deep-learning backbone design with ProteinMPNN sequence design
organization: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne; University at Buffalo; University of Washington; Massachusetts Institute of Technology

evidence.tested: Experiments reported stable, folded soluble designs and structural agreement with target folds.
evidence.unknown: This is a protein-design proof of concept with in-vitro biophysical and binding assays; the analogues are not native membrane receptors and do not demonstrate signaling, drug activity or therapeutic efficacy. The GPCR analogues tested binding to mini-Gs in conformation-designed constructs. The separate live-catalog record on designed proteins modulating dopamine D1 receptor signaling reports a different binder/target and signaling result; this paper reports soluble receptor-fold analogues and binding assays, not D1 signaling modulation.
evidence.ai_role: The deep-learning design pipeline generated soluble analogues of complex membrane-protein folds and the scaffolds into which native functional motifs were grafted. The study tested solubility, thermal stability, structural accuracy and selected binding functions experimentally, including conformation-specific A2A-receptor-like constructs.

title: MIMaL predicts and experimentally validates five yeast gene functions from protein–metabolite profiles
summary: MIMaL used tree-based regression and SHAP interpretation on yeast proteome/metabolome measurements, then clustered protein-control profiles across single-gene knockouts. It predicted functions for five genes, with experimental validation reported for all five. Two previously uncharacterized genes, YJR120W and YDL157C, were predicted to modulate mitochondrial translation; functions were also predicted and validated for SDH9, ISC1 and FMP52. The study additionally validated previously unrecognized protein links to citrate.
ai_technology: MIMaL: ExtraTrees regression of metabolite abundance from proteomic profiles, SHAP interpretation, and UMAP/OPTICS clustering of protein-control profiles
organization: Cedars-Sinai Medical Center; Medical College of Wisconsin; Stockholm University; University of Gothenburg

evidence.tested: MIMaL used tree-based regression and SHAP interpretation on yeast proteome/metabolome measurements, then clustered protein-control profiles across single-gene knockouts.
evidence.unknown: This was a yeast study using a prior 174-single-gene-knockout multi-omics dataset, with 348 condition profiles; it does not establish corresponding human gene functions. Five gene functions are reported validated, and the article specifically states YJR120W and YDL157C modulate mitochondrial translation. Some experimental validation used existing knockout strains and measurements; no independent replication is implied.
evidence.ai_role: A tree-based model predicted metabolite profiles from proteomic measurements; SHAP-derived protein-control values and clustering across knockout conditions were used to infer new protein–metabolite connections and gene functions. The researchers experimentally validated predicted citrate-control relationships and five gene-function predictions.

title: SIMMER-guided experiments identify gut bacterial strains that deplete methotrexate
summary: SIMMER combines reaction-chemistry and protein-sequence similarity to predict gut microbial species and enzymes responsible for drug biotransformations. For methotrexate (MTX), the model predicted candidate strains and enzyme sequences; researchers tested 42 gut bacterial isolates by HPLC. SIMMER predicted 13 isolates as MTX-metabolizing, and 10 of those tested isolates showed MTX depletion; the association was significant in the study (Fisher exact p=0.046). Predicted MTX-hydrolysis enzyme signatures were also enriched in stool samples of MTX nonresponders in an analyzed rheumatoid-arthritis cohort.
ai_technology: SIMMER, a computational reaction-similarity and protein-homology pipeline using chemical fingerprints, MetaCyc reactions and gut metagenomic sequences
organization: Gladstone Institutes; University of California, San Francisco; Chan Zuckerberg Biohub San Francisco

evidence.tested: For methotrexate (MTX), the model predicted candidate strains and enzyme sequences; researchers tested 42 gut bacterial isolates by HPLC.
evidence.unknown: The study reports species-level evidence for bacterial MTX depletion, but the enzyme predictions themselves were not individually purified or functionally validated. Only 13 of 42 tested isolates were predicted positive and 10 depleted MTX; predictions may have false positives, as the authors note. The RA association is observational and does not establish that microbial metabolism caused treatment nonresponse. The underlying fact that gut bacteria can metabolize MTX was already known; this result concerns species-level prediction and validation, not discovery of MTX metabolism itself.
evidence.ai_role: SIMMER proposed specific bacterial species and enzyme sequences for known drug transformations. The team tested its MTX predictions against an independent panel of 42 gut bacterial isolates and HPLC-measured drug depletion, and compared predicted enzyme presence with baseline stool metagenomes and later MTX response in an RA dataset.

title: AlphaFold structure analysis helps reveal PHGDH transcriptional activity linked to Alzheimer’s amyloid pathology
summary: AlphaFold-based structural analysis highlighted a helix-helix-turn-helix subdomain in PHGDH that resembles a TALE homeodomain, prompting tests of a previously unrecognized DNA-binding and transcriptional function. Experiments supported PHGDH binding to promoters and activation of IKKα and HMGB1 in astrocytes, independently of its metabolic enzyme activity. In mouse models and human brain organoids, PHGDH expression promoted amyloid pathology; a blood-brain-barrier-permeable inhibitor of its transcriptional function reduced amyloid pathology and improved measured behavioral deficits in mice.
ai_technology: AlphaFold structure prediction, followed by structural comparison of the predicted PHGDH fold
organization: University of California San Diego; collaborating biomedical research institutions

evidence.tested: AlphaFold-based structural analysis highlighted a helix-helix-turn-helix subdomain in PHGDH that resembles a TALE homeodomain, prompting tests of a previously unrecognized DNA-binding and transcriptional function.
evidence.unknown: The AlphaFold-derived structural resemblance generated the mechanistic hypothesis; experiments establish the reported PHGDH transcriptional and pathology effects in the tested models. The inhibitor and behavioral effects were tested in mice, not people. Human brain organoid findings are in vitro and do not establish clinical disease causation or treatment efficacy. PHGDH overexpression alone did not reproduce all Alzheimer’s disease features, and no human therapeutic outcome is reported.
evidence.ai_role: The researchers inspected AlphaFold-predicted PHGDH structure and identified a helix-helix-turn-helix subdomain resembling a TALE homeodomain, which motivated the hypothesis and targeted mutation tests for DNA binding. AlphaFold did not establish PHGDH function or disease causality; the transcriptional activity and pathology effects were tested through biochemical, cellular, organoid and mouse experiments.

title: iTARGEX analysis identifies ELG1 as a regulator of yeast transcription buffering and four protein-turnover regulators
summary: iTARGEX applied a mixture-regression model to gene-expression profiles from 1,484 single-gene deletion yeast mutants, associating transcriptomic changes with S-phase transcriptional buffering and global protein turnover. Experiments supported ELG1 as a previously unrecognized regulator of transcriptional buffering during S phase; the phenotype was reproduced in a second genetic background and rescued by a PCNA-D150E mutation. Follow-up protein-turnover measurements showed altered turnover in MRN1, UPF3, RAM1 and SSN3 deletion strains.
ai_technology: iTARGEX, a finite-mixture regression framework fitted by expectation maximization to single-gene-deletion transcriptomic data
organization: Academia Sinica, Taiwan

evidence.tested: Experiments supported ELG1 as a previously unrecognized regulator of transcriptional buffering during S phase; the phenotype was reproduced in a second genetic background and rescued by a PCNA-D150E mutation.
evidence.unknown: The study used budding yeast and pre-existing deletion-mutant transcriptome profiles, followed by experiments on selected candidates. ELG1's role in S-phase transcription buffering was reproduced in a second yeast genetic background and rescued by PCNA-D150E; the protein-turnover effects concern yeast deletion strains. These results do not establish corresponding human functions.
evidence.ai_role: iTARGEX associated gene-expression profiles from deletion strains with biological traits without requiring prior gene annotations and nominated candidate regulators. The researchers then performed S-phase transcription and protein-turnover experiments to test the model-prioritized candidates, supporting ELG1's role in transcriptional buffering and altered turnover for four deletion strains.

title: CAMIL regression predicts continuous homologous-recombination deficiency and tumor immune biomarkers from histology
summary: A self-supervised, attention-based deep-learning regression model predicted continuous homologous-recombination deficiency (HRD) scores and tumor-microenvironment biomarkers from H&E pathology slides. On TCGA internal validation, HRD classification AUROC exceeded 0.70 in five of seven cancer types; external CPTAC validation reached AUROC 0.81 for lung adenocarcinoma and 0.96 for endometrial cancer. In 2,297 colorectal-cancer patients in the DACHS cohort, continuous regression scores for leukocyte fraction and lymphocyte-infiltration-related signatures were independently prognostic in multivariable survival analysis.
ai_technology: CAMIL regression, a self-supervised contrastive-clustering and attention-based multiple-instance deep-learning model
organization: Technische Universität Dresden; University Hospital Dresden; collaborating clinical and pathology institutions

evidence.tested: On TCGA internal validation, HRD classification AUROC exceeded 0.70 in five of seven cancer types; external CPTAC validation reached AUROC 0.81 for lung adenocarcinoma and 0.96 for endometrial cancer.
evidence.unknown: Retrospective computational pathology analysis; the model predicts molecular and immune-related biomarkers from slides and does not replace confirmatory molecular testing or establish treatment selection benefit. HRD performance varied by cancer type, with weak internal performance in some cohorts. The reported survival associations in DACHS are prognostic associations, not evidence that using model predictions improves patient outcomes. Scores and endpoints were tested in the named datasets.
evidence.ai_role: The model analyzed whole-slide H&E images to estimate continuous HRD and tumor-microenvironment biomarker scores. The team compared regression with classification methods across cohorts, externally validated HRD predictions in CPTAC, and tested prognostic associations of predicted scores in a separate retrospective colorectal-cancer cohort.

title: An integrated Arabidopsis regulatory network predicts 13 previously unlinked reactive-oxygen-stress regulators
summary: Researchers integrated DNA-motif, chromatin-accessibility, TF-binding and expression evidence with supervised learning to build an Arabidopsis gene-regulatory network of 1,491 transcription factors and 1.7 million TF–target interactions. The network predicted candidate reactive-oxygen-species (ROS) regulators; loss- and gain-of-function phenotyping supported 13 regulators not previously linked to ROS or stress responses. Newly tested examples included WRKY55, WRKY47, AT2G33710 and AT5G57150. The paper also reports that 75% of its ROS-predicted TFs had ROS or physiological stress functions supported by either this study or prior evidence.
ai_technology: Supervised-learning integrated gene-regulatory network (iGRN) built from motif, open-chromatin, transcription-factor-binding and expression-based networks
organization: Ghent University; VIB Center for Plant Systems Biology; Bioinformatics Institute Ghent

evidence.tested: Newly tested examples included WRKY55, WRKY47, AT2G33710 and AT5G57150.
evidence.unknown: The iGRN integrated existing experimental data and the ROS findings were tested in Arabidopsis stress assays, not crop-yield or field-resilience trials. The 75% figure combines prior literature with new phenotypic tests; it is not a rate of independently replicated new discoveries. The new TF functions are limited to tested oxidative-stress conditions and mutant lines.
evidence.ai_role: The supervised integration model inferred TF–target regulatory links across multiple experimental input networks and predicted candidate TF functions, including ROS-response regulators. The investigators tested predicted TF candidates using Arabidopsis loss- or gain-of-function lines and ROS-specific phenotyping; these experiments supported 13 TFs without prior ROS/stress associations.

title: Longitudinal EHR machine learning identifies patients who may need autoimmune rheumatic-disease evaluation years earlier
summary: A random-forest model trained on longitudinal electronic health records from 161,584 people across two institutions identified records associated with high-specificity autoantibody testing for systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs). The model achieved AUROC 0.93 in internal validation and 0.87 on the external All of Us cohort. In a separate BioMe cohort, model probabilities tracked SARD and other autoimmune diagnoses; records could predict later autoantibody testing and rheumatology encounters up to five years before those events. The study also found higher autoantibody yield among model-prioritized individuals than under the comparison clinical-testing rate.
ai_technology: Random-forest machine-learning model using longitudinal electronic-health-record diagnoses, medications, laboratory results and vital signs
organization: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai; University of Maryland School of Medicine; Hospital for Special Surgery

evidence.tested: A random-forest model trained on longitudinal electronic health records from 161,584 people across two institutions identified records associated with high-specificity autoantibody testing for systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs).
evidence.unknown: The model predicts clinical suspicion and need for rheumatological testing, not a SARD diagnosis. The study was retrospective and opportunistic; autoantibody testing and rheumatology encounters are imperfect proxies for clinical need, and some diseases were not included in the training target. The authors state prospective studies are needed to determine whether model-guided testing improves care or outcomes. The five-year lead is retrospective prediction of later evaluation events, not proven earlier diagnosis or patient benefit.
evidence.ai_role: The model ranked patients by probability of receiving SARD-specific autoantibody testing, using clinical data preceding the test or rheumatology encounter. Investigators evaluated performance in internal validation, the external All of Us cohort and an independent BioMe cohort, and tested whether higher scores tracked diagnosed autoimmune disease and identified later testing or encounters earlier in retrospective records.

title: Deep learning detects elevated tissue-derived cfDNA across cancer and cirrhosis cohorts
summary: A study built a fragment-level methylation atlas from 521 noncancer tissue samples spanning 29 human tissue types and used it with cfSort, a supervised deep neural network, to estimate tissue composition in plasma cell-free DNA. Applying cfSort to patient data, the investigators found higher cfDNA fractions from the affected tissue in liver, lung, colorectal and stomach cancer and cirrhosis cohorts than in healthy controls; the estimated fractions also increased with cancer stage. The tissue-origin signal was reproduced on an independent whole-genome-bisulfite-sequencing dataset for liver cancer. In serial samples from four non-small-cell lung cancer patients receiving anti-PD-1 therapy, estimated liver or kidney tissue fractions tracked measured biochemical markers of organ injury.
ai_technology: cfSort, an ensemble of two dense deep neural networks trained on simulated mixtures using a fragment-level tissue methylation atlas
organization: University of California, Los Angeles; Stanford University; EarlyDiagnostics; University of Southern California; University of California, San Diego

evidence.tested: Applying cfSort to patient data, the investigators found higher cfDNA fractions from the affected tissue in liver, lung, colorectal and stomach cancer and cirrhosis cohorts than in healthy controls; the estimated fractions also increased with cancer stage.
evidence.unknown: The disease cohorts were retrospective and the clinical analyses demonstrate association and measurement feasibility, not prospective diagnostic benefit or improved outcomes. The clinical groups were 21 cirrhosis patients and 201 cancer patients, with 100 healthy controls; cross-platform liver-cancer validation used 24 cases and 32 controls. Anti-PD-1 injury monitoring involved only four NSCLC patients at three timepoints. The authors note that disease-specific methylation markers could improve cancer detection beyond tissue-of-origin fractions.
evidence.ai_role: The team used the supervised cfSort model to deconvolve methylation profiles in plasma cfDNA and estimate contributions from 29 tissue types. This enabled the reported comparison of affected-tissue cfDNA fractions in cancer and cirrhosis patient cohorts versus controls and longitudinal tracking of tissue-injury signals during immunotherapy. The atlas and model were also evaluated against simulated mixtures and independent methylation data.

title: EHR deep learning and sequencing identify two previously undiagnosed Noonan syndrome cases
summary: Investigators applied a deep-learning model to diagnosis text in the electronic health records of 92,428 pediatric patients. It flagged 171 patients above a prespecified Noonan syndrome risk threshold for chart review; genetic sequencing and specialist assessment identified two previously undiagnosed Noonan syndrome cases among evaluated patients, in addition to three patients diagnosed during the study period. The confirmed cases had pathogenic variants in Noonan-associated genes, including PTPN11 and LZTR1. This supplies real-world evidence that EHR-based model screening can surface rare-disease cases for clinical genetic evaluation.
ai_technology: Deep convolutional neural network trained on structured electronic-health-record diagnosis text to estimate Noonan syndrome risk
organization: Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center; University of Cincinnati College of Medicine; University of Wisconsin–Madison

evidence.tested: The confirmed cases had pathogenic variants in Noonan-associated genes, including PTPN11 and LZTR1.
evidence.unknown: This was a real-world retrospective screening evaluation at one pediatric biobank, not a prospective screening trial. Sequencing identified two cases among 83 patients evaluated, and the overall precision among the 171 high-risk patients was 2.92%; the model therefore required substantial chart review and genetic confirmation. Retrospective risk trajectories suggest possible earlier recognition but do not establish earlier care or improved outcomes.
evidence.ai_role: The previously developed deep-learning model scored 92,428 patient records and ranked 171 individuals above a prespecified risk threshold. The study team reviewed high-risk records, then used clinical genetic assessment and sequencing to evaluate patients without a prior diagnosis; these follow-up tests confirmed two previously undiagnosed cases. Model risk trajectories were also reconstructed from cumulative EHR diagnoses to assess whether the signal appeared before final diagnosis.

title: Machine learning identifies plasma protein signatures that predict onset of common and rare diseases
summary: Researchers used regularized machine-learning models to select sparse plasma-protein signatures for 10-year incidence across 218 diseases in 41,931 UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project participants. Five to twenty proteins improved held-out risk prediction over basic clinical information for 67 diseases and over clinical information plus routine assays for 52. The study identified TNFRSF17 as a specific predictor for future multiple myeloma and TNFRSF13B for monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. In bone-marrow single-cell data from 11 newly diagnosed myeloma patients and three controls, four of five myeloma predictor proteins were most highly expressed by plasma cells; FCRLB and QPCT elevation was attributable to malignant plasma cells. Proteomic signatures also replicated improved prediction for five of six diseases tested in EPIC-Norfolk.
ai_technology: LASSO feature selection and regularized Cox machine-learning models integrating plasma proteomics and clinical covariates
organization: MRC Epidemiology Unit, University of Cambridge; Queen Mary University of London; University College London; GSK Research and Development; Berlin Institute of Health at Charité; EPIC-Norfolk

evidence.tested: Five to twenty proteins improved held-out risk prediction over basic clinical information for 67 diseases and over clinical information plus routine assays for 52.
evidence.unknown: The disease predictions are observational risk associations, not causal mechanisms or clinical screening outcomes. Most protein signatures were not externally replicated; EPIC-Norfolk tested six diseases, with improved prediction replicated for five. The myeloma single-cell analysis involved 11 patients and three healthy controls and supports cellular expression attribution, not prospective validation of an assay. Absolute quantification with clinical-grade assays and further validation would be needed before clinical use.
evidence.ai_role: The authors applied a three-stage machine-learning framework—feature selection, hyperparameter tuning and held-out validation—to ~2,923 proteins in UK Biobank. It selected parsimonious protein signatures for 218 future disease outcomes and identified disease-specific predictors and shared predictors. For multiple myeloma, the model-selected five-protein signature and follow-up single-cell expression analysis linked four predictors to marrow plasma cells and showed malignant-cell-associated FCRLB and QPCT expression.

title: AstroREG maps functional enhancer–gene links in human astrocytes
summary: A CRISPRi and single-cell RNA-sequencing screen tested 979 candidate enhancers in cultured human primary astrocytes and identified 158 functional enhancer–gene pairs, including enhancers regulating genes implicated in Alzheimer disease. The study trained the EGrf random-forest model on the measured screen and used it to predict additional enhancer–gene regulatory interactions genome-wide; selected model-predicted interactions were then functionally assessed by CRISPRi and qRT–PCR.
ai_technology: EGrf random-forest enhancer–gene interaction model, trained on the AstroREG CRISPRi/single-cell RNA-sequencing screen
organization: University of New South Wales; University of Western Australia; Macquarie University; Monash University; University of Michigan

evidence.tested: A CRISPRi and single-cell RNA-sequencing screen tested 979 candidate enhancers in cultured human primary astrocytes and identified 158 functional enhancer–gene pairs, including enhancers regulating genes implicated in Alzheimer disease.
evidence.unknown: The primary CRISPRi screen and genome-wide model outputs are distinct evidence classes. The 158 reported enhancer–gene pairs came from the screen; genome-wide EGrf predictions are computational until tested. Figure descriptions report qRT–PCR follow-up for selected model predictions with independent duplicate transductions (n=4 per enhancer). The experiments used cultured astrocytes and do not establish enhancer causality in human Alzheimer disease or clinical relevance.
evidence.ai_role: The authors used experimentally measured enhancer–gene pairs to train EGrf, then applied the model to predict regulatory interactions genome-wide. Selected predictions were followed up by individual enhancer CRISPRi and qRT–PCR. Machine learning contributed the genome-wide extension of a functional astrocyte enhancer map; the initial 979-enhancer screen itself was experimentally measured.

title: Single-cell imaging and machine learning reveal a Cdk2–COP9 interaction that induces a senescence-like immune state in Drosophila cells
summary: A synthetic genetic-interaction and cell-morphology map covering more than 6,800 Drosophila genes supported machine-learning-based gene-function assignments across 47 modules. In follow-up, Cytoclass single-cell classification revealed a state-specific interaction between Cdk2 and COP9 signalosome knockdown: co-depletion arrested cell-cycle progression and produced a senescence-like phenotype with increased antimicrobial-peptide expression in cultured cells and hemocytes, including without bacterial infection.
ai_technology: Single-cell morphology classifier ensemble and machine-learning analysis of genetic-interaction profiles (Cytoclass; support-vector machines and random forest)
organization: German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ); Heidelberg University; University of Applied Sciences Bingen

evidence.tested: A synthetic genetic-interaction and cell-morphology map covering more than 6,800 Drosophila genes supported machine-learning-based gene-function assignments across 47 modules.
evidence.unknown: The findings are from cultured Drosophila cells and hemocytes; they do not establish mammalian or human disease mechanisms. The senescence-like phenotype and antimicrobial-peptide induction were measured after experimental RNAi co-depletion. The global module assignments and many network interactions are computational inferences; only selected interactions received targeted follow-up.
evidence.ai_role: The authors generated single-cell morphology and synthetic genetic-interaction profiles, used machine-learning-based function discovery to assign functions to genes in 47 modules, and applied Cytoclass state classification to reveal interactions hidden in bulk-average profiles. The state-specific Cdk2–COP9 interaction was followed up by double-RNAi assays, single-cell transcriptomics, beta-galactosidase and antimicrobial-peptide measurements.

title: Deep learning of salivary-gland biopsies identifies acinar CD8 T-cell infiltration associated with Sjögren disease
summary: A deep-learning model trained on digitized minor salivary-gland biopsy slides from five expert centres and externally validated at a sixth classified focus score and Sjögren disease in a retrospective cohort of 545 participants. Explainable-model analysis identified a histological pattern of CD8-positive T cells around acinar epithelial cells associated with Sjögren disease. External-validation AUROC was 0.89 for disease classification and 0.92 among patients negative for anti-SSA antibodies.
ai_technology: Deep-learning histopathology classifier with Shapley-value interpretation
organization: Scienta Lab; William Harvey Research Institute, Queen Mary University of London; University of Birmingham; National and Kapodistrian University of Athens; Newcastle University; Université Paris-Saclay; participating NECESSITY consortium centres

evidence.tested: A deep-learning model trained on digitized minor salivary-gland biopsy slides from five expert centres and externally validated at a sixth classified focus score and Sjögren disease in a retrospective cohort of 545 participants.
evidence.unknown: Retrospective multicentre cohort; external validation used one held-out expert centre. The authors state further validation is needed. The CD8 acinar-infiltration pattern was associated with disease classification and is not established as causal, pathognomonic, or clinically actionable. The study does not establish improved patient outcomes or replace expert pathology.
evidence.ai_role: The authors trained the deep-learning model on digitalized biopsy slides to classify focus score and Sjögren disease, tested generalization at a held-out centre, and used Shapley-value explanations to identify histological patterns associated with model decisions. The study reports acinar CD8-positive T-cell infiltration as a disease-associated pattern.

title: Deep-learning CT response score stratifies outcomes in lung-cancer immunotherapy cohorts
summary: A deep-learning radiomic pipeline generated a pretreatment CT response score (CTRS) for advanced non-small-cell lung cancer treated with PD-(L)1 checkpoint inhibitors. In an independent real-world test cohort, high-response-score first-line ICI-monotherapy patients had longer progression-free and overall survival after adjustment for baseline covariates including PD-L1 (adjusted HR 0.46 and 0.50). In a secondary analysis of 54 participants from a prospective sasanlimab trial, the score was associated with overall survival (adjusted HR 0.33) but not progression-free survival.
ai_technology: Three-dimensional hierarchical convolutional neural network feature extractor combined with a Cox survival model (CT response score, CTRS)
organization: Onc.AI; Pfizer; University of Pennsylvania; Moffitt Cancer Center

evidence.tested: In an independent real-world test cohort, high-response-score first-line ICI-monotherapy patients had longer progression-free and overall survival after adjustment for baseline covariates including PD-L1 (adjusted HR 0.46 and 0.50).
evidence.unknown: The real-world data were retrospective. Association of the score with survival among treated patients does not establish that the score predicts differential treatment benefit versus an untreated or alternative-treatment control. Clinical-trial analysis was secondary and small (n=54): PFS association was not significant, while OS association was significant. Authors say larger prospective studies are needed; no improved-care or deployment outcome is shown.
evidence.ai_role: The model learned image features from pretreatment CT/PET-CT scans and combined them with a Cox survival model to produce an imaging-only response score. Researchers evaluated the score in a held-out real-world cohort and in a secondary analysis of a prospective clinical-trial cohort; it stratified PFS/OS in the first and OS in the latter.

title: Machine learning identifies a high-risk diabetic cardiomyopathy phenotype linked to future heart failure
summary: Unsupervised clustering of 25 echocardiographic and biomarker variables in 1,199 ARIC participants with diabetes identified three phenogroups; the group with the greatest cardiac remodelling and neurohormonal-stress abnormalities had 12.1% five-year heart-failure incidence, versus 4.6% and 3.1% in the other groups. A deep-neural-network classifier trained to recognize this phenotype identified corresponding high-risk groups in the external CHS cohort (n=802) and UT Southwestern EHR cohort (n=5,071); phenotype classification was associated with incident heart failure in both.
ai_technology: Unsupervised hierarchical clustering and a deep neural network (DeepNN) classifier, with random forest variable-importance analysis
organization: University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center; Texas Heart Institute; Houston Methodist DeBakey Heart & Vascular Center; Duke University; National Heart Centre Singapore; University of Toronto; University of Colorado; Massachusetts General Hospital

evidence.tested: Unsupervised clustering of 25 echocardiographic and biomarker variables in 1,199 ARIC participants with diabetes identified three phenogroups; the group with the greatest cardiac remodelling and neurohormonal-stress abnormalities had 12.1% five-year heart-failure incidence, versus 4.6% and 3.1% in the other groups.
evidence.unknown: The cohorts were observational; association with future heart failure does not establish that model-guided intervention improves outcomes. The phenotype is an operational study definition, not a universally accepted diagnostic threshold. The authors describe potential preventive use, but it was not tested. The cohorts were external validations rather than prospective deployment trials.
evidence.ai_role: The authors used unsupervised hierarchical clustering of echocardiography and cardiac biomarkers to define outcome-associated diabetic-cardiomyopathy phenogroups, then trained and externally validated a DeepNN classifier to recognize the high-risk phenotype. Random forest permutation importance prioritized NT-proBNP, left-ventricular mass, Doppler measurements, left-atrial dimension and LV end-diastolic volume.

title: Deep learning identifies externally replicated fast and slow cognitive-progressor groups in early Alzheimer dementia
summary: Deep learning clustered cognitive and functional trajectories in 283 people with early dementia probably due to Alzheimer disease into fast- and slow-progressing groups. The trajectory groups were externally validated and independently replicated in a 2,779-person dementia cohort. A classifier using cross-sectional data at diagnosis predicted progression group in external validation with AUC 0.70 ± 0.01.
ai_technology: Deep-learning clustering of longitudinal cognitive/functional trajectories, followed by machine-learning classification from cross-sectional diagnosis data
organization: Fraunhofer Institute for Algorithms and Scientific Computing (SCAI); University of Bonn; Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School; Boehringer Ingelheim

evidence.tested: The trajectory groups were externally validated and independently replicated in a 2,779-person dementia cohort.
evidence.unknown: These are prognostic progression groups, not established biological disease subtypes or treatment-response predictors. The classifier had modest external discrimination (AUC 0.70 ± 0.01). Trial-size reduction and cost savings were estimated by emulating hypothetical enrichment and were not demonstrated in an actual clinical trial. The study does not show improved patient outcomes.
evidence.ai_role: Deep learning grouped patients using multivariate disease trajectories; the authors then trained a classifier to predict those progression subgroups from measurements available at diagnosis. The model-supported fast/slow progression groups were externally validated and independently replicated in a separate dementia cohort.

title: Deep-learning histopathology identifies tertiary lymphoid structure features linked to stage II colorectal cancer relapse
summary: SurvFinder analyzed 6,950 H&E slides from 1,604 stage II colorectal cancer patients across four cohorts and identified tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) as prognostic tissue features. Its multi-view model integrated TLS morphology and spatial location; explainable analysis highlighted TLS maturity and position near the tumor periphery as features associated with relapse-free survival and adjuvant-chemotherapy outcome patterns across the retrospective datasets.
ai_technology: SurvFinder, a multi-component deep-learning pipeline: WSINet for prognosis-associated tissue features, SegNet for TLS segmentation/subtyping, and MVNet for multi-view risk prediction
organization: Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center; Sun Yat-sen University; Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital; Johns Hopkins University; Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center

evidence.tested: SurvFinder analyzed 6,950 H&E slides from 1,604 stage II colorectal cancer patients across four cohorts and identified tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) as prognostic tissue features.
evidence.unknown: This was a retrospective analysis of patients enrolled in 2012–2018; results do not establish prospective clinical utility. Associations between predicted risk, TLS features and adjuvant-chemotherapy outcomes are observational and do not prove treatment benefit or that TLS features causally determine relapse. The authors identify absence of prospective validation and real-world deployment as limitations.
evidence.ai_role: Deep learning autonomously identified prognosis-associated tissue features in whole-slide images, segmented and subtyped TLSs, and integrated morphological and spatial features for risk prediction. Explainable-AI attribution identified TLS location near the tumor margin and TLS maturity state as important prognostic features.

title: Machine learning identifies new CYP2C9-inhibiting drugs and drug metabolites
summary: A structure-, dynamics- and physicochemical-feature machine-learning approach predicted CYP2C9 inhibition and experimentally identified four drugs—vatalanib, piriqualone, ticagrelor and cloperidone—as strong inhibitors, plus sertindole, asapiprant, duvelisib and dasatinib as moderate inhibitors in reported assays. Vatalanib had a reported CYP2C9 inhibition IC50 of 0.067 μM. Separate metabolism assays characterized CYP2C9-produced metabolites for abemaciclib, cloperidone, vatalanib and tarafenacin.
ai_technology: Machine-learning inhibitor predictors combining CYP2C9 structural/dynamics information with inhibitor physicochemical properties
organization: INSERM; CNRS and Université de Paris; Conservatoire National des Arts et Métiers; Université de Lorraine; Nantes Université

evidence.tested: A structure-, dynamics- and physicochemical-feature machine-learning approach predicted CYP2C9 inhibition and experimentally identified four drugs—vatalanib, piriqualone, ticagrelor and cloperidone—as strong inhibitors, plus sertindole, asapiprant, duvelisib and dasatinib as moderate inhibitors in reported assays.
evidence.unknown: Inhibition and metabolite findings are from the reported in vitro systems and do not by themselves establish clinically relevant drug–drug interactions, exposure changes, or patient harm. Reported inhibition strengths are assay-specific; clinical relevance depends on dose, exposure and context and requires pharmacokinetic/clinical assessment.
evidence.ai_role: The authors used machine-learning models to prioritize drug-like compounds for CYP2C9 inhibition testing. Follow-up in vitro assays identified the listed strong and moderate inhibitors; CYP2C9 metabolism assays separately characterized metabolites of four drugs.

title: Deep learning enables multi-site bone marrow adiposity genetics in UK Biobank
summary: Deep learning measured bone marrow fat fraction at four skeletal sites in UK Biobank MRI data; after quality control, 48,608 participants contributed to genome-wide analyses. In the white-participant meta-GWAS, the study reported 67, 147, 134 and 174 independent significant variants for femoral head, total hip, femoral diaphysis and spine, mapping to 54, 90, 43 and 100 genes, respectively. Analyses also identified site- and sex-specific genetic associations and added signals in multi-ancestry analyses.
ai_technology: Previously validated deep-learning models for MRI segmentation and bone marrow fat-fraction measurement
organization: University of Edinburgh; University of Lille; Heriot-Watt University; University of Southern Denmark; University of Dundee; University of Southern Denmark and collaborating UK Biobank institutions

evidence.tested: Deep learning measured bone marrow fat fraction at four skeletal sites in UK Biobank MRI data; after quality control, 48,608 participants contributed to genome-wide analyses.
evidence.unknown: The GWAS, transcriptome-wide and colocalization results are statistical associations and candidate gene mappings, not proof of causal mechanisms. Ancestry subgroup sizes differ, and results do not establish clinical utility or disease prevention. The deep-learning measurement method was established in an earlier study; this record concerns the distinct population-scale phenotype and genetic findings. A 2025 author correction fixed a misspelling of AKNA as ANKA; it did not alter the reported analysis or findings.
evidence.ai_role: The study applied deep-learning models to segment four skeletal regions and derive bone marrow fat-fraction phenotypes at UK Biobank scale. Those AI-derived measurements were the phenotypes used in the study's subsequent genetic association analyses; the paper's genetic findings are not themselves outputs of a generative model.

title: Deep learning maps previously unknown disease signals in ECGs across two health systems
summary: Researchers independently trained PheWASNet on ECG and electronic health-record data from Stanford Health Care and Cedars-Sinai to assess 1,243 disease phenotypes. In held-out patient splits at both centers, the study reported previously unrecognized ECG associations for disorders including respiratory failure, neutropenia and menstrual disorders (AUCs 0.86, 0.83 and 0.84 at Stanford, respectively). Cross-condition model-output analysis found that 35 of 37 strongly detectable non-cardiac phenotypes shared signals with only four other disease outputs, and simple ECG measurement models explained some findings.
ai_technology: PheWASNet, a multi-task deep-learning model based on a one-dimensional EfficientNet architecture
organization: Stanford University; Cedars-Sinai Medical Center; University of California, Los Angeles

evidence.tested: In held-out patient splits at both centers, the study reported previously unrecognized ECG associations for disorders including respiratory failure, neutropenia and menstrual disorders (AUCs 0.86, 0.83 and 0.84 at Stanford, respectively).
evidence.unknown: This retrospective EHR-linked study establishes model-detectable associations, not causal physiology, screening benefit or clinical utility. The disease labels are diagnostic codes associated with ECGs within 30 days; results may reflect comorbidity or care context. The authors caution that generalization to other health systems and populations is not assured. Some detectable signals were explained by simple conventional ECG measurements, and the paper does not claim that deep learning is required for every association.
evidence.ai_role: The researchers trained separate deep-learning models on raw 12-lead ECG waveforms linked to EHR diagnoses at two medical centers, then used held-out patient test sets to identify disease phenotypes whose signals were detectable from ECGs. Cross-phenotype prediction comparisons and simple-model analyses were used to characterize shared and interpretable signals.

title: Machine learning finds plasma protein signals up to 14 years before Parkinson diagnosis
summary: Using UK Biobank measurements of 2,937 plasma proteins, researchers found 446 dysregulated proteins in incident Parkinson cases and used machine learning to select a 23-protein panel for prediction. The panel achieved test AUCs of 0.78 in incident and 0.795 in prevalent cases; nine selected proteins were already dysregulated 10–14 years before diagnosis. In a separate Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative cohort, a 16-protein subset shared between platforms achieved validation AUC up to 0.76.
ai_technology: Support vector machine and other machine-learning models, with recursive feature elimination for panel selection
organization: Johnson & Johnson; UK Biobank; Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative collaborators

evidence.tested: Using UK Biobank measurements of 2,937 plasma proteins, researchers found 446 dysregulated proteins in incident Parkinson cases and used machine learning to select a 23-protein panel for prediction.
evidence.unknown: The result is a retrospective biomarker/prediction study, not a validated screening test or evidence that intervention based on the panel improves outcomes. The external PPMI analysis retrained and tested models in that cohort rather than evaluating a frozen UK Biobank model; validation AUCs varied by visit definition, and the reported maximum was 0.76. Protein associations and co-expression modules do not establish causal mechanisms. It is distinct from the earlier 2024 iRBD study in this ledger (DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-48961-3): separate cohorts and a different 23-protein/14-year result versus an eight-protein targeted panel and up-to-seven-year conversion finding; this record does not claim first discovery of presymptomatic plasma signals in Parkinson disease.
evidence.ai_role: Machine-learning classifiers were trained on UK Biobank plasma proteomic measurements to predict incident Parkinson disease; recursive feature elimination selected a 23-protein subset. The authors then tested the shared protein subset in the separate PPMI cohort using its own train/test split.

title: Machine learning and tear-fluid proteomics identify a six-protein ALS signature
summary: In discovery samples from 49 people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and 54 controls, mass spectrometry detected 876 tear-fluid proteins, of which 106 differed in abundance. Biostatistical and machine-learning analyses produced a six-protein signature (CRYM, PFKL, CAPZA2, ALDH16A1, SERPINC1 and HP). In an independent cohort of 51 ALS cases and 52 controls, Western blots replicated significant group differences for SERPINC1 and HP; their combination had the best reported in-silico discrimination.
ai_technology: Machine-learning models applied to data-independent acquisition mass-spectrometry proteomics and biomarker-panel discrimination
organization: Technical University of Munich; Helmholtz Munich; Ludwig-Maximilians University of Munich; University of Melbourne; University Medical Center Göttingen; Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences; German Center for Neurodegenerative Diseases

evidence.tested: In an independent cohort of 51 ALS cases and 52 controls, Western blots replicated significant group differences for SERPINC1 and HP; their combination had the best reported in-silico discrimination.
