This is an exploratory association in a small epilepsy-monitoring sample; the AI-derived ratings were not validated against human ratings or independently replicated, and do not establish causality.
ai_technology: GPT-5 large language model used to score free-text participant reports on ten cognitive dimensions
organization: The University of Osaka; The University of Tokyo; Juntendo University

evidence.tested: In nine participants undergoing intracranial EEG monitoring, GPT-5 scored reports from neurofeedback sessions; model-derived feedback-monitoring scores were associated with hippocampal ripple rates after adjustment for cognitive condition.
evidence.unknown: Only nine participants; no independent replication or human-rating comparison validated the GPT-5 scores. Prompt/model dependence and causal direction remain unresolved.
evidence.ai_role: GPT-5 converted short free-text reports into ten structured cognitive-dimension scores; the feedback-monitoring score was the only one of ten dimensions associated with ripple rate after FDR correction.

source_review.scope: Full 30-page Research Square v1 primary preprint, including Methods pp.18–19 and Results figure legend p.30, plus abstract and source metadata.

title: AlphaFold 3-guided mutagenesis identifies a candidate substrate-orienting enzyme residue
summary: For an enzyme studied in a plant natural-product pathway, the authors used an AlphaFold 3 structure model with substrate docking and molecular-dynamics analysis to nominate candidate pocket residues. Mutational tests found that replacing one predicted aromatic residue abolished measured activity, while a conservative aromatic substitution restored activity, supporting a role in substrate orientation. This is a bounded residue-level mechanistic result: the authors report that the mutations do not establish a comprehensive mechanism and the predicted protein and complex structures were not experimentally characterized.
ai_technology: AlphaFold 3 structure prediction with substrate docking and molecular-dynamics-guided residue selection
organization: Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology; University of Georgia; Max Planck Institute for Plant Breeding Research

evidence.tested: AlphaFold 3 structure modeling, putative-substrate docking and molecular-dynamics analysis nominated candidate residues; targeted mutations directly tested their contribution to activity. One aromatic-residue substitution eliminated measured activity and a conservative aromatic substitution restored it.
evidence.unknown: The predicted protein and complex structures were not experimentally characterized; authors state the mutational analysis is not comprehensive. No independent replication is reported.
evidence.ai_role: AlphaFold 3 structure modeling plus docking and molecular-dynamics analysis guided selection of residues for mutational testing, supporting a specific hypothesis about substrate orientation. The model was a guide to experiments, not an experimental structure or a complete mechanistic proof.

source_review.scope: Indexed primary publisher Results describing AlphaFold3-guided residue selection and mutational test, structural/mechanistic caveats, publication/version date and affiliations. No experimental reproduction.

title: Neural segmentation reveals persistent postsynaptic-density enlargement after potentiation
summary: In hippocampal slice neurons, StarDist neural-network segmentation identified postsynaptic densities for tracking over 16 hours. After CaMKII photoactivation, postsynaptic densities and spine heads enlarged rapidly; density enlargement persisted at 14 hours while spine-head expansion lasted about 6 hours. The original result was publicly posted on April 11, 2026, followed by a peer-reviewed version on November 20. The journal analysis included 6 activated and 5 control slice cultures, with thousands of nested synaptic measurements. Models were trained on a small manually annotated tile set and visually checked; held-out segmentation accuracy and independent replication were not reported.
ai_technology: StarDist convolutional neural network for star-convex image segmentation, adapted to PSD microscopy
organization: University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf

evidence.tested: StarDist-based segmentation identified PSDs in activated and control hippocampal-slice microscopy time series, with 6 activated and 5 control slice cultures and 2,948/2,953 PSD objects in the reported comparison. The model-supported imaging showed PSD enlargement remained significant at 14 hours, whereas spine-head expansion lasted about 6 hours.
evidence.unknown: Only a small manually annotated tile set was used for model training; predictions were inspected/retrained, but a held-out segmentation-accuracy metric is not reported. PSD counts are repeated objects nested within 11 slice cultures, not independent biological replicates. No independent replication is reported.
evidence.ai_role: Custom StarDist neural-network models segmented PSD microscopy, followed by Mastodon temporal tracking and fluorescence-based quantification of PSD/spine changes. Learned segmentation contributed to the structural time course; separate electrophysiological pathway results were not produced by this model.

source_review.scope: Actual bioRxiv v1 and journal full text: StarDist training/segmentation and Mastodon tracking Methods, Fig1 and morphology time course, first-preprint posted date, journal sample counts/affiliation; original StarDist primary abstract for learned-model identity.

title: A latent-state model links acute psychedelic treatment to sensory-guided mouse decisions
summary: A fitted generalized-linear-model hidden Markov model identified sensory-engaged and history-biased choice states in a mouse perceptual-decision task. Acute psilocybin or ketamine shifted occupancy toward sensory-engaged states while increasing response time and accuracy. First posted in September 2025 and published in Science Advances in November 2026, the work used different cohorts across analyses; the final drug comparisons included 42 psilocybin and 30 ketamine mice. State-performance relationships were checked within the study. The experiment does not establish independent replication, human therapeutic benefits or a uniquely causal interpretation of the inferred states.
ai_technology: Generalized linear model hidden Markov model (GLM-HMM) for latent decision-strategy inference
organization: Boston University

evidence.tested: The final paper reports mouse drug cohorts of 42 for psilocybin and 30 for ketamine. Repeated-measures behavioral tests show improved accuracy and longer response times at relevant doses, and GLM-HMM analyses report increased sensory-engaged state occupancy. State-specific accuracy/response-time associations provide within-study construct checks.
evidence.unknown: Inferred state-performance relationships were assessed within the study; independent validation of the state shift was not established. Sample denominators differ across versions and analyses. This acute mouse task does not establish human therapeutic benefit or a uniquely causal explanation of the latent states.
evidence.ai_role: An expectation-maximization-fitted GLM-HMM inferred latent sensory-engaged and left/right-biased states from trial-by-trial choices. State occupancy under treatment directly supports the reported strategy shift. Drift-diffusion and the separate five-fold L1 neural decoder are distinct analyses; their validation is not attributed to the GLM-HMM.

source_review.scope: Original bioRxiv v1 full Results/Methods and posted date; final primary journal full Results, Figure2 drug sample sizes and GLM-HMM Methods; preprint/final titles and affiliations. State and neural-decoder analyses distinguished.

title: ColabFold-supported binding tests identify CDKL5 interactions with synaptic scaffolds
summary: A preprint first posted 28 August 2025 used ColabFold/AlphaFold modeling to support a proposed interaction between the neuronal CDKL5 isoform and a SHANK1 PDZ domain. Fluorescence-polarization and NMR experiments supported direct binding, while disrupting the terminal binding motif abolished it; the preprint reported an affinity of 8.5 micromolar. The November 2026 journal version reports 7.6 micromolar for the same interaction and further cellular/neuronal context. These are versions of one result. AI supported a structural interaction hypothesis; binding assays provide the direct evidence. The distinct talin-binding result is not attributed to AI here, and the work does not establish clinical effects or treatment for CDKL5 deficiency disorder.
ai_technology: ColabFold/AlphaFold protein-complex modeling of the CDKL5 C-terminal peptide and SHANK1 PDZ domain
organization: University of Liverpool; University of Helsinki

evidence.tested: ColabFold-supported PDZ-binding hypothesis tested by fluorescence polarization, NMR and disruption of the terminal binding motif, with tests of other synaptic PDZ domains. The 2025 v1 reported SHANK1 affinity 8.5 micromolar; the 2026 journal version reports 7.6 micromolar. Both support the same specific direct-binding finding.
evidence.unknown: No atomic-resolution experimental structure of the predicted complex or patient-derived/in vivo disease validation is reported. Neuronal localization and spine effects use transfected/overexpression systems and do not establish treatment or clinical outcomes. The paper also reports talin binding; that result is not attributed to AlphaFold here.
evidence.ai_role: ColabFold generated a complex model supporting a sequence/motif-based CDKL5–SHANK1 interaction hypothesis, which was tested with binding and perturbation assays. AI is not credited with the separate talin finding or clinical effects.

source_review.scope: Author-institutional bioRxivv1PDF header and relevant ColabFold/binding Results independently extracted/read; final primary article abstract and relevant Results, model-use reference and metadata independently read. Numerical versions distinguished; no clinical reanalysis.

follow_up.note: Peer-reviewed journal version of the same PDZ-binding result. The final article reports SHANK1 affinity 7.6 micromolar, versus 8.5 micromolar in preprint v1; this numerical revision is preserved rather than backdated.

title: Machine learning links gut microbial modules with inflammatory and clinical features of major depression
summary: A single-center cross-sectional study of 102 inpatients with major depression and 38 controls used machine-learning feature selection on gut-microbiome profiles to identify nine biologically annotated microbial modules. Random forest with recursive feature elimination selected genera, and module scores were associated with inflammation and symptom dimensions. Functional pathways were inferred from 16S data rather than directly measured, and the associations do not establish causality or clinical utility. The small cohort and in-sample symptom associations require independent replication.
ai_technology: Random forest with recursive feature elimination; PLS-based multivariate modeling
organization: Sichuan Provincial People’s Hospital; University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; Deakin University

evidence.tested: Cross-sectional comparison of 102 MDD inpatients and 38 matched controls; feature selection and train/test evaluation of microbial profiles and clinical phenome measures; random forest/PLS-based biomarker discovery.
evidence.unknown: No independent external replication established; inferred functional potential is not measured microbial activity, and cross-sectional associations cannot establish causal effects or clinical benefit.
evidence.ai_role: Random forest with recursive feature elimination selected a parsimonious genus set within training data; PLS-based modeling linked microbial profiles to clinical and inflammatory measures.

source_review.scope: Publisher article-in-press PDF: abstract, introduction, full analysis strategy, participant and sample methods, AI/ML pipeline, and results including module/phenome associations.

title: Gaussian-process analysis identifies active Au–Ir–Rh regions in a measured electrocatalyst library
summary: An autonomous electrochemical platform measured 966 areas across Au–Ir–Rh alloy libraries and used Gaussian-process active learning to map hydrogen-evolution activity. A noise-aware model, rerun retrospectively on the completed dataset, recovered the activity trend after 140 sampled areas and identified high-activity regions near Au30Ir20Rh50 and Au10Ir35Rh55. The approximately 15% measurement requirement is a retrospective result, and the tested library does not establish long-term catalyst stability or broader performance. This record describes the 30 May 2026 arXiv preprint; publisher-deposited metadata confirms a same-title journal version dated 20 November 2026.
ai_technology: Multi-output Gaussian-process regression and cost-aware active learning for SECCM
organization: Ruhr University Bochum

evidence.tested: Autonomous measurements of 966 areas supplied ground truth; a noise-aware multi-output Gaussian-process campaign was rerun retrospectively, with activity-map predictions assessed after 140 sampled areas.
evidence.unknown: Long-term catalyst stability, external replication and transfer beyond the tested alloy library and conditions are not established by the reviewed material. Final journal full text was inaccessible; its deposited abstract matches the represented result.
evidence.ai_role: Active learning guides measurement selection during autonomous electrochemical screening and predicts composition–activity trends from partial measurements; it is directly linked to finding high-activity Au–Ir–Rh compositions.

source_review.scope: Original arXiv preprint full text: active-learning operation, completed measurement campaign, retrospective noise-aware rerun, composition/activity results; arXiv version metadata and publisher-deposited journal title/abstract/authors/date.

title: Geo-AI mapping reveals contrasting land cover and heat patterns across four Indonesian cities
summary: A Research Square preprint used Random Forest classification of 2025 satellite imagery to compare land cover, surface temperature and topographic wetness in four Indonesian cities. It found built-up land dominated Surakarta and Yogyakarta, while vegetation dominated Padang and Malang; Yogyakarta had the highest mean surface temperature in the analyzed scenes. Classification was checked using 200 higher-resolution-image reference points, with reported overall accuracy of 92.5–94.5%. These snapshot associations do not establish causal urban-heating effects or observed benefits from the proposed green-space planning recommendations.
ai_technology: Random Forest land-cover classification
organization: University of Brawijaya; Andalas University; State University of Malang; Bandung Institute of Technology

evidence.tested: Random Forest land-cover classification compared with 200 reference points from higher-resolution Google satellite imagery (50 per class); overall accuracy 92.5–94.5% and Kappa 90–93%. LULC classifications were combined with Landsat surface temperature and SRTM-based TWI analyses for four Indonesian cities using 2025 imagery.
evidence.unknown: Only four cities and 2025 scenes were analyzed; validation used 50 reference points per land-cover class. The proposed green-space allocation and heat/runoff implications have not been validated through observed planning or intervention outcomes.
evidence.ai_role: Random Forest classification provides the land-cover maps used to quantify urbanization and compare those patterns with satellite-derived surface temperature and terrain wetness across four cities.

source_review.scope: Source-provenanced original Research Square v1 full PDF/text: posting metadata, affiliations, learned operation, validation design, reported result and limitations.

title: Bayesian modeling estimates configuration-dependent uncertainty in printed PLA bending
summary: A Research Square preprint trained a Bayesian physics-informed neural network on bending data from 60 groups of printed PLA specimens and combined it with finite-element simulation. In ten within-study validation configurations, predicted uncertainty varied by raster angle and infill, with the 60-degree and reduced-infill configurations exceeding twice the estimated variation of the 0-degree configuration. All ten experimental validation values lay within the reported 95% intervals, but the sample is too small to establish precise uncertainty calibration. The result is limited to the studied printer, material and bending conditions, without separate-team replication or demonstrated service reliability.
ai_technology: Bayesian physics-informed neural network with Monte Carlo dropout embedded in finite-element analysis
organization: Amirkabir University of Technology

evidence.tested: The PINN was developed from experimental data for 60 FDM polylactic-acid specimen groups, with ten independent configurations evaluated. Reported R² was 0.9935, MAPE 1.85%, and 95% confidence intervals contained all ten experimental validation values. Reliability analysis estimated coefficient-of-variation uncertainty of 3.8–9.0% across configurations and corresponding safety factors of 1.11–1.30.
evidence.unknown: The ten configurations are within-study validation, not a separate-team replication. Sample size is limited; the results do not establish transfer to other printers, materials, component geometries, or load/service conditions.
evidence.ai_role: A physics-constrained neural network with Monte Carlo dropout estimates flexural-modulus distributions; sampled moduli are propagated through finite-element simulations to estimate configuration-dependent prediction uncertainty.

source_review.scope: Source-provenanced original Research Square v1 full PDF/text: posting metadata, affiliations, learned operation, validation design, reported result and limitations.

title: Machine-learning feature selection identifies student-performance factors in Nepal
summary: A study analyzed 1,021 survey responses from engineering students reflecting on their first year at colleges affiliated with Tribhuvan University in Nepal. A feature-selection vote including Random Forest and AdaBoost selected 21 candidate academic, psychometric and demographic factors, triangulated with 11 focus-group themes and expert review. The reported set included adaptation, motivation, residence and travel-time factors alongside academic measures. These context-dependent selections do not establish causal effects, externally validated predictive performance or transfer beyond the sampled institution system.
ai_technology: Random Forest and AdaBoost within a multi-method feature-selection vote
organization: Tribhuvan University

evidence.tested: Survey data contained 1,021 valid responses; quantitative feature selection used a voting threshold of three and produced 21 features, which were triangulated with 11 focus-group themes and expert review. Fourteen selected features were academic, four psychometric and three demographic.
evidence.unknown: Single-context sample from IOE-affiliated Tribhuvan University colleges; qualitative collection may contain bias; the authors explicitly say the selected determinants are not causal. No external prediction-performance validation is reported.
evidence.ai_role: Random Forest and AdaBoost were included in a multi-method feature-selection vote used to derive the reported student-performance correlates; qualitative focus-group themes and expert review were then used to triangulate them.

source_review.scope: Original journal PDF: posting and peer-review metadata, cohort/data collection, six-method feature-selection vote, triangulation, result categories and conclusions.

title: Patient-level tests evaluate a quantum-inspired transformer model for breast ultrasound lesion classification
summary: A classical GAN/vision-transformer system jointly segmented breast-ultrasound lesions and classified malignancy in two public clinical-image datasets. The paper reports patient-level separation and bidirectional BUSI/UDIAT cross-dataset F1 scores of 97.14% and 96.81%. This is retrospective evaluation of existing images, and the authors state that actual clinical conditions were not reproduced. Larger heterogeneous clinical populations and prospective workflow evaluation are needed; the quantum-inspired components do not establish physical quantum computation or advantage.
ai_technology: Quantum-inspired generative adversarial segmentation with a vision-transformer classification head
organization: Hindusthan Institute of Technology

evidence.tested: Patient-level validation on BUSI and UDIAT public breast-ultrasound image datasets, including cross-dataset testing in both directions; publisher reports cross-dataset F1 97.14% and 96.81%.
evidence.unknown: Prospective workflow performance, external validation by independent investigators, performance on larger and more heterogeneous populations, and clinical utility.
evidence.ai_role: Learned GAN image segmentation and a ViT classification head were evaluated on held-out patient images; the source explicitly describes the quantum-inspired components as classical operations, not physical quantum computation.

source_review.scope: Publisher Article in Press PDF: dataset and patient-level split methods, architecture and learned operations, cross-dataset validation results, limitations and data-availability statement.

title: Multimodal language models extract seizure semiology and support patient-held-out seizure classification
summary: An October 2025 preprint analyzed 90 video-EEG-confirmed events from 29 patients at one epilepsy-monitoring unit using vision-language and audio-language models to extract clinical features. With leave-one-patient-out testing, KNN using automated features achieved F1 and AUC of 0.76, below the classifier using expert features. Automated feature extraction itself had mean F1 of 0.51 against expert annotations, and the small retrospective cohort does not establish clinical utility or external generalization. A later journal version was dated November 2026; the detailed results here describe the accessible preprint.
ai_technology: InternVL vision-language models and Qwen audio/vision-language models with downstream KNN and other classifiers
organization: University of California, Los Angeles; University of Alabama at Birmingham

evidence.tested: Ninety video-EEG-confirmed events from 29 patients; open-source vision/audio-language feature extraction and leave-one-patient-out ES/NES classification. Automated-feature KNN F1/AUC were0.76, and feature extraction meanF1 was0.51 versus experts; all results are from the accessible preprint.
evidence.unknown: External multicenter performance, prospective clinical workflow utility and improvement in patient outcomes are unestablished. Detailed final-journal methods/results were not independently read.
evidence.ai_role: Vision-language and audio-language models extract clinical seizure semiology from patient video/audio; classifier evaluation shows moderate patient-held-out discrimination between video-EEG-confirmed epileptic and nonepileptic events.

source_review.scope: Europe PMC XML full text of medRxiv preprint, including methods, patient cohort, MLLM operations, LOPO protocol and results; publisher-deposited final journal abstract and DOI date metadata.

title: GWAS identifies a functional MSTN variant associated with higher lean mass in humans
summary: A genome-wide association meta-analysis of DXA-derived lean mass in about 79,000 people identified 63 loci, including a rare MSTN variant associated with higher leg lean mass. Supervised deep residual convolutional networks imputed missing DXA/MRI image-derived phenotypes from raw images for UK Biobank association analyses; statistical GWAS and researcher-led assays supplied the genetic and functional evidence. The findings are observational, largely from European-ancestry participants, and do not establish clinical benefit from myostatin inhibition.
ai_technology: Supervised deep residual convolutional neural networks for DXA/MRI image-derived phenotype imputation
organization: deCODE genetics

evidence.tested: Deep residual convolutional networks were trained on labeled DXA/MRI images with an 80/20 train/validation split; imputed phenotypes were used in GWAS. The main association analysis used BOLT-LMM; the paper also reports functional characterization of MSTN p.Ile225Thr.
evidence.unknown: The paper does not establish causal clinical benefit from myostatin inhibition; imputed phenotypes and observational genetic associations have limitations.
evidence.ai_role: Supervised deep residual convolutional networks imputed missing image-derived phenotypes from raw DXA and MRI images, increasing phenotype availability for the GWAS; the genetic association model and functional assays were separate statistical and experimental analyses.

source_review.scope: Publisher abstract, Results, UK Biobank imaging-processing Methods, Discussion limitations and publication metadata.

title: Learned expert skills improve shared control in a CT-guided biopsy robot
summary: A CT-guided biopsy robot used a variational autoencoder–hidden Markov model and dynamic motion primitives to learn procedural phases and trajectories from expert demonstrations. Its shared controller reduced interaction forces and targeting errors relative to manual, leader–follower and admittance control in phantom and rabbit experiments, with nine experiments per strategy; porcine work separately assessed robotic feasibility. These preclinical results do not establish safety or benefit in patients, and the learned skills came from a limited expert panel.
ai_technology: Variational autoencoder–hidden Markov model and dynamic motion primitives for expert-skill learning
organization: Shanghai Jiao Tong University

evidence.tested: Expert data were collected from a 31-doctor panel including ten experts. Phantom and rabbit control comparisons used nine experiments per strategy; porcine work assessed feasibility. Manual, leader–follower and admittance control were the comparators.
evidence.unknown: Clinical performance and patient benefit remain untested. Expert demonstrations and anatomical scenarios were limited, and phantom-to-living-tissue transfer remains a source-stated limitation.
evidence.ai_role: A variational autoencoder–hidden Markov model segmented latent procedural phases from expert skills; dynamic motion primitives reconstructed representative trajectories. These learned representations informed phase-adaptive shared control.

source_review.scope: Publisher abstract, robot/control Results, expert-skill learning Methods and Discussion limitations, with phantom, rabbit and porcine distinctions checked.

title: Artificial neural network analysis links immersion with self-efficacy in VR upper-limb training
summary: Artificial neural networks analyzed self-reports from 280 healthy adults who used a VR upper-limb training system. With ten-fold cross-validation, the ANN analysis ranked immersion above learning motivation as a predictor of task-specific self-efficacy, while linear structural-equation analysis ranked learning motivation higher. This preprint reports associations in young adults from one city, without causal evidence or rehabilitation outcomes.
ai_technology: Artificial neural networks with 10-fold cross-validation
organization: Fujian University of Technology

evidence.tested: ANN models used immersion, learning motivation, interactive experience, and perceived incentives to predict affective trust and task-specific self-efficacy; the study reports 10-fold cross-validation and RMSE. The underlying data are self-reports from 280 users.
evidence.unknown: All participants had normal upper-limb function, were aged 18–35 and came from one city. No causal effect or clinical rehabilitation improvement was tested. The manuscript inconsistently describes the system as immersive/non-immersive.
evidence.ai_role: The ANN analysis modeled nonlinear relationships among survey constructs and identified immersion as the strongest predictor of task-specific self-efficacy, complementing PLS-SEM and necessary configuration analysis.

source_review.scope: Research Square v1 full-text PDF: abstract, participant Methods, ANN analysis, cross-validation and limitations; Crossref version/publication metadata.

title: Cohort audit finds unstable performance in efferocytosis-related prognostic scores
summary: A retrospective audit rebuilt an efferocytosis-related head-and-neck-cancer prognostic analysis in 519 primary tumors after detecting non-primary rows in the original cohort. A Cox-LASSO workflow selected a nine-gene sensitivity score, but its exact composition recurred in none of 500 full-pipeline bootstrap samples and repeated nested cross-validation yielded a mean C-index of 0.587. Survival associations persisted in some analyses while external performance was inconsistent, and a fixed cutoff did not transfer. The authors treat both this reconstruction and the historical six-gene score as hypotheses, with overlapping prior cohorts, no demonstrated causal mechanism and no established clinical utility.
ai_technology: Cox LASSO prognostic scoring
organization: Loudi Central Hospital

evidence.tested: Retrospective prognostic-score audit in TCGA-HNSC primary tumors (n=519), two external cohorts, full-pipeline bootstrap (500 resamples), repeated nested cross-validation, and donor-aware single-cell analyses.
evidence.unknown: No prospective clinical or experimental validation; the nine-gene signature was unstable and a transportable threshold was not established. Public cohorts overlap with earlier work and are not independent sample-level replication.
evidence.ai_role: Cox-LASSO selected a nine-gene sensitivity score, while a locked six-gene score was audited. The model-based analysis is the clinical prognostic result; it does not establish causality or clinical utility.

source_review.scope: Primary publisher PDF: abstract, cohort definitions, Cox-LASSO Methods, bootstrap/nested-CV Results, external evaluation and limitations; publisher-deposited date metadata.

title: PLS-DA nominates exploratory serum-metabolite patterns in osteopenia
summary: Supervised PLS-DA and model-derived VIP feature scores helped nominate serum-metabolite patterns across bone-density groups in 220 adults. The study reported 30, 55 and 49 exploratory candidates for osteopenia versus controls, osteoporosis versus controls and osteoporosis versus osteopenia, using seven-fold cross-validation and permutation checks. All selected metabolites had FDR-adjusted q values above 0.05 and were retained under exploratory VIP, nominal-P and fold-change thresholds. The 135-person discovery and 85-person temporal replication groups came from one hospital; these findings do not establish prospective fracture prediction, external transport or clinical benefit.
ai_technology: Partial least-squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA)
organization: Wuhan Fourth Hospital; Wuchang University of Technology; Wuhan University; Fudan University

evidence.tested: PLS-DA group discrimination with seven-fold cross-validation and 200-permutation testing; VIP scores helped select exploratory serum-metabolite candidates across BMD groups.
evidence.unknown: All candidates had FDR-adjusted q>0.05; temporal replication was within the same hospital and study; no prospective fracture prediction, clinical benefit, or external transport was tested.
evidence.ai_role: Supervised PLS-DA learned separation between BMD groups; model-derived VIP scores contributed to candidate metabolite selection.

source_review.scope: Primary publisher PDF: abstract, cohort Methods, supervised PLS-DA training/VIP selection, cross-validation/permutation description, candidate q-value caveat and same-hospital temporal split.

title: IceCube DeepCore data constrain long-range neutrino interactions
summary: First located in an arXiv version posted January 3, 2026, this study received a journal version on November 20 with revised event-score bins. It uses trained boosted-decision-tree scores from IceCube’s pre-applied classification pipeline to group released DeepCore events for oscillation fits. Analyzing eight years of atmospheric-neutrino data, the authors find no evidence for the tested long-range interactions and report constraints on their coupling strengths. The result depends on the specified physical hypotheses and experimental systematics; the classifier identifies event topology and was not newly trained by these authors.
ai_technology: IceCube-pipeline boosted decision tree particle-identification classifier
organization: Institute of Physics, Bhubaneswar; Aligarh Muslim University; Homi Bhabha National Institute

evidence.tested: The arXiv v1 and peer-reviewed article analyze the released eight-year IceCube DeepCore high-purity νμ charged-current sample. The source describes a trained boosted decision tree that calculates a tracklike particle-identification score; the score defines mixed/tracklike event bins used in the fits. The published version reports constraints and no evidence for long-range interactions.
evidence.unknown: The search found no evidence for long-range interactions. Results depend on the released sample, detector/flux/cross-section systematics, and the tested interaction hypotheses. The paper states that the event sample selection/reconstruction procedures were already applied by IceCube and that the sample was used without modification; the evidence does not establish that these authors trained a new classifier for this paper.
evidence.ai_role: A trained boosted decision tree in the IceCube event-classification pipeline supplied particle-identification scores representing event tracklikeness. The study used these scores to define event-topology bins for its forward-folded oscillation fits. The study reused the IceCube golden-event sample without modification; do not attribute fresh model training to the paper’s authors.

source_review.scope: Official arXiv API identity and posting date; arXiv v1 and APS publisher PDFs, including abstracts, BDT particle-identification/binning Methods, main constraint results and conclusions.

title: Human-trained neural model predicts regulatory maps across 447 mammalian genomes
summary: Using an experimentally mapped human atlas of 5.33 million regulatory elements from 4,159 samples, researchers trained a cell-context-informed neural sequence model. It predicted cell-selective accessibility, generalized to observed mouse data and was applied to predict regulatory activity across 447 mammalian genomes. The human atlas was measured experimentally, while the broad cross-species maps remain computational predictions without validation in every species. Zenodo metadata dates this preprint November 20, 2026; the version record was created November 21, which does not establish a November 20 archive posting.
ai_technology: LegNet-based convolutional sequence model with transcription-factor-repertoire cell-context embeddings
organization: Altius Institute for Biomedical Sciences

evidence.tested: Sequence model assessed on held-out human biosamples, unseen ATAC-seq samples and mouse data; model reportedly identified the highest-activity cell type for ~85% of cell-selective DHSs.
evidence.unknown: Predictions are not experimentally confirmed in all 447 species. Concept DOI10.5281/zenodo.24208043 and version DOI10.5281/zenodo.24208044 describe the same work; metadata publication date2026-11-20 differs from archive-record creation2026-11-21.
evidence.ai_role: Deep-learning sequence-to-activity model, trained on the Atlas, predicts cell-selective regulatory DNA actuation from sequence and generalizes the predictions to mammalian genomes.

source_review.scope: Primary Zenodo version PDF: abstract, cell-context model Results, cross-species inference, LegNet-based Methods/training and limitations; Zenodo/DataCite identity, version and publication metadata.

title: AlphaFold homodimer predictions link truncation to different interface outcomes
summary: The May 9, 2026 preprint version compared 5,168 canonical/truncated human homodimer prediction pairs using AlphaFold-Multimer structures and interface-confidence scores. Among 234 pairs with high-confidence canonical homodimers, it classified 132 as conserved, 61 as interface-ablated and 41 as partially destabilized. These are computational classifications, without biochemical or cellular confirmation of the specific dimers. The later deposited abstract retains these headline proportions but revises interpretations of apparent interface emergence; those emergence and disorder claims are outside this entry.
ai_technology: AlphaFold Database; AlphaFold-Multimer
organization: Istanbul University

evidence.tested: Computational comparison of 5168 AlphaFold-predicted canonical/truncated homodimer pairs, including confidence-tier classifications and within-study robustness analyses; the represented three-class counts refer to the234 high-confidence canonical pairs.
evidence.unknown: No binding-affinity, cellular-complex or biochemical confirmation is established for individual predicted dimers. The later deposited abstract changes interpretation of apparent emergence; this entry represents only the common core classes documented in the May9v1.
evidence.ai_role: AlphaFold-Multimer predicts/scored homodimer interfaces; comparisons of canonical and truncated-isoform structures yield the represented interface classes.

source_review.scope: May9v1 primary PDF abstract, Results class counts, AlphaFold-Multimer Methods and limitations; comparison with current publisher-deposited Crossref abstract to bound version-dependent claims.

title: Cholesterol dysregulation contributes to hematopoietic failure in PARN-mutant zebrafish
summary: Researchers found expanded hematopoietic stem/progenitor populations and reduced mature blood cells in PARN-loss zebrafish; cholesterol-pathway inhibition rescued expansion and anemia, and cholesterol-pathway activation was also observed in patient-derived iPSCs. Ilastik interactive machine learning generated image probability maps, followed by CellProfiler/Otsu segmentation, to quantify blood-lineage staining and cell counts supporting the phenotype and treatment comparisons. This AI role concerned image-based measurement; pathway identification and rescue conclusions also relied on experimental and transcriptomic assays. The treatment findings remain preclinical, and the iPSC observations do not establish patient benefit.
ai_technology: Ilastik interactive machine learning for bioimage analysis
organization: CHEO Research Institute; University of Ottawa

evidence.tested: Ilastik probability maps plus CellProfiler segmentation were used to quantify WISH/o-dianisidine staining and distinguish labeled-cell counts in zebrafish hematopoietic phenotyping; biological rescue results were experimentally tested in PARN-loss zebrafish and pathway activation was recapitulated in patient-derived iPSCs.
evidence.unknown: Not stated in the reviewed Image analyses Methods: the incremental effect of ML segmentation versus manual/non-ML quantification. Clinical treatment benefit is not established by the zebrafish rescue and patient-derived iPSC experiments.
evidence.ai_role: Interactive ML image segmentation measured stained/fluorescent blood-lineage markers and cell counts that support the PARN-mutant hematopoietic phenotype; it was not used to identify the cholesterol pathway.

source_review.scope: Publisher article abstract; selected hematopoietic phenotype, cholesterol/rescue Results; Image analyses Methods; author affiliations. Supplementary material was not reviewed.

title: Predicted enzyme structures support shared substrate gates in C-glycosylation
summary: Analysis of structural models for 56 C-active UGT enzymes found acceptor gates throughout the set and two enzymes lacking a discernible donor gate; AlphaFold3 and source-labeled RobettaFold models supported variable open/closed gate conformations. These predictions extended a gating hypothesis derived from experimental structures and molecular simulations, rather than independently measuring dynamics across all enzymes. For maize ZmUGT708A6, crystallography, biochemical/mutational tests and QM/MM calculations supported a stepwise C-glycosylation mechanism involving water-mediated stabilization of a high-energy sigma complex. The AI contribution concerns comparison of predicted gate architectures; direct mechanistic tests focused on selected enzymes and substrates.
ai_technology: AlphaFold 3; RobettaFold
organization: Freie Universität Berlin; Technical University of Denmark

evidence.tested: The predicted gate conformations were compared across 56 UGT models; mechanistic propositions were tested with crystallography, biochemical assays, mutational data, QM/MM and pH/substrate activity experiments.
evidence.unknown: Predicted conformations across the 56 enzymes are not direct measurements of their dynamics. Supplementary model-generation details were not assessed here; the reviewed experimental/mechanistic scope centers on selected enzymes and substrates.
evidence.ai_role: AlphaFold3 and source-labeled RobettaFold structural models were compared to assess gate architecture/conformational variability across 56 C-active UGTs; experimental structures and simulations established the core gating/mechanistic hypothesis.

source_review.scope: Publisher article abstract; selected gate-architecture and reaction-mechanism Results; computational/crystallographic Methods; contributions and affiliations. Supplementary model-generation material was not reviewed.

title: Neural-potential simulations clarify a phosphonium/HFIP catalyst for CO2 conversion
summary: Researchers synthesized phosphonium-salt/HFIP catalysts for converting CO2 and epoxides into cyclic carbonates, reporting yields of 86–96% for monosubstituted and 66–88% for disubstituted epoxides at 25 °C and 1 atm CO2. Matlantis PFP v5.0.0, a trained neural interatomic potential, sampled the liquid-mixture structure; radial-distribution analysis supported strong association between HFIP and bromide. The calculated density differed from experiment by about 5%, while NMR and conventional DFT calculations provided complementary structural/mechanistic evidence. AI supported characterization of the new catalytic system; catalyst preparation and performance were experimentally established.
ai_technology: Matlantis Preferred Potential Framework (PFP) v5.0.0, TeaNet-inspired neural network interatomic potential
organization: University of Alicante; University of Almería; University of Salerno; University of Camerino

evidence.tested: Catalytic performance was experimentally measured across phosphonium/HFIP mixtures and multiple epoxide substrates. PFP neural-potential molecular dynamics modeled the DES organization; DFT and NMR provided complementary mechanistic evidence.
evidence.unknown: The approximately5% density discrepancy limits the model check; no uncertainty-calibrated validation of every simulated intermolecular feature was assessed. AI supplied mechanistic support rather than autonomous catalyst selection, and external replication was not reviewed.
evidence.ai_role: The learned PFP potential predicts energies for atomic configurations and enabled molecular-dynamics sampling of catalytic-mixture structure and intermolecular organization, supporting the hydrogen-bond mechanism interpretation.

source_review.scope: Primary ACS Omega full-text XML via Europe PMC: abstract; catalyst-mixture organization and density/RDF Results; computational Methods4.8–4.9; publication dates and author affiliations. Supplementary material not reviewed.

title: Sonopet aspirates support genomic and epigenomic profiling of skull-base meningioma
summary: In a prospectively collected paired feasibility series of seven patients, Sonopet aspirate and standard-resection skull-base meningioma specimens produced comparable sequencing yield, read quality and tumor purity. Copy-number profiles were highly concordant (Lin’s CCC0.99;95% CI0.76–1.00), whereas somatic variant-burden agreement was weaker and imprecise (CCC0.53;95% CI−0.28–0.99); promoter methylation was closely correlated. Learned Dorado models interpreted nanopore sequence/modified-base signals, and the ClairS-TO neural ensemble called somatic variants for the comparison. This small specimen-feasibility study, partly funded by Stryker, does not establish improved patient outcomes or independent replication.
ai_technology: Dorado high-accuracy and modified-base models; ClairS-TO trained neural-network ensemble
organization: The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center; Mayo Clinic

evidence.tested: Prospective paired specimen comparison in seven patients. Copy-number concordance CCC 0.99 (95% CI 0.76–1.00); somatic SNV burden CCC 0.53 (95% CI −0.28–0.99); promoter methylation reported as closely correlated.
evidence.unknown: Somatic-variant agreement has wide uncertainty in seven patients; intratumoral heterogeneity is a possible explanation, not established here. Prospective specimen collection is not prospective clinical-outcome validation; separate replication and patient benefit were not assessed in this series.
evidence.ai_role: Dorado learned models base-called genomic and methylation signal; ClairS-TO trained neural networks estimated somatic variants, enabling the comparison of aspirate and resection profiles.

source_review.scope: Publisher article abstract; paired-specimen Methods; Dorado and ClairS-TO bioinformatic Methods; concordance Results; affiliations and funding/competing-interest declaration. Supplementary file not reviewed.

title: Physics-informed neural model predicts cervical cancer progression in retrospective cohorts
summary: Researchers at Vellore Institute of Technology report a physics-informed neural model for two-year progression-free survival prediction in cervical cancer, evaluated retrospectively in a 20,287-patient analytical cohort and two external Indian cohorts totaling 15,967 patients. The primary abstract reports internal time-dependent AUC 0.91 and external AUCs 0.87 and 0.86; the 2,663-patient 2023 temporal subset is included within the 3,043-patient held-out test set. Model-derived clusters with differing survival outcomes remain hypotheses requiring prospective validation. This source check covers the publisher abstract and publication metadata; it does not establish prospective patient benefit or causal biological mechanisms.
ai_technology: Physics-Informed Neural Surrogate Learning (PI-NSL), a neural model with a variational physics encoder, differentiable PDE solver and dynamic risk operator
organization: Vellore Institute of Technology

evidence.tested: Retrospective internal held-out and historical external evaluation of progression-free survival prediction; reported latent patient-cluster survival differences.
evidence.unknown: Prospective clinical benefit and causal interpretation of clusters are not established. Full-paper methods and supplements were not assessed in this bounded independent review; broad geographic transfer is not established by the reported Indian cohorts.
evidence.ai_role: PI-NSL uses neural representations constrained by a mechanistic PDE system to estimate patient-specific parameters and predict progression-free survival; its latent representations support the reported patient clustering.

source_review.scope: Publisher article-in-press abstract, affiliations and publication metadata; full paper not assessed by independent reviewer

title: Random forest classifies eight infant illnesses in a retrospective Bangladesh dataset
summary: A Daffodil International University study compares four supervised models on 2,552 infant health records covering eight illness categories, assembled from hospital records and caregiver reports in Bangladesh. The publisher abstract reports 99.22% accuracy and 99.04% macro F1 for an optimized random forest using a stratified 80:20 split, with cross-validation, bootstrap and calibration analyses. These are retrospective internal evaluation results; clinical deployment, independent external validation and improved caregiver or patient outcomes are not established by the reviewed abstract. This source check covers the publisher abstract and metadata.
ai_technology: Random forest; logistic regression; decision tree; XGBoost; SHAP
organization: Daffodil International University

evidence.tested: Retrospective internal 80:20 train–test evaluation of eight illness classes in 2,552 infant records, with cross-validation, bootstrap and calibration analyses; all figures source-reported.
evidence.unknown: Full methods were not assessed in this bounded review. Independent external performance, prospective utility and patient benefit are not established by the reviewed abstract.
evidence.ai_role: Supervised random forest learns classification from symptom and demographic variables; other classifiers provide comparisons and SHAP supports feature interpretation.

source_review.scope: Publisher abstract, affiliations, article type and publication metadata; full paper not assessed by independent reviewer

title: Machine learning and cell assays prioritize FASN in a smoking–male-infertility study
summary: Researchers at Meishan City Second People’s Hospital integrated three infertility transcriptomic datasets with network toxicology and used LASSO and support-vector-machine recursive feature elimination to prioritize candidate genes. The publisher abstract reports a genetic association between higher predicted FASN expression and male-infertility risk and increased FASN mRNA after cigarette-smoke-condensate exposure in mouse TM4 Sertoli cells. These findings nominate FASN for functional investigation; they do not show that FASN mediates smoke-induced reproductive injury or establish a treatment. This source check covers the publisher abstract, affiliations and publication metadata; full methods were not assessed.
ai_technology: LASSO; support vector machine recursive feature elimination (SVM-RFE)
organization: Meishan City Second People’s Hospital

evidence.tested: Transcriptomic candidate selection and MR/SMR genetic associations, plus a within-study RT-qPCR assay reporting increased FASN mRNA in mouse TM4 Sertoli cells after smoke-condensate exposure.
evidence.unknown: The source explicitly states that FASN-mediated smoke-induced injury is not established. Full-paper methods and supplements were not assessed; human causal mediation and therapeutic benefit are unestablished.
evidence.ai_role: LASSO and SVM-RFE select candidate genes from integrated target and transcriptomic features, helping prioritize FASN for genetic analyses and a bounded cell-expression test.

source_review.scope: Publisher abstract, affiliations, publication metadata and visible ethics/data statements; subscription full paper not assessed

title: Vocabulary app with Qwen tutoring shows a short-term score advantage in eight classes
summary: A twelve-week teaching study randomized four matched pairs of university tutorial classes to a vocabulary application or non-adaptive word lists. The application bundled Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct examples, wav2vec2.0 pronunciation feedback and rule-based review scheduling. Among 92 completers from 100 allocated students, class-adjusted posttest scores favored the application by 6.6 points on a 100-point test (95% CI 1.3–11.9). This is a prospective comparison of the complete instructional package, not an isolated effect of AI. Eight classes, repeated test items, complete-case analysis and no delayed-retention measure limit generalization.
ai_technology: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; wav2vec 2.0 speech model; VocabPilot EDU 2.1.4
organization: City University Malaysia

evidence.tested: March–June 2025 twelve-week application use after matched-pair class allocation, followed by week 12 testing. 100 students allocated, 92 analyzed (46 per condition); eight classes with four per arm. A class-random-intercept model estimated 6.6 points adjusted advantage, 95% CI 1.3–11.9, p=.022.
evidence.unknown: The complete package includes deterministic scheduling, mobile delivery, language-model dialogue and speech feedback; the contribution of each component was not isolated. Same-item pre/post testing, only eight clusters, attrition and self-reported control study time constrain inference. Long-term retention and transfer to broader language performance were not tested.
evidence.ai_role: A fixed named Qwen instruction model generated target-word examples/explanations, with output checks and instructor audits; a local wav2vec2.0 acoustic model supplied pronunciation practice feedback. The scheduling/recommendation rules themselves are not learned AI.

source_review.scope: Independently recovered 24-page primary publisher PDF; read allocation, named model/intervention, measures/procedure, reported adjusted results and limitations. Original article publication metadata and publisher indexed journal peer-review statement checked. No raw-data reanalysis.

title: EEG–fMRI feature fusion distinguishes CELF-defined language difficulty in a retrospective cohort
summary: Pairwise learned classifiers fused EEG microstate and fMRI-connectivity features to distinguish CELF-defined language difficulty from controls in 173 participants. The authors report 78.4% balanced accuracy under nested cross-validation with training-only feature selection. This is within-cohort discrimination, not a prospective screening result or evidence of a causal language mechanism. SHAP interpretation used an original non-nested model rather than the most frequent nested classifier. The main Methods body and complete fMRI preprocessing were unavailable in the reviewed publisher snapshot; subgroup counts do not fully describe the 173-person sample.
ai_technology: Random forest and Gaussian Naive Bayes feature fusion; nested classifier selection
organization: Beijing Technology and Business University; Beijing Wuzi University

evidence.tested: Complete primary abstract and Appendix C describe 173-person nested evaluation, training-only screening/FDR and inner selection across 4221 model/fusion configurations. Most frequent nested pair was RF+GaussianNB; full-sample balanced accuracy 78.4%.
evidence.unknown: Main Methods body, full fMRI preprocessing and hyperparameter grids not assessed. Listed age subgroups 5–17 sum to 165 versus 173 overall aged 5–21; exact remaining allocation not specified in the reviewed tables. External/prospective clinical performance, causal neural interpretation and benefit remain unestablished.
evidence.ai_role: Learned classifier pairs combine EEG and fMRI features; nested selection evaluates their ability to discriminate language-test-defined groups. Correlated features and SHAP attributions do not establish biological mechanisms.

source_review.scope: Independently read original publisher abstract and accessible acquisition/quality, nested-validation/permutation, adjustment and SHAP appendices, plus 10-page supplementary model/age tables. Main Materials/Methods body was absent; ordinary PDF route returned HTML. No full-main-paper review claimed.

title: Sensor LSTM predicts part dimensions in an injection-molding campaign
summary: A shared bidirectional LSTM with four regression heads predicted weight and dimensions from injection-molding sensor sequences. The campaign collected 132 molding cycles, with 124 retained for regression. On a selected 24-cycle comparison subset, the model reported average MAPE 0.27%. This is an evaluation on the study’s campaign, with epoch selection using held-out folds. Comparators used different evaluation units and protocols, so the reported errors do not establish general model superiority. Generalization across molds, materials, machines and production periods remains untested.
ai_technology: Bidirectional LSTM shared encoder with task-specific MLP regression heads
organization: Clemson University; University of Delaware; University of South Carolina

evidence.tested: Actual molded-part weight, length, width and thickness measurements in a controlled single-factor process campaign. LSTM evaluation used shuffled-cycle five-fold splits and retained each fold’s best epoch on that fold; the cross-method comparison used selected cycles and separate setting-level DOE evaluation.
evidence.unknown: Fold-based epoch selection and selected comparison cycles limit untouched-test interpretation. The protocols/units differ across comparators, so average MAPE 0.27% versus 0.95%/2.03% is not a matched-protocol estimate of universal superiority. No independent production deployment or broader process transfer is established.
evidence.ai_role: The shared LSTM learns temporal sensor features after each complete molding cycle; four MLP heads map them to measured part quality attributes. This is a manufacturing measurement-prediction result, not a newly discovered material property.

source_review.scope: Original complete publisher Methods/Results text independently read, including 132-cycle campaign, 124-cycle regression, selected 24-cycle comparison and fold-based epoch selection. Publication date and affiliations authenticated in original HTML metadata. No raw sensor reanalysis.

title: Machine learning prioritizes blood markers associated with neuralgia and depressive symptoms
summary: LASSO and random forest prioritized four blood-expression markers shared by postherpetic-neuralgia and depression datasets. A separate 240-person clinical study found higher candidate-marker expression in neuralgia with depressive symptoms; serum LTF/sCD40L discrimination had AUC 0.818 within the 120 neuralgia patients. Symptoms were defined by PHQ-9 rather than a formal psychiatric interview. These are candidate associations, not a causal pain–depression mechanism or validated clinical diagnosis. The public-data four-gene model was refitted in its comparison cohort, so it was not fixed-coefficient external validation.
ai_technology: LASSO feature selection; random forest; logistic biomarker modeling
organization: Shanxi Medical University; The People’s Hospital of Chongzuo; Sun Yat-sen University; Foshan Women and Children Hospital; Southern Medical University; South China University of Technology

evidence.tested: Learned selection of LTF, HLA-DPA1, CACNA2D4 and CD40LG was followed by new human blood expression/protein assays in four clinical groups of 60 each. Within PHN-only participants (n=120), the combined serum marker score had AUC 0.818 for PHQ-9-defined symptoms.
evidence.unknown: Cross-sectional biomarkers and symptom thresholds do not prove causality, formal MDD diagnosis, prospective screening benefit or treatment effects. The discovery transcriptomic cohorts are small and initial screening exploratory. Public-data comparison coefficients were re-estimated.
evidence.ai_role: LASSO and random forest prioritize the transcriptomic candidates subsequently measured as human clinical biomarkers. Learned selection is distinct from WGCNA/network enrichment and from the later descriptive clinical associations.

source_review.scope: Primary source-provenanced article text independently read for transcriptomic model selection, coefficient-refit limitation, human clinical cohort/assays/results, limitations, affiliations and date. The represented claim concerns human biomarker associations; no animal intervention efficacy is claimed. No underlying-data reanalysis.

title: Machine-learning feature selection prioritizes two coronary-disease-associated genes
summary: XGBoost, SVM recursive feature elimination and Boruta narrowed transcriptomic candidates to DYRK2 and SIGIRR, whose expression was lower in coronary heart disease. The study analyzed 141 discovery samples and 24 samples in a second public dataset, then confirmed lower expression in newly collected clinical samples from 5 patients and 5 controls. Both public datasets informed final gene selection, so the second dataset was not an untouched diagnostic test. Single-cell associations were exploratory; the work establishes neither causal gene roles nor clinical diagnostic utility.
ai_technology: XGBoost, support-vector-machine recursive feature elimination, and Boruta feature selection applied to transcriptomic data
organization: The 941th Hospital of Joint Logistic Support Force of Chinese People’s Liberation Army

evidence.tested: XGBoost/SVM-RFE with fivefold tuning and Boruta selected features from141 PBMC samples (93 CHD/48 controls). Final DYRK2/SIGIRR selection additionally used expression/AUC criteria in24 public samples (13/11). New clinical qPCR samples (5/5) showed lower expression of both genes.
evidence.unknown: The second public dataset informed feature selection and is not an untouched final diagnostic evaluation. Ten qPCR samples support expression patterns only. Causal mechanisms, independent replication and clinical utility remain unestablished; single-cell data included only2 CHD and2 control donors.
evidence.ai_role: The intersection of XGBoost, SVM-RFE and Boruta selected17 common features from231 candidates; additional cross-dataset criteria narrowed these to DYRK2 and SIGIRR, followed by new expression measurements.

source_review.scope: Full primary v1 PDF: data acquisition, machine-learning feature selection, cross-dataset filtering, RT-qPCR Methods and Results3.2/3.8; official bioRxiv first-posted metadata. Model, gene-expression and clinical-utility claims distinguished.

title: Inverse optimal control infers shared and patient-specific squat objectives after knee replacement
summary: Bi-level inverse optimal control inferred individual and shared movement-objective weights from recorded squats in six people after total knee replacement. Center-of-mass height and balance were dominant fitted terms, while balance weights varied across subjects; these are model-dependent inferences rather than direct measurements of neural control. The June 15, 2026 preprint reported within-sample trajectory reconstructions. A November 22 revision added leave-one-subject-out testing within the same six-person dataset, reporting mean RMSE 7.36° and correlation 0.95. Neither version establishes prediction from preoperative data, external-cohort generalization or improved clinical outcomes.
ai_technology: Bi-level inverse optimal control learning latent movement-objective weights from observed trajectories; OpenSim Moco forward model with PRIMA outer optimization
organization: University of Liège

evidence.tested: Version 1 fitted individual and pooled objective weights to existing CAMS-Knee squat recordings from six participants, collected 64–87 months after surgery, and compared reconstructed hip, knee and ankle trajectories with those recordings. Its fitted center-of-mass-height and balance terms were dominant in most cases; balance weights ranged from 0.0950 to 0.4158. The version-2 abstract and author update note report leave-one-subject-out fitting on five subjects and testing on the sixth, repeated across the same cohort, with mean RMSE 7.36°, normalized RMSE 17.75% and Pearson correlation 0.95.
evidence.unknown: The inferred objective weights depend on the chosen cost terms, mechanical model, local optimization and simplified actuation; they do not directly measure human motor-control objectives. No independent external cohort, prospective prediction from preoperative inputs, improved patient outcome or independent replication is established. Uniform ligament parameters and imperfect movement-timing reproduction remain limitations.
evidence.ai_role: Inverse optimal control learns the weights of hypothesized movement objectives from observed human trajectories, enabling patient-specific and shared objective inference and reconstruction of squat kinematics. The fixed mechanical simulator and PRIMA optimization routine alone are not the enabling learned result.

source_review.scope: Independently read the complete primary version-1 article sections on inverse weight estimation, cohort, recovered weights, trajectory validation and limitations, plus version-2 primary abstract and author Summary of Updates. Version-2 full article body was not inspected. Version-specific text distinguishes the original within-sample result from later same-cohort cross-validation; the API repeats updated abstract content under earlier metadata.

title: A Bayesian nonparametric model identifies short-lived frequency-selective states in motor-cortex MEG
summary: A Bayesian nonparametric mixture model inferred brief frequency-selective activity states in a public resting-state MEG dataset from one left motor-cortex parcel. The first preprint version, posted December 23, 2025, reported two aperiodic and five oscillatory states with marked variation in occupancy, frequency and power across people. Its Methods and Results disagree on whether the cohort contained 64 or 65 participants. A June 2026 revision retained the broad state decomposition but changed numerical frequency estimates; the November 2026 abstract retains the broad finding. These are model-inferred signal patterns, without independent neural-state ground truth, external replication or demonstrated behavioral/clinical meaning.
ai_technology: Bayesian nonparametric Dirichlet-process Gaussian mixture model with time-delay embedding and stochastic variational inference
organization: Ruhr University Bochum

evidence.tested: A DP-GMM fitted to time-delay-embedded observations was evaluated against thresholding and a time-delay HMM on synthetic signals with known labels, then applied to one left motor-cortex parcel in public resting MEG. Version 1 reported two aperiodic and five oscillatory states, peaks near 9.5/11.5/19.5/22.0/26.5 Hz and median mean lifetimes 0.202–0.263 s; these are historical v1 estimates. Version 3 retained the state-count pattern but revised frequency assignments. V1 Methods says 64 participants while its concatenation account and Results say 65.
evidence.unknown: The empirical state labels are inferred by the model and depend on embedding choices, activity selection and post-processing; there is no independent neural-state ground truth or external replication. The original 64/65 cohort discrepancy and later revised state-frequency estimates limit numerical interpretation. No causal link to cognition, disease or clinical outcomes is established.
evidence.ai_role: The DP-GMM clusters time-delay-embedded signal vectors and prunes inactive states, enabling unsupervised group-level decomposition of the MEG data. PSD candidate peaks guided embedding setup and k-NN post-processing was used.

source_review.scope: Independently read primary version-1 Methods for mixture learning, inference/post-processing and empirical cohort, plus Results 3.4/figures 6–7 and posting footer. Checked version-3 cohort and revised empirical state-frequency text and version-4 primary abstract/posting date. Primary version metadata confirms the first result-bearing date; later numerics are not retroactively attributed to version 1. Version-4 full body was not exposed in the retrieved page.

title: Transformer-assisted bibliometric analysis maps changes in Italian computer science
summary: A study combined learned co-authorship and text representations with topic clustering to analyze a roster of 1,229 Italian computer-science scholars and publication records from 1980–2025. It identified three model-derived periods spanning foundational work, computer vision/machine learning, and later applied AI/health informatics. An ancillary Genoa pilot introduced 15 recommended researcher pairs, with four joint projects reported within six months. The topic patterns depend on metadata and analytical thresholds, 44.2% of paper abstracts were missing, and the small uncontrolled pilot does not establish a causal collaboration benefit.
ai_technology: Node2vec, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence transformer, BERTopic/HDBSCAN, Falcon and Gemini topic-label generation
organization: Utrecht University; University of Genoa

evidence.tested: The framework models 1,229 Italian CS scholars. Forecast backtesting trained on 2010–2020 and tested on 2021–2023 for 130 authors and 6,084 forecasts (reported SES MAE 7.75 vs. moving-average 8.08). In the University of Genoa pilot, 15 system-flagged researcher pairs were introduced at a showcase; the authors report four started joint projects within six months.
evidence.unknown: Generalization beyond this national disciplinary population, metadata/disambiguation bias and model-dependent topic labels remain limitations. The15-pair pilot lacks a controlled comparator; a locked model and pre-specified prospective evaluation protocol are not established.
evidence.ai_role: Graph and transformer representations are combined to identify semantic similarity and temporal topics; this enables the reported field-evolution patterns and candidate collaboration recommendations, with LLMs used to label discovered topics.

source_review.scope: Original PLOS full text: source population/metadata gaps, learned embeddings/topic modeling, longitudinal patterns, backtesting, ancillary collaboration pilot, affiliations and date.

title: A retrospective prostate-cancer messaging study finds different strengths in GPT-4 and clinician replies
summary: A retrospective study compared clinical-team replies with a GPT-4-based bot for 158 prostate-cancer patient inquiries. Clinicians rated team replies higher on completeness, correctness and clarity, while bot replies scored higher on empathy and more often required major editing. Four LLM graders favored bot replies and showed lower inter-grader agreement than clinician graders. The reviewed publisher abstract describes an evolving rubric and response-quality evaluation, without establishing patient outcomes, prospective workflow utility or clinical safety effects; full Methods were inaccessible.
ai_technology: GPT-4-based patient-message drafting bot and LLM-based graders
organization: Mayo Clinic; Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Cornell University

evidence.tested: Retrospective comparative assessment of replies to 158 prostate-cancer patient inquiries, using three human evaluation rounds and one LLM-grader round. Clinicians rated team replies higher in completeness, correctness and clarity; the bot higher in empathy; bot replies required major edits more often. LLM graders favored bot replies and showed low agreement (alpha 0.07–0.18) versus clinician graders (0.53–0.81).
evidence.unknown: The article abstract does not establish that patients received the generated replies, any effect on patient outcomes, or prospective clinical utility. Full Methods were not accessible from the Nature article route during this check; the rubric changed across the clinician rounds.
evidence.ai_role: A GPT-4-based bot drafts responses in a specific oncology workflow and LLM graders evaluate the same response set; the study measures concrete strengths and limitations of this AI-assisted communication task.

source_review.scope: Publisher original abstract, publication/acceptance metadata and author affiliations; detailed full Methods not accessible.

title: Imbalance-aware modelling identifies severe-crash patterns in Selangor records
summary: A study used Random Forest, XGBoost and SVM to analyze 6,978 fatal or serious crash reports from Selangor, Malaysia, covering 2012–2020,with one stratified 70:30 split and training-only class balancing. The selected class-weighted Random Forest had 81.66% accuracy but only 20.53% recall and 30.10% precision for serious crashes. Tree-model feature importance emphasized collision type, while other rankings varied by model; low-capacity motorcycle involvement was described separately through record frequencies. The dataset excludes minor-injury crashes and lacks exposure denominators, so these associations do not establish causality, population risk or transfer beyond one state and split.
ai_technology: Random Forest, XGBoost and SVM with undersampling, SMOTE or class weighting
organization: Sunway University; Universiti Sains Malaysia

evidence.tested: Dataset of 6,978 fatal/serious crashes (2012–2020), with 70:30 stratified train/test split and resampling/weights applied only to training data. The selected RF with class weights achieved 81.66% overall accuracy, serious-crash recall 20.53% and precision 30.10%. Feature importance ranks collision type highly for RF/XGBoost; road surface type tops SVM permutation importance. Low-capacity motorcycles are the largest vehicle share among the analyzed fatal/serious crash records, particularly loss-of-control on bitumen.
evidence.unknown: The analysis excludes slight-injury crashes, covers only Selangor, uses one train/test split, and has no vehicle-registration or vehicle-kilometre exposure denominators. The motorcycle frequency is descriptive and not evidence of increased per-vehicle risk; feature importance is not causal.
evidence.ai_role: Supervised classifiers with class-balancing methods improve recognition of the underrepresented serious-crash class and support model-based feature/risk-profile analysis of the 2012–2020 crash dataset.

source_review.scope: Original publisher reference PDF: cohort/severity definitions, stratified split and training-only balancing, class-specific performance, feature analysis and exposure/single-split limitations.

title: Machine learning reveals distinct neural control of morning and evening body-temperature rhythms in Drosophila
summary: The February 2026 THERM-D preprint used learned fly localization in camera images to track temperature-preference rhythms over several days. Body temperature was inferred from flies’ positions on a temperature gradient, rather than directly measured by thermal imaging, and targeted genetic perturbations implicated CRYPTOCHROME-negative clock neurons in the morning temperature rise without the same evening effect. Author-maintained software documents a trained YOLOv8 object detector supporting fly localization. These are Drosophila findings, not an established human mechanism; the later November 2026 journal version is distinct from the preprint summarized here.
ai_technology: YOLOv8 object-detection model in the THERM-D computer-vision workflow
organization: University of California, Davis; University of Würzburg; Okayama University

evidence.tested: Continuous computer-vision BTR measurement with genetic clock disruption and targeted Gal4 neuronal manipulations in Drosophila; control comparisons tested separate morning/evening circuits.
evidence.unknown: Generalization beyond Drosophila and human relevance are unestablished. Preferred ambient position is a body-temperature proxy for these small ectotherms; the exact frozen preprint software/model snapshot was not identified.
evidence.ai_role: The preprint uses learned camera-image localization to derive fly positions and temperature-preference time courses. The version-linked author software release identifies a trained YOLOv8 detector and ONNX bounding-box inference; exact frozen weights used for the February preprint were not established.

source_review.scope: Original February2026 preprint XML: assay, fly-position/temperature proxy, neuronal perturbation results, affiliations and dates; bioRxiv API v1 history; author v0.1.0 README and ONNX detection code. Final journal metadata used only for version distinction.

title: Learned wing sensing supports damage detection and lift recovery in a flapping robot
summary: A prototype flapping-wing robot used integrated wing sensors with a learned Kriging surrogate to reconstruct wing motion and a linear SVM to classify damaged states. The SVM achieved 94.6% accuracy on 168 held-out samples, and a separate damaged-wing bench demonstration increased flapping frequency within 0.1 seconds to restore average lift near the intact baseline. These are device-specific physical sensing and control results, with calibration and comparison against binocular-vision measurements. They do not establish autonomous free-flight performance, generalization across robot designs or sustained field operation.
ai_technology: Physics-informed Kriging surrogate model and linear support vector machine (SVM)
organization: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; City University of Hong Kong; The University of Tokyo

evidence.tested: The Kriging model was calibrated using two signal cycles and evaluated on other cycles at each frequency against binocular-vision measurements; reported mean unit-pitching-angle error was below 10% and maximum flapping-angle error 1.1%. For fault diagnosis, 504 samples trained a linear SVM and 168 test samples yielded 94.6% accuracy across normal and three failure states. The authors also report a damaged-wing feedback demonstration with frequency rising from 12.9 to 19.3 Hz in 0.1 seconds and average lift restored near the intact baseline.
evidence.unknown: Generalization to other wing structures, sensor builds, operating conditions, and untethered flight; evidence for field deployment or sustained operational use.
evidence.ai_role: The physics-informed Kriging surrogate maps measured voltage/current amplitudes and flapping frequency to wing-motion angles; a linear SVM classifies faults from the derived signal features. These learned operations support the experimentally demonstrated intrinsic motion sensing, fault classification and lift-compensation control.

source_review.scope: Original final-journal PMC/EuropePMC XML: learned Kriging/SVM operation, image-referenced wing-motion checks, train/test sample counts, damage-feedback lift results, device-calibration limitations, affiliations and date.

title: AlphaFold3 modeling supports a functional COG4–Syntaxin 5 interface
summary: A preprint abstract reports that AlphaFold3 modeling placed COG4 against a Syntaxin5 loop/linker region, supporting a proposed interface in Golgi membrane trafficking. Targeted substitutions, co-precipitation and cell-based rescue assays linked that interface to protein glycosylation and Golgi organization. This is an abstract-scoped source check: full Methods, sample sizes and detailed controls were inaccessible, and no organism-level or clinical effect is established.
ai_technology: AlphaFold 3
organization: University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences

evidence.tested: The primary abstract reports targeted interface substitutions, co-precipitation, rescue, glycosylation, localization and Golgi-morphology assays in cells.
evidence.unknown: Full Methods, sample sizes and detailed experimental controls were not assessed because primary full-text routes were inaccessible. The reviewed material does not establish organism-level or clinical effects.
evidence.ai_role: AlphaFold3 predicted a COG4–Syntaxin5 contact arrangement; the reported cell perturbations test the functional interface described by that model.

source_review.scope: Complete publisher-deposited Crossref and bioRxiv v1 abstracts, posted date and author affiliations; full primary PDF/XML access attempts were blocked, so full Methods were not read.

title: XGBoost links focused-attention meditation to frontal EEG coherence patterns
summary: XGBoost and four feature-importance analyses characterized EEG differences between focused-attention meditation and instructed mind-wandering in 26 experienced meditators.
