The authors report 83% classification accuracy and higher-frequency power/coherence patterns, with reduced delta activity among the important features. Evaluation used repeated participant splits with calibration epochs from test participants added to training, so the result does not establish fully uncalibrated transfer. The small, previously collected dataset supports an association rather than a causal mechanism or clinical benefit.
ai_technology: XGBoost with SHAP and permutation feature importance
organization: University of Haifa; University of California, San Diego; University of Wisconsin-Madison

evidence.tested: Previously collected EEG from 26 meditators; 50 repeated 80/20 participant splits, with 21 training and 5 test participants. Calibration epochs from test participants were included in training. Source-reported accuracy 83%, AUROC 0.79, F1 0.74.
evidence.unknown: One small dataset and selected frontal electrodes; no external validation or uncalibrated unseen-participant performance. Feature importance does not establish causal neurophysiology.
evidence.ai_role: XGBoost classifies recorded cognitive states and model-importance analyses identify EEG power/coherence features associated with the state contrast.

source_review.scope: Primary PMC full JATS: abstract, participant/data selection, performance evaluation, test-participant calibration, feature-importance Results and limitations; publication metadata.

title: SVM analysis links liquid ordering at interfaces to slower crystal growth
summary: A support-vector classifier of local atomic environments helped reveal how interface-induced ordering of liquid reduces atomic mobility and slows crystal growth in silicon and copper simulations. The learned structural quantity supported a growth model that predicted temperature-dependent rates beyond the fitted temperature range more effectively than the compared Wilson–Frenkel model. These are atomistic simulation and model-comparison results, with material/interface-specific limits rather than demonstrated industrial-process performance.
ai_technology: Support-vector machine encoding of local atomic environments
organization: Stanford University

evidence.tested: SVM trained on 10,000 balanced atomic-environment examples; applied to 27.5 million held-out simulation data points. Crystal-growth models fitted at higher temperatures were compared against newly computed lower-temperature growth rates in silicon, with silicon/copper interface analyses.
evidence.unknown: Simulation results depend on the atomistic models and interfaces studied; general industrial applicability and independent experimental confirmation of the full learned mechanism were not established in this review.
evidence.ai_role: A trained SVM supplies a local structural softness coordinate that separates liquid/crystallizing environments and enables analysis of interface ordering, atom mobility and growth kinetics.

source_review.scope: Primary publisher full article: abstract, SVM/local-structure Results, classifier training and temperature-extrapolation Methods, model comparisons, publication metadata and affiliations.

title: Neural reconstruction supports rewritable two-dimensional DNA data storage
summary: A molecular storage demonstration encoded image data in synthetic DNA sequence and rewritable metadata in DNA-backbone nicks. GatedConvolution and EdgeConnect neural inpainting helped reconstruct images after sequencing/readout errors, alongside non-neural detection, smoothing and enhancement steps. Experiments reconstructed an image library and erased/re-wrote metadata, demonstrating a bounded physical storage capability. Image inpainting produces approximate visual reconstructions and does not establish lossless recovery of arbitrary data or universal data-erasure guarantees.
ai_technology: GatedConvolution and EdgeConnect neural image inpainting
organization: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign; Dorna Robotics

evidence.tested: Synthetic-DNA storage/readout of images, computational reconstruction using neural inpainting and other processing, and experimental metadata erasure/rewriting. Reconstruction was assessed in the demonstrated image-storage setting.
evidence.unknown: Visual image reconstruction is approximate and setting-dependent. The main article was reviewed; detailed supplementary algorithm protocols and general reliability/privacy guarantees were not assessed.
evidence.ai_role: Existing neural inpainting models replace masked, corrupted image pixels during decoding of experimentally read molecular data; they are components of a broader experimental storage platform.

source_review.scope: Primary publisher main article abstract, storage/reconstruction Results, named neural-inpainting workflow, main Methods, publication date and author affiliations; supplementary algorithms not reviewed.

title: Random forest predicts three-month outcomes after stroke thrombolysis
summary: Random-forest models predicted three-month functional outcome after intravenous thrombolysis in a retrospective 488-patient stroke cohort, with additional evaluation on two cohorts from another center. Day-seven NIHSS was the most important predictor, so this is a post-treatment prognosis result rather than a tool for choosing initial thrombolysis. Reported performance varied across cohorts; the study does not establish improved treatment decisions or patient outcomes.
ai_technology: Random forest with SHAP, LIME and eli5 explanations
organization: Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Hospital; Shanghai Eighth People’s Hospital; Fudan University

evidence.tested: 488 patients split 70/30 for training/testing, with 10-fold cross-validation described; internal test mean F1 0.825 for RF versus 0.653 SVM and 0.777 logistic regression. Additional retrospective cohorts contained 316 conventional and 114 wake-up-stroke patients.
evidence.unknown: No prospective decision-impact test or independent replication. Day-seven predictors are unavailable at treatment selection. Text and tables report inconsistent feature counts (16 versus20) and training sample totals (341 versus342); external metrics are source-reported and do not prove universal superiority.
evidence.ai_role: A trained random forest combines clinical variables to predict three-month modified Rankin outcome; explanation methods identify influential features, especially day-seven NIHSS.

source_review.scope: Cached original Frontiers full main text: publication metadata, cohort definition, Methods, model splitting/tuning, Results including external validation, and limitations; supplements not independently read.

title: Neural and radiomics score fusion estimates lung-nodule invasiveness
summary: A neural image model and radiomics SVM estimated invasive versus non-invasive or minimally invasive adenocarcinoma in surgically confirmed ground-glass lung nodules. Maximum-score fusion reached a reported AUC of 0.90 in a 127-nodule test cohort from a second center, compared with 0.83 for the neural model and 0.87 for radiomics alone. This retrospective, selected surgical cohort supports diagnostic discrimination, without establishing screening performance or clinical benefit; several fusion strategies were compared on the reported test cohort.
ai_technology: Recurrent residual U-Net, transfer-learned CNN, radiomics SVM and maximum-score fusion
organization: Taizhou University; Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center

evidence.tested: 373 pathology-confirmed nodules from323 patients:246 nodules/229 patients for training and validation at Taizhou;127 nodules/94 patients at Fudan for independent testing. Source reports maximum-fusion AUC0.90 (95%CI0.84–0.95) and accuracy80.3%; segmentation pretraining used257 LIDC-IDRI nodules.
evidence.unknown: Retrospective selected stage-I surgical nodules, multiple nodules treated independently, small cohorts and varying scanner parameters. The report compares fusion choices on the same test set, so that performance is not a separately confirmed frozen-choice estimate. No prospective clinical-utility or survival benefit.
evidence.ai_role: A recurrent residual U-Net segments nodules, a transfer-learned CNN predicts invasiveness, and an SVM classifies selected radiomics features; their prediction scores are fused.

source_review.scope: Cached original Frontiers full main text: publication metadata, cohort inclusion, segmentation and classifier Methods, fusion strategies, Results tables2/3 and limitations; supplements not independently read.

title: CNN stages liver fibrosis from non-contrast MRI in rats
summary: A convolutional neural network classified three liver-fibrosis stages from non-contrast T1-weighted MRI in a 99-rat study. The primary abstract reports stage-specific test AUCs of 0.76, 0.88 and 0.79 after an 80/20 split of one selected image per rat. These animal-model results do not establish human diagnosis; full reference-standard procedures and rat grouping for the separate segmentation evaluation were not available in the reviewed primary abstract.
ai_technology: nnU-Net segmentation and convolutional neural network classification
organization: Qingdao University; The Affiliated Hospital of Qingdao University

evidence.tested: 99 male Wistar rats and2628 MRI slices. The abstract describes a70/30 image split for segmentation (test Dice0.8477), and one maximum-diameter image per rat with80/20 stage-stratified image selection for classification. Reported class accuracies0.73/0.89/0.84 and AUCs0.76/0.88/0.79.
evidence.unknown: Primary abstract and indexed publisher excerpts only; no full article/supplement retrieved. Exact histologic reference/rater protocol and segmentation grouping by rat remain unverified; slice-level splitting may inflate segmentation results. Prospective animal acquisition does not establish prospective frozen-model performance or human transfer.
evidence.ai_role: nnU-Net delineates liver regions and a CNN learns MRI features to classify no, early or progressive liver fibrosis in the induced rat model.

source_review.scope: Primary PubMed XML complete abstract, publication history and author affiliations; corroborating publisher-indexed excerpts retained by researcher. Full publisher article unavailable; no full Methods claim.

title: Neural imaging screen detects cardiotoxicity signals in human-derived heart cells
summary: A ResNet50 image model screened human induced-pluripotent-stem-cell-derived cardiomyocytes for compound-associated toxicity signals. Follow-up mitochondrial-respiration assays supported cell-level liabilities for selected screen hits that simple staining measurements had missed. A further comparison separated proteasome inhibitors with similar biochemical potency but different neural toxicity scores. These are in vitro safety signals, with the core results already present in the March2021 preprint; they do not establish human cardiac risk or clinical safety.
ai_technology: ResNet50 convolutional neural network on the PhenoLearn platform
organization: Tenaya Therapeutics; Stanford University; Dana Solutions

evidence.tested: Original preprint and journal Methods describe image-based training/validation and a separate validation plate, screening1280 bioactive compounds plus1280 diverse compounds. Selected hits underwent secondary mitochondrial-respiration assays; proteasome activity was measured for a ten-inhibitor comparison. The cell experiments support the bounded measured result, beyond recovery of known liabilities alone.
evidence.unknown: Cell-line/model-specific in vitro results; technical replicates and model-development validation are not independent clinical replication. Unknown-target-library hits remain phenotypic signals. Human exposure, arrhythmia risk and therapeutic safety were not established; no novel chemical toxicity mechanism is claimed.
evidence.ai_role: A ResNet50 learns staining-image patterns from control and known-toxic conditions, produces a phenotypic toxicity score for screening compounds, and prioritizes hits for orthogonal cell assays.

source_review.scope: Original bioRxiv v1 full JATS Methods/Results, primary history API; corresponding eLife PMC full JATS model Methods, selected-hit orthogonal validation and proteasome comparison. First public core result dated2021-03-24; journal publication2021-08-02. No priority beyond located versions claimed.

title: Hospital audit study identifies limits of learned access explanations
summary: A hospital-field evaluation examined a machine-learning-based Explanation-Based Auditing System using staff access logs and scenario checks. The tool explained an average98.09% of accesses as appropriate; this measures explanation coverage, rather than breach-detection accuracy. Analysis linked many unexplained accesses to missing staff metadata and exceptional workflows, identifying limits that remained despite high overall coverage. This single-hospital evaluation does not establish fewer privacy breaches or generalizable detection performance.
ai_technology: Supervised learning in an Explanation-Based Auditing System (EBAS)
organization: University of Toronto; Mackenzie Richmond Hill Hospital

evidence.tested: Original paper abstract plus the author’s thesis chapter4, explicitly identified as the same2020 article, document a2017–2018 hospital study.13 clinical/non-clinical staff were selected for review, with additional constructed appropriate/inappropriate scenarios and longitudinal audit-output analysis. A seven-day analysis linked most unexplained accesses to absent role/department metadata.
evidence.unknown: Article full text was not retrieved; detailed Methods were checked in the author’s later thesis, not silently treated as the publisher version. Tool internals were black-box and the source does not expose a reproducible trained-model architecture. Coverage is not sensitivity, specificity or accuracy against comprehensive breach ground truth. One hospital and partly constructed scenarios; no measured breach reduction.
evidence.ai_role: The thesis identifies EBAS as a supervised-learning tool that combines electronic records and staff/scheduling data to generate learned access explanations; the study evaluates its outputs and operational failure patterns rather than training a new algorithm.

source_review.scope: Primary PubMed complete abstract and electronic publication date; author-deposited2022 doctoral thesis chapter4 original Methods and Results, including explicit relationship to the2020 article, EBAS identity, staff/scenario validation and unexplained-access analysis. Publisher full article remains unavailable.

title: Random-forest digital pathology quantifies P2RY12 differences in lung carcinoma subtypes
summary: The November22 v2 of a preprint first posted June17 describes a QuPath random forest trained on manually annotated tumor, stromal and immune cells for tumor-specific P2RY12 quantification. In a cohort containing319 lung adenocarcinomas and157 squamous-cell carcinomas, P2RY12 was higher in squamous carcinomas and discriminated subtype (AUC0.916); digital measurements were concordant with microscopic scoring. Classifier training used project-wide annotations and ROC validation was internal; the reviewed v2 does not establish a significant overall-survival association, independent-cohort validity or treatment benefit.
ai_technology: QuPath random-forest tissue-classification model
organization: University of Lübeck

evidence.tested: Random-forest tissue classification supported tumor-cell staining quantification. Manual scoring and digital measurements were compared; subtype ROC/cutoff assessment used internal bootstrap and repeated cross-validation, with no independent cohort.
evidence.unknown: Classifier training used annotations from the project, while bootstrap/cross-validation assessed the biomarker cutoff internally; no independent cohort is established. The reviewed v2 reports nonsignificant survival association. The cached v1/v2 API abstracts both state nonsignificance, so no claim is made that v1 significance was reversed.
evidence.ai_role: A trained QuPath random forest categorized cells as tumor, stroma or immune, allowing automated quantification of tumor-cell P2RY12 staining across tissue microarrays.

source_review.scope: Primary bioRxiv latest v2 PDF: abstract; QuPath random-forest tissue-classification Methods; retrospective cohort, ROC/statistical Methods and survival Results. Primary API v1/v2 version metadata/abstracts were compared; v1 full Methods not reviewed.

title: Spatial models map malignant territories and immune exclusion in salivary gland cancer
summary: A preprint used scVI and cell2location models to integrate single-cell references with Visium HD measurements from four salivary-gland adenoid cystic carcinoma sections from three patients. The spatial analysis inferred ordered malignant-cell states, millimeter-scale tumor territories, enrichment of immune signatures in stroma, and B7-H4 transcript enrichment in tumor nests. Cell-type abundances and lineage ordering are model-based inferences; the small descriptive cohort requires larger-cohort, protein-level and clinical validation, and does not establish a treatment effect.
ai_technology: scVI variational-inference model; cell2location hierarchical Bayesian spatial deconvolution
organization: University of New Mexico; Centrillion Biosciences

evidence.tested: scVI/cell2location-derived spatial mapping was checked against histologic annotations and marker patterns; permutation-based territory analysis tested spatial organization against random mixing.
evidence.unknown: Only four sections from three patients were studied, and spatial bins are not independent patient replications. Model-inferred cell abundances/trajectories do not establish causal lineage transitions; larger-cohort, protein-level and clinical confirmation remain needed under the source conclusions.
evidence.ai_role: Learned scVI batch correction and cell2location probabilistic deconvolution mapped cell types to 10-µm spatial bins, enabling spatially resolved lineage and immune analyses.

source_review.scope: Primary bioRxiv v1 PDF: abstract; scVI latent-model training and cell2location reference/spatial-abundance Methods; selected territory, histologic/marker and immune-signature Results; limitations and affiliations. Supplementary analyses not independently reproduced.

title: Single-nucleus proteomics identifies regulators of protein transport
summary: A preprint first posted June18,2024 linked protein-abundance variation across3,412 macrophage-like-cell nuclei to LPS-induced nucleocytoplasmic transport, then tested16 candidate regulators by knockdown;13 conditions changed transport in the expected direction. DIA-NN v1.8.1 neural-network processing identified and quantified proteins from mass-spectrometry data, while weighted PCA and statistical associations drove downstream candidate nomination. The November22,2026 v2 retains this measurement role and13-of-16 result. AI supported proteomic measurement rather than directly predicting regulators; the findings concern a cell-model study, not a demonstrated clinical intervention.
ai_technology: DIA-NN v1.8.1 neural-network-based data-independent acquisition proteomics processing
organization: Northeastern University; Parallel Squared Technology Institute

evidence.tested: DIA-NN processed mass-spectrometry measurements; 13/16 targeted knockdown conditions changed transport in the predicted direction.
evidence.unknown: The incremental contribution of DIA-NN versus another processing pipeline was not assessed here. Only13 of16 perturbation conditions changed transport in the expected direction; this is not confirmation of every candidate or evidence of clinical benefit.
evidence.ai_role: Neural-network-based DIA-NN searches used in-silico-predicted spectral libraries to identify and quantify proteins, enabling high-depth proteomic measurement used for regulator prioritization.

source_review.scope: Primary latest bioRxiv v2 PDF: DIA-NN raw-search Methods and knockdown Results; v1 PMC primary XML abstract/computational Methods/Results; primary DIA-NN method-paper XML for neural signal/noise processing; primary API version history. Versions retain3,412 nuclei and13/16 directional effects.

title: AI-guided spatial genomics maps variant-intolerance regions in the cardiac sarcomere
summary: A preprint first posted October7,2025 combined AlphaFold-family structures, AlphaMissense scores and observed clinical/population variants to map disease-associated regions in six cardiac sarcomeric genes. The reviewed November22,2026 v3 explains that selected high- and low-scoring predicted substitutions enlarged the variant analysis by50%, revealing nine additional candidate regions, including signals absent from observed-data-only analyses. These additions are predicted variant labels, not additional patients; the population databases overlap and the HCM registry subset differs from the full cardiomyopathy registry. ClinVar and clinical-onset checks were retrospective, and prediction-dependent regions require further validation rather than establishing causal mechanisms or prospective clinical prediction.
ai_technology: AlphaFold2/3; ColabFold; AlphaMissense pathogenicity predictor
organization: Stanford University; ETH Zurich

evidence.tested: Retrospective spatial scans used SHaRe data (over17,000 cardiomyopathy patients, including12,326 HCM and4,427 six-gene variant carriers), overlapping population databases, predicted structures and selected AlphaMissense substitutions. ClinVar annotations and clinical-onset associations supplied retrospective cross-checks.
evidence.unknown: The nine additional signals depend on selected in-silico substitutions and require further validation. gnomAD and UK Biobank overlap, so their cohort sizes are not summed as unique people. Predicted labels do not establish HCM-specific causality/severity, and ClinVar/cohort checks are not prospective clinical validation or independent research replication.
evidence.ai_role: AlphaFold-family structure prediction and AlphaMissense pathogenicity scoring provided model outputs used to expand variant cohorts and locate 3D regions of disease-associated enrichment.

source_review.scope: Primary latest bioRxiv v3 PDF: model/AlphaMissense selection and variant-augmentation Methods; population-overlap/cohort descriptions; selected spatial/clinical Results and candidate-region limitations. Compared with v1 PDF sections and primary API version history; v2 body was not independently read.

title: Machine learning selects CeCoBi and CeIrBi for thermoelectric calculations
summary: An ICGM-led study used learned SISSO descriptors and other machine-learning models to screen half-Heusler compositions, selecting CeCoBi and CeIrBi for first-principles follow-up. The October 9, 2026 arXiv v2 reports calculated intrinsic power factors of 5.26 and 8.39 mW m−1 K−2 at 673 K under a constant relaxation-time assumption. These calculations support electronic transport potential, not measured performance, complete stability or the predicted thermoelectric figure of merit: lattice thermal conductivity, phase/mechanical/dynamical stability and synthesis remain for later work. A February 1 preprint already described the screening workflow; the journal accepted the work on November 20.
ai_technology: SISSO symbolic regression; random forest; XGBoost; neural networks; Bayesian hyperparameter optimization
organization: Institute Charles Gerhardt Montpellier, University of Montpellier; CNRS; ENSCM

evidence.tested: Within-study DFT electronic-structure and transport calculations for two SISSO-selected compositions; power factors assume relaxation time10−14s. CeCoBi is calculated narrow-gap and CeIrBi semimetallic.
evidence.unknown: The authors explicitly defer full phase, mechanical and dynamical stability and lattice thermal conductivity calculations. No synthesized materials, measured power factors or complete DFT zT validation are established.
evidence.ai_role: SISSO predicts high zT for CeCoBi and CeIrBi from learned descriptor–property relations; these selections motivate their explicit DFT follow-up.

source_review.scope: arXiv v2 primary full HTML Methods context, Results3.4.1–3.4.6 and Conclusion; v1 cached abstract/introduction; APS accepted-paper abstract and date metadata

title: Transcriptomic classifier shows limited cross-dataset Long COVID discrimination
summary: A bioRxiv preprint from the Institute of Bioinformatics and collaborators analyzes six RNA-sequencing datasets from Long COVID and recovered patients. Its primary abstract reports mean AUC0.664 for an RBF support-vector classifier across six leave-one-batch-out folds. Gene hypotheses were derived from three selected higher-performing folds and then used for pathway and interaction analyses; these do not establish causal mechanisms, effective drugs or clinical utility. This review covers the primary abstract and metadata; full-text HTML and PDF access were blocked.
ai_technology: RBF-kernel support vector classifier; SHAP
organization: Institute of Bioinformatics, Bangalore; Indian Council of Medical Research; University of Delhi

evidence.tested: Retrospective leave-one-batch-out discrimination across six transcriptomic datasets, mean AUC0.664; SHAP-derived features from three selected folds support hypothesis generation.
evidence.unknown: Full methods, patient counts, leakage controls and batch-specific performance were not assessed because full-text routes were inaccessible. Experimental mechanisms, drug benefit and clinical utility are not established.
evidence.ai_role: The learned RBF support-vector classifier distinguishes Long COVID from recovered-patient transcriptomic profiles across held-out batches; SHAP nominates features for further analyses.

source_review.scope: Primary bioRxiv v1 abstract, author affiliations and posted date; full HTML/PDF routes returned403 and were not reviewed

title: Machine-learning regression assists dual-mode ochratoxin A sensing
summary: A study led by COMSATS University reports a cerium–cobalt metal-organic-framework sensor for ochratoxin A, combining fluorescence and electrochemical measurements with machine-learning regression of fluorescence data for quantitative analysis. The publisher abstract reports real-sample recoveries of101.31–102.05% for fluorescence and103.05–105.50% for electrochemistry, checked against HPLC. This is a bounded experimental analytical result; the reviewed abstract does not name the regression algorithms or establish broad field deployment. Full subscription methods were not assessed in this review.
ai_technology: Supervised machine-learning regression of fluorescence measurements (algorithms not named in reviewed abstract)
organization: COMSATS University Islamabad; University of the Punjab; Islamic University of Madinah; King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals; Chinese Academy of Sciences

evidence.tested: Initial dual-mode sensor experiments and real-sample recovery analysis, with HPLC comparison; the source says regression models analyze fluorescence data quantitatively.
evidence.unknown: Named regression algorithms, training/test partitions and their incremental contribution were not stated in the reviewed abstract; subscription full methods were not assessed. Broad food-matrix generalization and field use are not established.
evidence.ai_role: Learned regression maps fluorescence measurements to quantitative analyte predictions, supporting the reported sensor analysis; generative writing/code assistance acknowledged elsewhere is a separate role.

source_review.scope: Primary publisher abstract, affiliations, publication metadata and visible AI-assistance statement; subscription full methods not assessed

title: Single-cell modeling identifies a BRCA-enriched fallopian secretory-cell state
summary: A University of Cambridge-led preprint uses MetaCell clustering to analyze 168,679 fallopian-tube cells from 34 women, including 15 BRCA1/2 carriers, and identifies secretory-cell states enriched among carriers with high TP53 and histone expression. A trained QuPath image classifier also supports the spatial p53 analysis; matched protein measurements found increased DNA-damage markers in selected samples. These findings support a bounded replication-stress association, without establishing prospective cancer prediction or causal malignant transformation. This represents the August 27, 2026 first preprint; a November 22 revision is the same study.
ai_technology: MetaCell unsupervised graph-based single-cell clustering; QuPath trained cell-type image classifier
organization: University of Cambridge; University College London; Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust; Francis Crick Institute; University of British Columbia

evidence.tested: Single-cell transcriptional analysis of 55 samples from 34 women, including 15 BRCA1/2 carriers, plus within-study p53 immunohistochemistry and matched multiplex protein-marker measurements.
evidence.unknown: The study does not establish prospective cancer-risk prediction, causal transformation or clinical utility. Protein validation uses a subset of slides, and the cohort is modest; all figures and associations are source-reported.
evidence.ai_role: MetaCell estimates homogeneous transcriptional states from noisy single-cell data, helping reveal rare secretory-cell subpopulations. Separately, QuPath uses a classifier trained on annotated epithelial, stromal and red-blood/debris examples to assign cell types for spatial p53 analysis.

source_review.scope: Cached primary bioRxiv v1 full source XML: cell-state results, replication-stress validation, MetaCell and QuPath Methods, affiliations and publication tags; bioRxiv version metadata

title: Peritumoral ultrasound features improve prediction of breast-cancer nodal metastasis
summary: DenseNet-121 neural networks and random-forest radiomics models were evaluated on ultrasound images from 479 women with pathology-confirmed breast cancer. Including tissue around the tumor improved axillary-node metastasis prediction: the combined-region image-only CNN had a reported test AUC of 0.912, compared with 0.748 for the tumor-only CNN. The combined CNN also reached AUC 0.95 in an additional 16-patient cohort described as prospective, but this single-center paper reports inconsistent training/test counts and does not establish clinical benefit or the biological basis of the imaging association.
ai_technology: DenseNet-121 convolutional neural network; random-forest radiomics with Boruta feature selection
organization: Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences; Peking University Shenzhen Hospital; Ultimage Lab; Peng Cheng Laboratory

evidence.tested: A single-center study used 2,395 images from 479 patients and histopathologic nodal labels. The combined image-only CNN reported test AUC 0.912 versus 0.748 for tumor-only images; differences from corresponding radiomics models were not statistically significant. A further 16-patient cohort reported combined-CNN AUC 0.95.
evidence.unknown: The abstract/image-acquisition description gives training/test counts 343/136, whereas the population description/table gives 359/120. Locked-model timing before new outcomes in the additional cohort is not established by the reviewed Methods. The authors call for larger multicenter/different-machine studies and biological investigation; clinical benefit was not tested.
evidence.ai_role: DenseNet-121 learns image features to classify pathology-confirmed nodal metastasis; Boruta-selected radiomic features feed random forests. Comparing input regions identifies the study-specific predictive information gained from peritumoral tissue.

source_review.scope: Original full-text source: abstract, publication metadata, relevant model/feature selection and validation Methods, Results and limitations. Supplementary files not assessed.

title: A learned twelve-gene signature stratifies lung-adenocarcinoma survival in archived cohorts
summary: Cox screening and random-survival-forest selection identified a twelve-gene immune-related score associated with overall survival in 954 lung-adenocarcinoma patients across four archived datasets. A 204-patient discovery cohort was followed by GEO validation cohorts totaling 309 patients and a 441-patient TCGA cohort; high-score groups had worse survival and distinct inferred immune profiles. Validation used a separate median cutoff in each cohort, and these retrospective associations do not demonstrate treatment-response prediction, clinical benefit or causal immune mechanisms.
ai_technology: Random survival forest variable hunting; Cox regression risk scoring
organization: Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University

evidence.tested: GSE31210 supplied 204 discovery patients; GSE41271 and GSE50081 supplied 309 validation patients, and TCGA supplied 441. Cox screening followed by random-survival-forest selection produced twelve genes for a Cox-weighted score. High-score groups had worse survival in both validation groups (reported HR 1.66 in GEO and 1.93 in TCGA); inferred immune profiles were also compared.
evidence.unknown: Each validation cohort used its own median cutoff, so this is not locked-threshold clinical validation. The authors identify the retrospective design and absence of immunotherapy-response data as limitations and call for prospective validation. Immune abundance is inferred and associations do not establish causality. An inconsistent GEO AUC/confidence-interval sentence is not used for performance claims.
evidence.ai_role: A random survival forest selects prognostic immune-related genes after Cox screening; the selected genes define the survival-risk score whose associations and immune profiles are tested in archived clinical datasets.

source_review.scope: Original full-text source: abstract, publication metadata, relevant model/feature selection and validation Methods, Results and limitations. Supplementary files not assessed.

title: Cell-free DNA fragmentomes distinguish lung cancer in two clinical cohorts
summary: A LASSO-regularized classifier using genome-wide cell-free DNA fragmentation distinguished lung cancer in a prospectively collected 365-person clinical cohort, with cross-validated AUC 0.90. A fixed model was evaluated in an independent group of 385 non-cancer individuals and 46 lung-cancer patients, while a separate multimodal model was evaluated only within the original cohort. These results establish a diagnostic proof of concept, not screening benefit: a 2022 commentary questioned extrapolation from mostly symptomatic patients, and the authors agreed that screening-cohort development and validation were still needed.
ai_technology: DELFI fragmentomics; principal-component features and LASSO-regularized logistic regression
organization: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine; Herlev and Gentofte Hospital; Bispebjerg Hospital; Aarhus University Hospital; Herning Regional Hospital; Netherlands Cancer Institute; Delfi Diagnostics; Hvidovre Hospital

evidence.tested: Among 365 analyzed LUCAS participants, model training/evaluation used 158 without prior/baseline/future cancer and 129 with baseline lung cancer. PCA within training folds compressed fragment-size features; LASSO logistic regression included chromosomal-arm measures, with repeated fivefold cross-validation. A final model and cutoffs were applied to 385 non-cancer individuals and 46 predominantly early-stage lung-cancer patients from separate collections. The main-cohort AUC was 0.90 (95% CI 0.86–0.94).
evidence.unknown: Most LUCAS participants were symptomatic and all had suspicious imaging; prospective collection does not establish prospective evaluation of a frozen model. The combined fragment/clinical/CEA model was not evaluated in the external cohort. A 2022 commentary challenged screening extrapolation, and the authors described the work as proof of concept needing screening-population validation; clinical benefit, sensitivity to very small lesions and safety of pre-CT triage were not established.
evidence.ai_role: PCA is fitted within training folds, and LASSO-regularized logistic regression learns a cancer-risk score from fragmentome and chromosomal-arm features. A fixed learned model then predicts cancer status in an independent cohort.

source_review.scope: Original publisher full-text article: abstract, Methods (study populations, model and cross-validation), relevant Results, limitations, author affiliations and publication date. The two 2022 comment/reply texts were also read; supplementary files not assessed.

follow_up_review.scope: Read the full original 2022 Matters Arising commentary and author reply through NCBI PMC BioC; this is a bounded follow-up check, not continuous monitoring.

title: Seasonal climate forecasts support advance prediction of European West Nile outbreaks
summary: An XGBoost model combined seasonal climate forecasts with past human-case and environmental data to estimate annual West Nile outbreak occurrence in Greece and 887 regions across 14 European countries. In held-out European years 2022–2024, it identified 81 of 91 first-recorded outbreaks in regions unaffected during training. This was an out-of-time evaluation of surveillance data, with variable false alarms and a marked decline in Greek municipal performance in 2025; it does not establish improved public-health outcomes.
ai_technology: XGBoost gradient-boosted classification; SHAP, SAGE and ALE interpretation
organization: University of Patras

evidence.tested: Models trained on 2010–2021 were tested on later years (Greece 2022–2025; Europe 2022–2024). Rolling-origin development used earlier years only for preprocessing, feature selection and threshold setting. The European model identified 81/91 first-recorded regional outbreaks; Greek municipal AUCs were 0.94, 0.96, 0.92 and 0.74 across the four test years.
evidence.unknown: Out-of-time evaluation is not evidence that a frozen model was deployed prospectively. Forecast skill and false alarms varied by region/year; Greece deteriorated in 2025. Reporting/surveillance intensity differed across countries, and entomological or near-real-time data were unavailable. Mechanistic causation and public-health benefit were not tested.
evidence.ai_role: XGBoost learns an annual region-level outbreak classifier from pre-season climate forecasts and historical/environmental predictors. SHAP, SAGE and ALE describe learned predictive contributions rather than causal drivers.

source_review.scope: Original full-text source: abstract, publication metadata, relevant model/feature selection and validation Methods, Results and limitations. Supplementary files not assessed.

title: Triage models flag opioid misuse in an enriched retrospective emergency cohort
summary: First posted as a July 2025 preprint and journal-published in February 2026, this study reports machine-learning identification of opioid misuse from data available at emergency-department triage. Among 1,123 analyzed encounters, the latest 169 formed a temporal test set; gradient boosting reported AUROC 0.88, AUPRC 0.89 and F1 0.77 against expert chart-review labels. The single-center cohort was deliberately enriched for opioid misuse, and overlapping model confidence intervals and absent prospective or fairness validation limit claims about routine screening or patient benefit.
ai_technology: Random forest; gradient boosting; additional supervised classifiers on triage-time EHR features
organization: University of Illinois Chicago; University of Wisconsin Madison

evidence.tested: The retrospective cohort covered September 2020–March 2023 and was chronologically partitioned 70/15/15 for training, validation and testing. Models used structured triage/history data and expert-adjudicated labels. The latest 169 encounters were held out; gradient boosting achieved AUROC 0.88, AUPRC 0.89 and F1 0.77. Models performed comparably to opioid-related diagnosis codes entered by encounter end; these codes were not a triage-time comparator.
evidence.unknown: Enriched sampling does not estimate routine-population prevalence or predictive values. Most performance confidence intervals overlapped; model superiority was not established. The authors call for prospective multi-site calibration and bias/fairness checks before clinical trials. The demographic-table totals are inconsistent with the repeatedly stated 1,123 analyzed encounters; subgroup claims are not used.
evidence.ai_role: Supervised classifiers learn associations between information available at triage and manually assigned opioid-misuse labels, permitting temporal hold-out assessment of early identification without waiting for encounter-end diagnosis codes.

source_review.scope: Original journal full text: cohort selection, chronological partition, triage feature processing, model Methods, Results, limitations and date/preprint metadata; original medRxiv v1 metadata and abstract compared. Supplements not assessed.

title: Simulated low-field MRI retains pathology-detection signals with reduced small-lesion sensitivity
summary: First posted in July 2021 and journal-published that December, this study used DenseNet-121 classifiers to compare pathology detection in 3T MRI and simulated 64mT-quality images from glioma, stroke and multiple-sclerosis datasets. Patient-separated tests reported similar slice-level AUCs, including 0.97 versus 0.98 for low-grade glioma, while simulated low-field sensitivity declined for smaller lesions. The transformation had limited paired-image and radiologist checks, but omitted field-dependent tissue contrast and device artifacts; these simulations do not establish diagnostic equivalence or clinical performance of an actual low-field scanner.
ai_technology: DenseNet-121 convolutional neural network for pathology detection
organization: University of Pennsylvania

evidence.tested: A non-neural image transformation was fitted using three hydrocephalus patients and checked in three additional patients; three radiologists compared paired real/simulated images from ten MS patients. DenseNet-121 classifiers were trained separately on original/simulated images for low-grade glioma (76 subjects), high-grade glioma (259), stroke (28) and MS (20), using approximately 9:1 patient-separated train/test splits. Reported slice-level AUCs were respectively 0.97/0.98, 0.96/0.95, 0.94/0.94 and 0.90/0.87.
evidence.unknown: The simulation approximates resolution/noise but not all field-strength contrast or device-specific artifacts. Separate disease classifiers perform simple lesion detection, not differential diagnosis or full radiologic assessment. Small test cohorts and degraded detection of small lesions limit generalization; prospective actual-device trials and patient benefit were not established.
evidence.ai_role: DenseNet-121, initialized with ImageNet weights, learns lesion-present versus lesion-absent image classification. Comparing held-out original and simulated datasets probes a specific imaging-performance question; the image transformation itself was conventional rather than learned.

source_review.scope: Original journal full text: transformation and radiologist checks, model architecture, patient-separated training, Results, Discussion limits and publication metadata; original medRxiv v1 metadata/abstract compared. Supplements not assessed.

title: EntireAxon reveals coexisting patterns of axonal degeneration in a cell-culture model
summary: Initially reported in an August 2020 preprint and subsequently journal-published in 2021, EntireAxon combined neural image segmentation and temporal classification to track cortical axons in an in-vitro hemorrhagic-stroke model. The study found that axonal swellings preceded fragmentation and that granular, retraction, swelling and transport patterns could occur together. The finding is limited to unmyelinated axons and hemin exposure; small image-label validation sets, weak fragment segmentation and absent in-vivo confirmation limit generalization.
ai_technology: EntireAxon U-Net/ResNet-50 segmentation ensemble; attention-based recurrent neural network
organization: Fraunhofer Research Institution for Marine Biotechnology and Cell Technology; University of Lübeck; University Hospital Leipzig; Medical Laser Center Lübeck; University of Warwick

evidence.tested: A U-Net/ResNet-50 ensemble learned pixel classes for background, axons, swellings and fragments from 33 labeled images and was compared with human labels on eight validation images. Its segmentation quantified newly recorded degeneration time courses from six independent cortical-neuron cultures per condition. An RNN analyzed temporal class transitions and was checked with ten-fold cross-validation over 162 labeled examples, supporting the finding that four degeneration patterns coexist and swellings precede fragmentation.
evidence.unknown: The CNN fragment-class F1 was only 0.301 and the validation labels shared an annotator with the training labels. RNN folds were not established as independent by culture/biological replicate in the reviewed Methods. The source limits the biology to unmyelinated cultured axons and hemin-induced injury, notes that other hemorrhage products may differ, and does not establish in-vivo mechanisms or clinical benefit.
evidence.ai_role: The CNN segments axon structures in time-lapse images; the RNN learns temporal changes in segmentation-class histograms. These operations provide the measurements and pattern classifications used for the new in-vitro biological finding.

source_review.scope: Original bioRxiv v1 full text: abstract/date/affiliations, CNN architecture and labeling, validation Methods, RNN cross-validation, biological time-course/pattern Results and limitations. Journal primary XML abstract and publication metadata checked for the shared finding; supplements not assessed.

follow_up.note: Journal version retains the core observation of swellings preceding fragmentation and four axonal-degeneration patterns; publication is not independent replication.

title: Polarimetric collagen features classify breast-tumor regions in a limited tissue study
summary: First posted in May 2021 and journal-published in 2022, this study used logistic regression on polarimetric second-harmonic-generation and texture features to distinguish tumor from normal breast-tissue regions. From one microarray originally containing 45 cores from 12 patients, the analysis retained 15 normal and 20 tumor cores; prediction on two held-out cores from that same array reported 91.3% subimage accuracy. Random subimage cross-validation and the small core-level hold-out do not establish patient-independent diagnosis, external validation or clinical benefit.
ai_technology: Logistic-regression classifier on polarimetric second-harmonic-generation and collagen-texture features
organization: University of Toronto; University of Toronto Mississauga; Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, University Health Network; National Centre of Pathology; Vilnius University; Light Conversion

evidence.tested: A binary logistic-regression classifier used 33 image-derived features and 544 normal/543 tumor subimages, evaluated using 1,000 repeated stratified five-fold partitions. Two cores (one normal, one tumor) were set aside before training; subimage prediction in these cores reported accuracy 91.3% and F1 90.7%. The original publisher PDF Fig. 5 and Results report cross-validation accuracy 94.2%; those performance measures are not interpreted as patient-level accuracy.
evidence.unknown: The Methods treat subimages as data points without establishing patient/core-grouped cross-validation. Held-out prediction uses only two cores from the same microarray; external or patient-independent validation was not established. Adipose/no-signal areas and two rare stromal tumor cores were excluded, and subimage size affects predictive performance. Clinical utility, prospective workflow performance and patient benefit were not tested.
evidence.ai_role: Logistic regression learns a normal-versus-tumor classifier from collagen ultrastructure statistics and texture features measured by widefield P-SHG microscopy, linking the learned operation to a specific ex-vivo tissue classification result.

source_review.scope: Original bioRxiv v1 abstract/date/affiliations and original journal publisher PDF: abstract, classification Results, Fig. 5/table, Statistical analysis and machine learning Methods, tissue-microarray Methods and Discussion. PDF Fig. 5 also visually checked. Supplementary files not assessed.

ai_technology: SL-XGBRanker (monotonic-constrained gradient-boosted decision trees)

evidence.ai_role: A learned gradient-boosted model combines mechanistic and pharmacogenomic features to rank drug dependencies, placing ceralasertib second for held-out MBD4.
evidence.tested: Retrospective GDSC2 cell-line drug-response associations and leave-one-DDR-anchor-out evaluation of a learned drug-prioritization model. The TP53-mutant ceralasertib comparison contains 11 MBD4-loss and 619 wild-type cell lines.
evidence.unknown: The reviewed study does not establish causal MBD4-dependent drug sensitivity or clinical benefit; isogenic perturbation/rescue and prospective clinical evaluation remain outstanding. Existing pharmacogenomic measurements enter model features and do not independently validate its predictions.

organization: CrisPRO.org; New York University

source_review.scope: Primary v1 and v2 full-text Methods, pharmacogenomic results, ranker evaluation and limitations; independently retrieved bioRxiv version metadata. Organization field follows the represented v1 affiliations; v2 lists CrisPRO.ai.

summary: A preprint combined the gradient-boosted SL-XGBRanker with retrospective pharmacogenomic analyses to prioritize drug hypotheses for MBD4 loss of function. In existing GDSC2 measurements, TP53-mutant MBD4-loss cell lines were associated with greater ceralasertib sensitivity than wild-type comparators (11 versus 619 lines; reported BH-FDR q=0.036); the ranker placed ceralasertib second when MBD4 was held out during training. The ranking includes pharmacogenomic features from these datasets, so the association is not an independent experimental validation of the model. The small observational cell-line study establishes neither causal synthetic lethality nor clinical benefit; isogenic knockout/rescue experiments remain necessary. The represented findings appear in the November 12 first public version; a November 20 revision changes author affiliations while retaining the central findings.
title: Learned ranking prioritizes ceralasertib for MBD4-deficient cell lines

ai_technology: AIROGS challenge winning deep-learning fundus-image classifier

evidence.ai_role: A learned image classifier supplied glaucoma scores used in external diagnostic evaluation.
evidence.tested: External existing-cohort diagnostic evaluation; not a prospective test of clinical benefit.
evidence.unknown: Clinical benefit and deployment outcomes are unestablished. The reported ROC-derived operating point is cohort-specific; prospective validation remains needed. Direct full-text access was blocked; bounded publisher-indexed Methods and Results were reviewed.

organization: The Rotterdam Eye Hospital; Erasmus Medical Center; Radboud University Medical Center; Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel

source_review.scope: Primary PubMed abstract/date/affiliations and publisher-indexed DL-algorithm-development, Validation dataset, participant ROC-threshold Results and Discussion passages. Direct publisher full-text fetch403; no full-PDF review claimed.

summary: An existing deep-learning fundus-image classifier was evaluated on 19,088 eyes from 9,837 Rotterdam Study participants, including 201 eyes with perimetric glaucoma. Eye-level sensitivity was 70.6% at 95% specificity, with ROC-AUC 0.911. Among 61 true positives with earlier images,33 were flagged before diagnosis. This retrospective evaluation of a prospectively collected cohort does not establish improved patient outcomes; image quality affected false positives. The reported specificity operating point was derived from this cohort’s ROC analysis, rather than a separately locked clinical cutoff.
title: AIROGS classifier detects glaucoma in retrospective Rotterdam validation

ai_technology: Multilingual neural-network language models (including mBERT, XLM-R and NLLB); ridge-regression brain encoding

evidence.ai_role: Learned multilingual embeddings supply a common feature space for brain-response models and cross-language transfer tests.
evidence.tested: Cross-participant and held-out-language encoding on fMRI data; existing 12-language data and 27 new participants across nine languages. Reviewed v2 uses nested regularization and sequential validation with controls for temporal structure.
evidence.unknown: Fine-grained language differences and causality remain unresolved. Small cohorts and selection by response reliability constrain conclusions. The 2026 journal version was not reviewed in full.

organization: University of Milano-Bicocca; Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Harvard University

source_review.scope: Primary bioRxiv v2 archived full text through Europe PMC: language models, encoding design, participant selection, Results and limitations. Primary v1 metadata/abstract establishes earlier core result date; v2 Methods are not asserted identical to v1. Final 2026 Nature full text inaccessible.

summary: Multilingual neural-language-model embeddings enabled ridge-regression models of fMRI language-network responses that transferred to held-out languages across a 21-language study. The study combined existing data in 12 languages with newly collected data in nine more, supporting a shared representational component related to meaning. Small samples per language, reliability-based filtering and modest predictive correlations limit generalization; the results establish neither identical processing across languages nor a causal universal neural code. The core result was public in the February 2, 2025 preprint; the reviewed November 18, 2025 revision added analyses. A November 23, 2026 journal announcement is later source context, with final journal Methods not reviewed.
title: Multilingual model representations predict shared brain responses across languages

ai_technology: Hierarchical mixture-of-experts classifier (logistic-regression experts)

evidence.ai_role: A tree of trained logistic-regression experts predicts subtype labels from gene expression and transfers mouse taxonomy to human nuclei, enabling the subtype-specific disease comparison.
evidence.tested: Existing mouse/human transcriptomic data; 24,419 mouse reference cells, five-fold cell-stratified validation and a held-out test; human depletion comparison uses eight control and seven Parkinson’s donors with donor-aware mixed models.
evidence.unknown: Causal susceptibility, in-vivo human projections and therapeutic benefit are not established. Cells are not independent donor replicates; cross-species annotation may constrain inferred subtype identity.

organization: Northwestern University; Shirley Ryan AbilityLab; Karolinska Institutet; University of California, San Diego; McGill University

source_review.scope: Primary v1 full-text HMoE training/validation and Human transfer Methods, human population-depletion/MASC Methods, subtype Results and limitations; primary bioRxiv API date independently checked. Numerical drug-target and inferred projection claims not admitted as independent findings.

summary: A hierarchical mixture-of-experts classifier transferred mouse dopaminergic-neuron labels to human single-nucleus datasets, identifying an Anxa1-associated population. The preprint reports this population was more depleted in Parkinson’s disease than comparator subtypes in a postmortem analysis of eight control and seven Parkinson’s donors. The model uses logistic-regression experts trained on a mouse reference; donor-aware abundance models support an association rather than a causal mechanism. Cross-species label transfer, small donor cohorts and retrospective tissue limit generalization; inferred connectivity and candidate drug targets are not direct human tracing or demonstrated therapy.
title: Cross-species classifier identifies a human dopaminergic subtype depleted in Parkinson’s disease
